articles.full_text:
ANI
                
23 Oct 2026, 21:31 GMT+10
            
New Delhi [India], October 23 (ANI): Banks have passed on 93 basis points (bps) of lending rate reductions to borrowers against the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) cumulative 125 bps cut in the policy repo rate between February 2025 and March 2026, according to the RBI's October 2026 Bulletin released on Friday.
The Bulletin highlighted that the weighted average lending rate (WALR) on fresh loans declined by 93 bps during the period, reflecting the transmission of monetary policy easing to bank lending rates.
According to the RBI study, the reduction comprised an 80 bps interest rate effect and a 13 bps composition effect, indicating that both changes in lending rates and shifts in the composition of bank credit contributed to the overall decline.
'In response to a cumulative reduction of 125 basis points (bps) in the policy repo rate, the WALR on fresh lending declined by 93 bps, with interest rate effect of 80 bps and composition effect of 13 bps during February 2025 to March 2026,' the Bulletin stated.
The study, titled 'Transmission to Lending Rates of SCBs: Price versus Composition Effects in WALR,' examined how changes in lending rates and credit composition across banks and sectors influence the transmission of monetary policy.
It noted that movements in aggregate lending rates reflect both repricing of loans and changes in credit composition, highlighting the importance of considering both factors while assessing monetary policy transmission.
Meanwhile, the Bulletin's State of the Economy article highlighted that India's economy continued to demonstrate strength, supported by high-frequency indicators across industrial and services sectors.
However, renewed geopolitical tensions in West Asia and supply chain disruptions have intensified global inflationary pressures, prompting major central banks to raise policy rates.
The Bulletin also noted that India's headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation increased in September, driven by broad-based rises in food, fuel and core inflation components.
On the external sector, double-digit growth in merchandise exports during the first six months of FY27 helped narrow the trade deficit, while foreign direct investment (FDI), external commercial borrowings (ECB) and remittance flows strengthened in August.
Separately, the Bulletin highlighted continued double-digit credit growth in the non-banking financial company (NBFC) sector at the end of December 2025, alongside improving asset quality reflected in declining non-performing asset ratios.
The RBI clarified that views expressed in the Bulletin articles belong to their respective authors and do not necessarily represent the central bank's official position. (ANI)

Higher oil prices have strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep rates elevated for longer, raising the cost of holding bullion, which does not pay interest. Investors are watching the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting and next week’s PCE inflation data; markets largely expect no rate change, while the probability of a December hike stands at 80%. At a glance

articles.title: Pound Holds Firm Above 1.3400 On Hot UK Inflation Data - TradingPedia
articles.summary: Pound Holds Firm Above 1.3400 On Hot UK Inflation Data  TradingPedia
articles.full_text:
Key Moments
- GBP/USD traded around 1.3405 in early Asian dealings on Friday, extending modest gains above the 1.3400 level.
- UK CPI accelerated to 3.5% YoY in September, its highest reading in 11 months, reinforcing expectations of a more hawkish Bank of England.
- Markets are pricing a 98% chance of a 25 bps BoE rate increase to 4.0% next month, with another similar move anticipated in December.
GBP/USD Supported by Stronger UK Inflation and BoE Expectations
The GBP/USD pair was modestly firmer near 1.3405 in early Asian trade on Friday, with the Pound edging higher against the Dollar after a hotter UK September Consumer Price Index (CPI) reading boosted expectations for a more aggressive policy stance from the Bank of England (BoE). Investors are also awaiting the UK Retail Sales release later in the session.
Data from the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday showed UK inflation at an 11-month high, driven in large part by higher petrol and diesel prices. Headline CPI rose 3.5% year-on-year in September, up from 3.1% previously and above forecasts of 3.4%. Core CPI inflation also gained momentum, rising to 2.8% year-on-year from 2.6% in August, beating the 2.7% market consensus.
Rate Path: BoE Seen Hiking Twice, Fed Expected to Pause, Then Move
Interest rate markets are almost fully aligned with a BoE rate increase at the next policy meeting on November 5. According to LSEG data, pricing currently reflects a 98% probability that the central bank lifts its key rate by 25 basis points to 4.0% next month. This would represent the BoE’s first rate hike since 2023. Positioning also suggests that traders broadly anticipate another 25 basis point increase at the BoE’s final meeting of the year in December.
On the U.S. side, Federal Reserve (Fed) Chair Kevin Warsh did not provide explicit guidance on the timing of any further rate rises. A Reuters poll indicated that the Fed is widely expected to keep rates unchanged at its upcoming October gathering, with nearly all surveyed economists projecting that the next move will come in December. The survey highlighted that policymakers are signaling patience, even as persistent inflation continues to justify a firmer policy stance.
Sterling Dynamics Versus the Euro: ING Sees Independent GBP Strength
Analysts at ING argue that the Pound’s performance in EUR/GBP reflects more than just domestic political factors. They note that “it seems like sterling is riding on the coat-tails of PM Andy Burnham’s popularity. In reality, it looks like there is both independent sterling strength and independent euro weakness at play in EUR/GBP.”
ING acknowledges that “earlier this summer, we had felt that sterling gains would not last,” but adds that “greater market confidence in a Bank of England tightening cycle – we look for 25bp hikes in February and November – makes sterling a high-carry European currency.”
Looking ahead, the bank expects only limited market reaction to upcoming fiscal news, remarking that “next week’s UK budget looks unlikely to derail the recent EUR/GBP break below 0.8400.” With “the euro still having plenty of room to drop on French politics,” ING sees potential for the cross to remain under pressure, concluding that “EUR/GBP can stay offered in a 0.8360-0,8430 range for the time being.”
Greene’s Comments Reinforce a Hawkish BoE Bias
Greene’s 7.4/10 FXS Speechtracker score is in line with the historic average, pointing to a consistently hawkish, but not intensifying, tone. The focus on stalled wage disinflation at levels seen as incompatible with 2% inflation, alongside the view that policy should move proactively to counter second-round effects, underpins a preference for keeping policy restrictive for longer. This stance limits near-term downside for the Pound.
Greene’s observation that the risk of second-round effects is now viewed as greater than previously, even as forward-looking indicators signal pay growth moving closer to 3.5%, suggests that the labor market is still judged too tight to justify easing. References to stronger-than-expected economic resilience and signs that labor market slack may have already peaked further support a hawkish reading. This combination points to a delayed timeline for eventual rate cuts and implies that the Pound may remain relatively well-supported against both the Euro and the Dollar.
Technical Picture: GBP/USD Maintains Bullish Structure Above 100-Day SMA
From a technical perspective, GBP/USD retains a slightly bullish profile on the daily chart, with spot trading above the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and well above the middle line of the Bollinger Bands. The pair is inching toward the upper Bollinger band, indicating a possible test of near-term resistance, while the 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI) stands at 58.6, comfortably in positive territory and below overbought thresholds. This configuration suggests that there is still scope for further upside before momentum becomes overstretched.
| Technical Level | Indicator | Level | Implication | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Immediate resistance | Upper Bollinger band | 1.3412 | Daily close above may extend the recent recovery | 
| First support | 100-day SMA | 1.3390 | Initial cushion on corrective pullbacks | 
| Secondary support | Bollinger middle band | 1.3275 | Deeper downside support within bullish structure | 
| Major support | Lower Bollinger band | 1.3140 | Key level expected to limit larger corrections | 
On the topside, resistance is initially defined by the upper Bollinger band at 1.3412. A decisive daily close above this area would likely validate further gains and continuation of the current recovery phase. On the downside, the 100-day SMA at 1.3390 provides the first line of support, followed by additional buffers around the Bollinger middle band near 1.3275 and the lower band around 1.3140. These levels are expected to help contain dips while the broader bullish tone remains in place.

articles.title: WTI crude oil hits $100 as Saudi supply fears keep oil markets on edge - Gulf News
articles.summary: WTI crude oil hits $100 as Saudi supply fears keep oil markets on edge  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
Libya pipeline shutdown adds to oil price pressures and supply uncertainty
US crude traded at $100 a barrel on Friday, Oct. 23, while Brent hovered above $113, as traders weighed threats to Saudi Arabian supplies and fresh disruptions in Libya.
As of 1:08 pm Tokyo time, US oil benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) hit $100 a barrel, up 53 cents, or 0.53 percent, as per industry tracker OilPrice.com.
Brent stood at $113.60, up 39 cents, or 0.34 percent, while Murban crude rose $4.20, or 3.81 percent, to $114.40.
Oilprice.com crude forward contract rates are delayed by 10 minutes.
The snapshot followed a volatile morning. Investing.com, reported Brent at $113.96 and WTI at $100.17 at 11:02 am in Tokyo on Friday.
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil is a high-quality crude oil primarily used as a refining feedstock to produce fuels like gasoline and diesel, and as a core pricing benchmark for the US oil market.  
The key concern was escalating fighting involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on Thursday, heightening anxiety over the security of the world’s largest crude exporter. The evacuation itself did not establish that Saudi oil production had been interrupted.
Fighting intensified as the Houthis pushed toward Bab Al-Mandab, the shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Concerns about further energy-supply disruptions helped lift Brent’s Thursday settlement to its highest level since May 4.
Libya added another source of uncertainty. A pipeline valve connecting the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port was shut, reducing production at both fields, the head of the country’s National Oil Corporation told Reuters.
The prolonged energy-price shock is also increasing the cost of shielding consumers from expensive fuel.
Japan is considering scaling back gasoline subsidies as early as December because funding could run short, local media reported Friday, citing two ruling-party officials familiar with the discussions. The emergency program began in March following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Keeping average regular gasoline prices near 170 yen per litre is costing Japan several billion dollars a month and rapidly drawing down a 3.1-trillion-yen supplementary budget approved in June.
A proposal under discussion could allow average pump prices to rise to around 175 yen in December and 180 yen in January. No final decision was reported.
Traders are watching whether the Saudi-Houthi escalation produces actual damage to energy infrastructure or further shipping disruption, and how quickly Libyan output can recover.
Those developments will help determine whether the latest price surge persists or unwinds.
For consumers, Japan’s subsidy debate illustrates the broader stakes: sustained high crude prices can strain both household budgets and the public finances used to cushion fuel costs — even before governments withdraw support,

articles.title: Asian shares wobble as tech rout boosts bonds, dents rate hike bets - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Asian shares wobble as tech rout boosts bonds, dents rate hike bets  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
AI generated
SYDNEY – Asian shares fell on Oct 23 as concerns over the enormous funding needs of artificial intelligence hammered tech and led to the biggest daily rally in US Treasuries in more than three years, with investors fleeing to sovereign bonds and safe-haven currencies.
Markets also sharply pared back expectations of further policy tightening from the US Federal Reserve, stripping out almost a full quarter-point rate hike for 2027 amid concerns a bursting AI bubble could derail the data centre investment boom and hobble the United States economy.
A December rate rise is no longer fully priced, with the implied probability falling to 85%.
That was despite elevated oil prices, with Brent hitting a five-month peak at US$114 a barrel on Oct 23.
Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies as fears grow that the conflict in the Middle East could escalate sharply.
MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan fell 0.3% on Oct 23, bringing its weekly loss to 2.7% and marking a fourth straight week in the red.
Japan’s Nikkei dropped 1.3% and was down a whopping 5% for the week.
South Korea’s KOSPI skidded 1.7%, on course for a 4.3% weekly decline, with memory chipmaker SK Hynix down 2.5% on the day.
Taiwan’s stock market was closed due to a typhoon.
An index of mainland Chinese blue chips lost 1.1% on Oct 23 to hit the lowest level since July 2025.
The index was down about 20% from its peak in late June. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.1% after dropping 3% on Oct 22.
Charlie McElligott, managing director for cross-asset strategy at Nomura Securities International in New York, said in a note that AI is under sustained pressure.
“US Treasury bonds are – gasp – working as your hedge again, as the market seems to be real-time repricing the probabilities of a US growth scare off the back of the AI reset.”
On Wall Street, the Nasdaq slumped more than 2% as Meta shares lost nearly 8% after the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures, and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the technology.
Tesla shares fell 3.1% as the electric carmaker cut its 2026 capital spending plans.
“The question is whether selling accelerates or markets stage another familiar reversal,” said Chris Weston, head of Research at Pepperstone.
“There’s nothing more emotive than a falling market where buyers refuse to engage. Sellers don’t need a fresh catalyst when deteriorating price action itself encourages more selling.”
Treasuries shine
As equities tumbled, money flowed into safe haven US Treasuries, sending yields plunging across the curve overnight.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield slid more than 19 basis points, the biggest drop since March 2023, before steadying at 4.9591% on Oct 23, back below the closely watched 5% level.
That was also due in part to the ongoing sell-off in French bonds, whose benchmark yield climbed 6 basis points overnight to 5.0601%, the highest level since 2002.
“The US 10-year yield gapped back below 5% with some conviction. We’re not convinced it keeps on going,” said Padhraic Garvey, ING’s regional head of research for the Americas.
“We’re minded to expect it to snap back above (5%), as we still have inflation/fiscal deficit/AI boom underpinnings to navigate. And we have the US midterm elections approaching as an excuse for trouble. But it will need some degree of calm in the risk space first.”
The two-year Treasury yield slumped nearly 19 basis points overnight and were last flat at 4.6566%.
Government bonds in Asia also rallied. The yield on 10-year Japanese government bonds fell 9 basis points to 2.790%, while Australia’s 10-year yield dropped 10 basis points to 5.164%.
In currency markets, safe havens such as the yen and Swiss franc gained. The dollar fell 0.2% to 156.44 yen on Oct 23, after slumping 0.9% overnight.
The dollar also slipped 0.1% to 0.8196 Swiss francs, the lowest in a month, after an overnight fall of 0.5%.
Gold failed to catch any safe haven demand though, and was flat at US$4,021.99 an ounce on Oct 23 after a nearly 3% drop overnight. REUTERS

articles.title: Gold drops below $4,000 as ‘haven’ asset joins market sell-off - Financial Times
articles.summary: Gold drops below $4,000 as ‘haven’ asset joins market sell-off  Financial TimesCurrent price of gold as of October 23, 2026  FortunePrecious metals tumble despite falling yields as Hormuz tensions intensify - Kitco PM Report  KitcoGold falls to more than two-month low as oil-fuelled inflation fears weigh  ReutersGold Falls Below $4,000 for the First Time Since July. What’s Next?  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Gold dipped below $4,000 a troy ounce on Friday for the first time since July, capping a tough week for the precious metal, in the latest sign that it was no longer functioning as a haven asset.
Bullion prices fell as low as $3,986.50 on Friday before recovering some ground, having lost 2.8 per cent on Thursday. Prices are down 3.3 per cent ths week.
Gold’s fall, “despite the risk-off backdrop”, is a “notable divergence”, said analysts at Berenberg.
It is often used as a haven investment, while lower bond yields are typically positive for the metal, which does not offer a yield itself.
But while investors rushed into US Treasuries and other perceived havens on Thursday amid concerns over the AI boom, and even though investors have pared back their expectations for US interest rate rises recently, gold has still sold off this week.
Gold’s fall amid the broad risk-off sentiment in markets comes after it was used as a speculative asset by traders last year. This helped push its price to a record high of more than $5,400 a troy ounce in January, before it tumbled by more than a fifth as some of those traders have exited.
The Berenberg analysts said that the last time bullion had been this weak when Treasury yields were posting such a large fall was in December 2008, around the depths of the global financial crisis.
Demand for gold ETFs fell back in the first half of the year before rebounding in the third quarter after strong September sales. Berenberg said that whether the gold price closes above or below $4,000 an ounce on Friday would be significant, as “a confirmed close below $4,000 would likely trigger further ETF outflows and technical selling across the gold equity complex”.
Gold mining stocks have had their worst week in seven months, with BHP and Rio Tinto both falling more than 8 per cent.
In addition to this week’s pattern of trading, gold has generally been hit this year by markets sharply increasing their expectations of interest rate rises by the US Federal Reserve.
Erik Norland, chief economist at derivatives exchange CME Group, said that the largest contributing factor to the decline in precious metals prices this year was the shift in expectations from rate cuts to rate increases.
But he said that it was “astonishing” that prices were still significantly higher than at the beginning of 2025. He attributed this to the combination of budget deficits rattling confidence in bond markets, rising inflation, geopolitics and buying by central banks.
Central bank gold buying in September rose to the highest monthly level since November 2024, according to provisional data from the World Gold Council. The figures were compiled by the trade association using central bank and IMF data.
Several fund managers said last week at the FT’s precious metals summit that they still expected a rebound for gold.
John Reade, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, said at the summit that prices of gold were being buffeted by the war and the fallout on markets.
“Higher interest rates have made investing in gold somewhat less attractive. High energy prices have . . . damaged consumers’ ability to buy gold,” said Reade. “Fundamentals have mattered more this year in the absence of safe-haven purchases.”

articles.summary: Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentresOil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Oil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April.
The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran.
Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”
The oil price later eased back slight to sit about 2.7% up at just over $116 a barrel. Brent crude had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”
Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

What’s driving the selloff in precious metals  LivemintSilver Futures Fall to Lowest This Year as Oil Prices Fuel Inflation Risks  WSJAhmedabad: Silver falls to ₹1.98 lakh per kg, lowest in 10 months  The Times of IndiaGold, Silver Prices Sink: Why Are Precious Metals Losing Glitter? articles.full_text:
Silver prices showed no signs of recovery as the white metal extended its losing streak in Friday’s trade, falling another ₹6,800 per kg to ₹1,92,800, its lowest level since December 2025.
MCX gold prices were also down marginally, declining 0.29%, while hovering around a nearly three-month low of ₹1.40 lakh per 10 grams. Precious metals have faced heavy selling pressure in October as the Middle East conflict showed no signs of easing, keeping the possibility of further US Federal Reserve rate hikes in focus.
The weakness has deepened October losses, putting both metals on track for a second consecutive monthly decline. Rising bond yields, driven by elevated crude oil prices, have emerged as a key challenge for precious metals, fueling concerns that the US Federal Reserve could tighten monetary policy further.
Last week’s US consumer and producer inflation data came in hotter than expected, largely as energy costs continued to climb. This has strengthened the case for tighter monetary policy, although Fed officials are still expected to hold rates steady at their October 27–28 meeting.
US inflation has remained stubbornly high, prompting the Federal Reserve to raise its short-term interest rate in September for the first time in three years.
Gold is traditionally considered a hedge against inflation and a safe-haven asset during geopolitical uncertainty. However, higher interest rates reduce its appeal as investors turn towards yield-bearing assets.
Brent crude climbed towards $115 per barrel on Friday, approaching the four-year high of $115.25 reached on May 4. Escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi targets and reports of possible renewed US strikes against Iran have heightened concerns over oil supplies from the Middle East.
Market expectations of a rate hike at the Fed’s October 27–28 meeting stood at 9%, while the probability of a hike in December was 81%, according to CME’s FedWatch Tool. Investors are also awaiting US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, due on October 29 for fresh clues about progress towards its 2% inflation target.
The European Central Bank is scheduled to meet on Thursday amid political upheaval in France and an Iran war that has kept energy prices above $100 per barrel, leaving inflation risks elevated.
Considering Friday’s low, silver prices were down 7.5%, putting the metal on track for a fifth consecutive weekly loss. Silver has plunged ₹56,000 from its August peak of ₹2,48,800 per kg.
From its record high of ₹4,20,048 per kg, the metal has lost more than half its value. The sharp correction follows a 170% surge in silver prices in 2025. Gold has also witnessed a steep decline, falling ₹23,000 per 10 grams from August peak of ₹1,64,773.
Jateen Trivedi, vice president and research analyst at LKP Securities, said, “Gold continued its downward trend, declining more than 3.5% this week to around ₹1,42,800, as COMEX Gold corrected towards $4,000 amid growing expectations of a US interest rate hike.
"Higher rate expectations and elevated bond yields continue to weigh on bullion by increasing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets. Going ahead, the Fed’s policy decision next week will be the key trigger, with the rate outlook and policy guidance likely to determine gold’s near-term direction," he further added.

OpenAI is reportedly close to securing another mega round of private funding, rather than plowing ahead with an IPO. The AI lab is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in a round led by Coatue and investors in UAE, sources told CNBC.
This follows a similar report by Bloomberg a month ago which said the AI lab was working on raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Terms are still being negotiated, both outlets report, so they could ultimately change. CNBC reports that the UAE funding could also be coupled with a deal to secure more computing capacity for OpenAI from the UAE, too. OpenAI declined comment.
Should OpenAI command a valuation of more than $1 trillion with this round, it would break records as the most valued private company ever. That valuation would also raise the bar even higher for OpenAI’s forthcoming IPO. OpenAI filed confidential paperwork for an IPO in June, after its last raise in March valued the ChatGPT maker at $852 billion post-money.
That high valuation could also have ramifications for Anthropic’s IPO, which many believe is closer to materializing. (Rumors suggest we could see Anthropic’s public S-1 filing any day now.) The latest reports have Anthropic seeking a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation for its public debut, CNBC reports. Anthropic raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation in May in what many believed at the time would be its last big round before an IPO. It also filed confidential paperwork in June.

articles.title: USD/JPY Forecast: Is Rising Japanese Inflation Supporting the Yen? - StoneX
articles.summary: USD/JPY Forecast: Is Rising Japanese Inflation Supporting the Yen?  StoneX
articles.full_text:
As the trading week comes to an end, one of the most relevant developments in the FX market has been the renewed strength of the Japanese yen. This can be seen in the recent performance of USD/JPY, which has fallen nearly 1.0% over the last two trading sessions, highlighting a meaningful recovery in the Japanese currency against the U.S. dollar.
For now, the selling pressure observed around the pair is being driven primarily by the loss of momentum in U.S. Treasury yields. This has been reinforced by Japan's latest inflation data, released toward the end of the week, which has started to strengthen expectations of a potentially more aggressive Bank of Japan in the coming months. As a result, the yen has managed to recover part of the ground lost in previous months and, as long as these catalysts continue to support the Japanese currency, selling pressure around USD/JPY could remain relevant in the sessions ahead.
Is the Dollar Beginning to Lose Strength?
A loss of momentum around the U.S. dollar became increasingly evident throughout the week. Part of this dynamic has been driven by the moderation observed in 10-year U.S. Treasury yields, which temporarily moved below the 5.0% area.
This development is important because lower yields reduce part of the relative attractiveness of dollar-denominated investments. As a result, demand for the U.S. currency may also begin to soften in the short term.
The impact has already started to become visible in the behavior of the DXY, the index that measures the strength of the dollar against its main peers. In recent sessions, the index has retreated consistently, moving away from its yearly highs and currently trading near the 102-point area. This decline suggests that demand for the dollar has begun to moderate after several weeks of relatively solid strength, a dynamic that appears closely linked to the loss of momentum in the U.S. bond market.
Source: TradingEconomics
This behavior is particularly relevant because, as part of the relative advantage of holding dollar-denominated assets begins to fade, other currencies such as the yen have started to recover ground. In fact, the recent strength observed in the Japanese currency appears closely tied to this loss of relative attractiveness within U.S. financial markets.
As long as Treasury yields continue moving within a moderation phase, the yen could continue recovering part of the ground lost throughout much of 2026. Under this scenario, selling pressure around USD/JPY may remain an important factor influencing the pair in the short term.
Do Japan's Inflation Data Matter?
In addition to the weakness observed in the dollar, investors have also been paying close attention to Japan's latest inflation release. Annual inflation rose to 2.1%, reaching its highest level of 2026 and maintaining a relatively consistent upward trend over recent months.
This remains important because inflation is now developing slightly above the 2.0% target established by the Bank of Japan, a situation that could start generating greater concerns about inflationary pressures within the Japanese economy.
Source: TradingEconomics
The data have also started to influence monetary policy expectations. Only a few weeks ago, markets were pricing more than a 90% probability that the Bank of Japan would leave its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% during the October 28 meeting. However, by the end of the week that probability had fallen toward 80% area.
At the same time, expectations for the December meeting now imply close to a 60% probability that interest rates could rise to 1.50%.
Source: Centralbankwatch
This suggests markets are increasingly positioning for a more aggressive Bank of Japan over the coming months. Although Japanese rates remain relatively low compared to the current 4.0% reference rate in the United States, it is important to remember that Japan has maintained exceptionally low rates for decades.
For this reason, any gradual shift toward a more restrictive monetary policy stance could begin to alter investor perceptions regarding yen-denominated assets. If this process continues, the interest-rate differential between Japan and other major economies could gradually narrow, eventually becoming a meaningful catalyst for demand for the Japanese currency.
As a result, if the Bank of Japan continues moving toward a more aggressive stance than markets have been accustomed to over recent years, selling pressure around USD/JPY could remain an important theme even beyond the short term.
USD/JPY Technical Forecast
Source: StoneX, Tradingview
- The bearish bias is becoming relevant once again: Although USD/JPY had recently entered a phase of short-term neutrality after partially breaking the bearish trendline developed over previous months, recent price action has once again given prominence to selling pressure. As a result, the broader bearish structure is regaining relevance within the daily chart. As long as price continues approaching key support zones, the long-standing bearish trendline could once again become the dominant technical structure during the weeks ahead.
- MACD: The MACD histogram continues to trade slightly below the 0 neutral line, a reading that reflects weakening momentum within short-term moving averages. If this dynamic remains intact, it could continue supporting a more established bearish bias in the sessions ahead.
- RSI: A similar picture can be observed in the RSI, whose line remains below the 50 neutral level. This suggests that selling momentum has started to regain traction and supports the possibility that the bearish bias could remain relevant in the short term.
Key Levels:
- 158.86 – Key Resistance: A level that aligns with the 200-period simple moving average and represents the most important upside barrier in the short term. A sustained move above this reference could significantly alter the current technical structure and open the door to a more consistent bullish trend over the coming weeks.
- 157.38 – Near-Term Barrier: A level that coincides with the base of the recent consolidation range and also develops near the 50-period simple moving average. This could become the main level to monitor in the event of short-term bullish corrections.
- 155.30 – Key Support: A support zone established during previous weeks that remains one of the most important downside barriers on the chart. Price action returning toward this level could restore the dominance of selling pressure and reinforce the relevance of the broader bearish trendline as the market's primary technical structure over the coming weeks.

Global oil prices surged by around 3% on Friday, with Brent crude breaking above $117 a barrel for the first time since March 19, as escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East heightened concerns over global energy supplies and prompted investors to reassess the risk of market disruptions.
The rally reflected growing uncertainty over crude oil production and transportation, particularly the potential impact of regional conflicts on vital maritime shipping routes.
US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude also recorded significant gains, rising 3.6% to $103.05 a barrel, as concerns over supply constraints continued to support prices.
After-hours Trading Prices

Geopolitical risks drive oil market rally
The latest gains came as tensions across the Middle East intensified, raising concerns about the security of energy supplies and the possibility of disruptions to crude oil shipments through strategically important waterways.
These developments have increased what market participants call the geopolitical risk premium, the additional amount investors are willing to pay for oil amid the possibility of supply interruptions, higher transportation costs or threats to major export routes.
The oil market remains particularly sensitive to developments involving major producing countries and the maritime corridors that carry crude to international markets. Any disruption to these routes could tighten available supplies and increase costs for refiners and consumers.
Brent heads towards a third consecutive weekly gain
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, climbed above $117 a barrel, putting it on course for a third consecutive weekly advance.
Meanwhile, WTI strengthened to $103.05 a barrel, extending its gains as traders weighed the potential consequences of regional instability for the global supply-demand balance.
The simultaneous rise in both benchmarks underscores the extent to which geopolitical uncertainty is influencing energy market sentiment, with investors closely monitoring developments that could affect production, exports and shipping operations.
Global energy supplies remain in focus
The rally highlights the vulnerability of global energy markets to geopolitical shocks, particularly when uncertainty surrounds key producing regions and major maritime routes.
If supply disruptions materialise, oil prices could face further upward pressure. However, the scale and duration of any additional gains will depend on how events unfold, the actual impact on physical oil flows and the market’s assessment of available supplies.
For now, traders remain focused on developments in the Middle East as they assess the risks to global crude availability and the potential implications for energy costs and the wider economy.

articles.title: Silver Breaks Below $55 as Fed Decision Looms for Next Market Test - FXEmpire
articles.summary: Silver Breaks Below $55 as Fed Decision Looms for Next Market Test  FXEmpire
articles.full_text:
Silver finds itself with an improving interest-rate backdrop, but an unresolved question about industrial momentum. This week’s verified monetary change was a decline in Treasury yields, from a 5-year yield of 2.52% down to 2.33%, while the 10-year measure slipped from 2.74% to 2.64%. This does ease the opportunity cost of holding precious metals, although it does not necessarily establish a corresponding gain in the price of silver. In fact, we have seen silver continue to drop.
Industrial Demand?
The industrial side requires a different type of time horizon, though. The Federal Reserve’s latest production release, published on October 16, showed September manufacturing output rising 0.3% after a revised 0.2% loss in August. Output was 1.1% above September 2025 readings. This dated background information gives us an idea that manufacturing is perking up a bit, but it does not necessarily translate to more silver demand quite yet.
The chart just below will put that signal in context, as the manufacturing index moved from 98.1 in April to 98.4 in September, with an August setback between the July and September advances. Manufacturing capacity utilization was 75.9% in September, below the longer-term 78.2% average. Put together, the figures suggest a limited recovery with spare capacity.
Some Scenarios
The most supportive combination would be easing real yields along with resilient activity. For the weekly outlook, this distinction matters a bit. The favorable monetary environment can encourage investment demand, while manufacturers may still be a bit cautious if final demand is uncertain. Stronger production, on the other hand, can improve the industrial case even when monetary conditions remain somewhat restrictive.
Unemployment Claims
Thursday’s unemployment claims report illustrates why the growth picture remains somewhat mixed. Initial claims declined to 194,000 for the week ending October 17, while continuing claims increased to 1.728 million for the week ending October 10. These are differently dated measures, but they give us an idea of what is going on through the broader U.S. economy.
Inflation complicates the outlook for industrial margins and financing as well. September final-demand producer prices rose 1.3% month over month, seasonally adjusted, and 6.3% year over year, unadjusted, in the October 15 release. These are broad producer-price measures, not a silver input-cost index, so silver should just be thought of as a bit of a component in the larger picture. Persistent cost pressure could squeeze some manufacturers or encourage restrictive monetary policy, so these numbers will be watched.
Federal Reserve Meeting
Next week’s first major test is the Federal Reserve decision on Wednesday, October 28, scheduled for 2 p.m. Eastern, with a 2:30 p.m. press conference. A policy message that permits real yields to stay lower could help silver’s monetary argument. A renewed emphasis on inflation could restrain the market, as tighter monetary policy continues to work against it.
On October 29, there is the BEA advance third-quarter GDP and September personal income and outlays announcement, coming out at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. GDP can help us assess demand and investment conditions. The personal income and outlays release supplies PCE inflation and household-spending evidence. For silver, resilient real demand with moderating inflation would be a favorable combination.
The third-quarter Employment Cost Index follows on Friday at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. Compensation pressure can have a major influence on policy persistence and manufacturers’ operating costs. CFTC positioning also deserves interest, as the October 30 report is scheduled for 3:30 p.m. Eastern and ordinarily reflects the preceding Tuesday.
Technical Setup
Lower real yields do offer some support, but stronger industrial-demand claims need further evidence. Looking at the price numbers, it certainly seems as if silver continues to see downward pressure. From a technical standpoint, we broke below a major support level on Friday to smash through that $55 level. This opens up much lower silver pricing, perhaps even driving silver towards the $70 level.
This breakdown is a continuation of the bearish pressure we have seen since silver peaked in January, reaching above $120 an ounce. At this point, this market seems to be entering another leg lower and, quite frankly, needs the Federal Reserve statement or press conference to somehow give it hope.

articles.title: Gold Price Forecast: Can XAU/USD Recover Above $4,000 as Fed Decision Looms? - Mitrade
articles.summary: Gold Price Forecast: Can XAU/USD Recover Above $4,000 as Fed Decision Looms?  Mitrade
articles.full_text:
Gold prices have entered a critical phase as XAU/USD briefly fell below the psychological US$4,000 level on Friday, 23 October 2026, extending Thursday's sharp selloff.
Spot gold dropped to approximately US$3,987 during Asian trading before recovering towards US$4,015. The decline followed a nearly 3% fall on Thursday, when bullion broke below US$4,100 and approached US$4,020.
The selloff comes amid growing concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) investment valuations, elevated oil prices, persistent inflation risks and uncertainty surrounding the Federal Reserve's next interest rate decision.
Despite falling US Treasury yields, gold has struggled to attract sustained buying interest, suggesting that broader market deleveraging and inflation concerns may be outweighing traditional safe-haven demand.
For Australian investors, the key question is whether gold can establish support around US$4,000 or whether the recent breakdown signals a deeper correction towards US$3,800.
Gold Price Today: Key Market Highlights
- Immediate resistance: US$4,030–US$4,050, followed by US$4,100.
- Key support: US$4,000, followed by US$3,940–US$3,960 and US$3,800.
- US Treasury yields: The benchmark 10-year yield fell below 5% on 22 October as investors moved towards government bonds.
- Federal Reserve outlook: Markets are assessing the likelihood of further monetary tightening amid conflicting signals from inflation and economic growth.
- Market sentiment: Technology-stock volatility, AI investment concerns and rising oil prices have increased uncertainty across financial markets.
- Next major catalyst: The Federal Reserve's October policy decision, scheduled for 28 October 2026.
Why Is the Gold Price Falling Despite Rising Market Uncertainty?
Gold is traditionally considered a defensive asset during periods of financial uncertainty. However, its recent performance demonstrates that safe-haven demand does not always translate into higher prices.
Three major factors are influencing the current gold market.
1. AI Stock Selloff Triggers Broader Market Deleveraging
Concerns about the sustainability of AI-related capital expenditure have contributed to renewed selling pressure across US technology stocks.
As equity market volatility increases, investors may liquidate profitable or liquid positions to meet margin requirements and reduce overall portfolio exposure.
Gold is particularly vulnerable to this type of short-term selling because it is highly liquid and can be converted into cash quickly.
This helps explain why bullion has declined alongside equities despite increased demand for defensive assets.
The recent rise in the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) also highlights growing investor anxiety.
If technology-stock weakness continues, gold could experience further liquidation pressure even if the broader economic outlook deteriorates.
2. Rising Oil Prices Increase Inflation Risks
Escalating tensions in the Middle East have pushed energy prices higher, raising concerns about renewed inflationary pressure.
Higher oil prices can increase transportation, manufacturing and consumer costs, complicating the Federal Reserve's efforts to control inflation.
For gold investors, the implications are mixed.
On one hand, persistent inflation may strengthen demand for gold as a long-term store of value.
On the other hand, higher inflation could encourage the Federal Reserve to maintain restrictive monetary policy or raise interest rates further.
Because gold does not generate interest income, higher real interest rates can reduce its attractiveness relative to interest-bearing assets.
This creates a challenging environment in which geopolitical uncertainty may support gold demand while monetary policy expectations place downward pressure on prices.
3. Falling US Treasury Yields Offer Limited Support
On Thursday, 22 October, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield fell below the important 5% threshold, while the two-year yield also declined sharply.
Lower Treasury yields would normally provide support for gold by reducing the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
However, gold continued to fall.
This divergence suggests that short-term liquidity requirements, portfolio adjustments and uncertainty surrounding inflation may currently be more influential than the decline in bond yields.
A sustained recovery in gold may therefore require not only lower yields but also greater stability across equity and currency markets.
Federal Reserve Outlook: Could the October Rate Decision Trigger a Gold Rebound?
The Federal Reserve's upcoming monetary policy announcement is likely to be a major catalyst for XAU/USD.
The decision is scheduled for 28 October 2026, following the central bank's two-day policy meeting.
Investors will focus on whether policymakers signal a pause in further tightening or maintain concerns about persistent inflation.
Scenario 1: The Fed Signals a Less Hawkish Outlook
If the Federal Reserve emphasises slowing economic activity, weaker employment conditions or tighter financial conditions, expectations for additional rate increases could decline.
Such a development may put downward pressure on US Treasury yields and the US dollar.
This could create a more supportive environment for gold, particularly if the metal manages to hold above US$4,000.
Under this scenario, XAU/USD may attempt to recover towards US$4,050 and US$4,100.
Scenario 2: The Fed Maintains a Hawkish Stance
If policymakers remain concerned about energy-driven inflation, markets may continue to anticipate restrictive interest rates.
A stronger US dollar or a rebound in Treasury yields could limit gold's recovery.
In this scenario, a renewed break below US$4,000 may expose the next support region around US$3,940–US$3,960.
A more sustained decline could eventually bring US$3,800 into focus.
Scenario 3: Stagflation Concerns Intensify
A particularly complicated outcome would involve slowing economic growth alongside persistently high inflation.
This combination, commonly described as stagflation, can create conflicting pressures for gold.
Although gold has historically attracted interest during certain inflationary and stagflationary periods, aggressive monetary tightening and forced asset sales can still produce substantial short-term declines.
Investors should therefore avoid assuming that stagflation will automatically result in higher gold prices.
Gold Technical Analysis: Is US$4,000 the Most Important Support Level?
Gold's technical outlook has weakened following its breakdown below US$4,100.
After consolidating around the US$4,100–US$4,200 region earlier in October, XAU/USD experienced a sharp decline that brought the US$4,000 psychological level into focus.
Source: Tradingview
Friday's brief move below US$4,000 suggests that bearish momentum remains significant.
However, the subsequent recovery also indicates that some buyers are willing to enter the market at lower prices.
Source: Tradingview
Key Gold Support and Resistance Levels
Bullish Outlook: Gold Holds Above US$4,000
If gold stabilises above US$4,000 and establishes a series of higher intraday lows, a technical rebound may develop.
The first important upside area lies around US$4,030–US$4,050.
A decisive move above this region could encourage further buying towards US$4,100.
However, a sustained recovery above US$4,100 would provide stronger evidence that the recent selling pressure is easing.
Until then, rebounds may remain vulnerable to renewed selling.
Bearish Outlook: Gold Breaks Below US$4,000 Again
If XAU/USD falls below US$4,000 and fails to recover, the market could revisit Friday's low near US$3,987.
Further weakness may expose the US$3,940–US$3,960 support zone.
A sustained breakdown below this area could increase the likelihood of a move towards US$3,800.
Under a more severe medium-term correction, US$3,400 could become a longer-range technical reference, although reaching this level would require substantial additional selling pressure.
The direction of the next sustained move will likely depend on the interaction between monetary policy expectations, energy prices and overall financial market sentiment.
How to Trade Gold Price Movements with CFDs in Australia
Gold contracts for difference (CFDs) allow traders to speculate on gold price movements without owning physical bullion.
Unlike purchasing gold bars or coins, CFD trading involves taking a position on the price difference between opening and closing a trade.
Traders can potentially participate in both rising and falling markets, although losses are possible in either direction.
Trading a Potential Gold Rebound
Traders expecting a recovery may monitor whether XAU/USD stabilises above US$4,000 and breaks through nearby resistance.
A bullish setup could become more convincing if gold reclaims US$4,050 and buying momentum improves.
However, an intraday recovery alone does not confirm a sustained trend reversal.
Trading a Potential Gold Breakdown
Traders expecting further downside may focus on whether gold breaks below US$4,000 again and fails to recover.
A sustained move beneath nearby support could indicate additional bearish momentum.
Nevertheless, short positions can also face significant losses if gold rebounds sharply following unexpected economic or geopolitical developments.

Did Regulators or Markets Drive the Solidigm IPO Halt?
Solidigm's factories have little room to expand output as AI memory demand climbs.
FSS Governor Lee Chan-jin said officials were weighing whether the IPO needed review under minority shareholder protection rules.

Can SK Hynix Fund a US Fab and Bigger Payouts?

Separately, a listing could have valued Solidigm on its own, a growth story SK Hynix says its valuation misses.
Payouts were already rising, as the board approved a 40 trillion won buyback and share cancellation program in August.
The company also raised its return target to over 50% of cumulative free cash flow through 2027.
The statement names no replacement for the IPO. SK Hynix is still deciding when, how much, and how to finance any investment.
Meanwhile, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) had already faced a chip-led AI selloff earlier this week.
In the US, the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.6% Thursday, its weakest session since June, CNBC reported.
AI data center operators also slid, with CoreWeave down 10% Thursday and Australia's NextDC nearly 40% lower Wednesday.
In contrast, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC he does not expect a memory chip glut by 2029.
SK Hynix said it would detail payout plans with its third-quarter results, which a filing shows are due Oct. 28.
Korea's chip exports rose 222.5% from a year earlier in early October. Yet the KOSPI fell 20.72% in 10 sessions through Oct. 20.

articles.summary: Japan's CPI data reinforces rate-hike expectations; yen's rally fails to sustain, but institutions remain bullish in the medium term  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
On Friday (October 23), during the Asian session, the USD/JPY pair rebounded from a more-than-one-month low reached earlier in the session—around 156.00—after Japan released consumer inflation data.
However, the current exchange rate has failed to hold above 157.00, and the week is still on track to post a sizable weekly decline.
Rising inflation in Japan has boosted the yen, but the rally has failed to sustain.
According to the latest data from Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the nationwide Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 2.1% year-on-year in September, accelerating from 1.9% in the previous month. Excluding volatile fresh food, the core CPI also increased by 2.1%, marking the strongest reading since December 2025.
In addition, the core CPI—excluding fresh food and energy—rose to 2.5% month-on-month, hitting a 10-month high and providing further justification for the Bank of Japan to continue raising interest rates.
This provided some support to the yen, but the initial market reaction quickly faded.
The U.S. dollar staged a modest rebound, drawing some bargain-hunting at lower levels and lifting USD/JPY from a more than one-month low near 156.00.
Demand for the U.S. dollar has rebounded, but upside potential remains limited.
Although Federal Reserve officials have recently indicated there is no urgent need for an immediate rate hike, traders appear confident that the U.S. central bank will raise rates again this year.
The CME Group's FedWatch tool indicates that the probability of a rate hike in December stands at around 80%. Inflation risks stemming from rising energy prices also bolster the outlook for further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve.
In addition, the further escalation of tensions in the Middle East has kept geopolitical risk premiums elevated, boosting demand for the safe-haven U.S. dollar and providing tailwinds for USD/JPY.
However, upside appears limited, as traders remain hesitant ahead of next week's key central bank events.
Institutional Perspective
Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG) forecasts the USD/JPY exchange rate at 155 by the end of the fourth quarter of 2026, 153 in the first quarter of 2027, 151 in the second quarter, and 149 in the third quarter. The Bank of Japan has raised its policy rate to 1.25%, with another rate hike most likely in December, followed by an accelerated pace that could bring the rate to 2% by 2027.
Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group believes that the narrowing U.S.-Japan interest rate spread, the yen's perceived significant undervaluation by the United States, and the potential risk of coordinated intervention will cap any substantial appreciation. Should the exchange rate break above 160, the likelihood of warnings and intervention from both Japanese and U.S. authorities would increase, and the 200-day moving average would also act as a resistance level. Sustained appreciation would require the Bank of Japan to continue raising interest rates and restoring confidence in fiscal discipline. With near-term risks having eased further, the yen is expected to strengthen gradually over the medium term.
Westpac forecasts that the USD/JPY exchange rate will fall to 156 by December 2026 and further to 151 by December 2027. The yen's recovery is expected to be concentrated in 2027 and will not hinge on rapid Fed rate cuts—assuming U.S. interest rates remain unchanged throughout 2027.
Westpac stated that the Bank of Japan's ongoing normalization efforts, coupled with Japanese inflation data supporting further rate hikes, will gradually narrow the U.S.–Japan yield spread. At the same time, the yen's long-term undervaluation and potential capital repatriation provide support. In the short term, the currency may remain influenced by U.S. Treasury yields and global risk sentiment; however, over the medium to long term, the yen is expected to appreciate against the U.S. dollar, with the overall trajectory leaning toward gradual strengthening.
Next Week's Focus: Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan Meetings
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its interest-rate decision at the conclusion of its two-day monetary-policy meeting on October 28, followed by the highly anticipated Bank of Japan meeting (October 29–30).
Traders will also be watching the U.S. third-quarter GDP preliminary estimate and the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, both scheduled for release next Thursday. These data are expected to bolster demand for the U.S. dollar and provide meaningful momentum for USD/JPY.
Meanwhile, market participants will remain on high alert, as speculation mounts that further depreciation of the yen could prompt direct intervention in the foreign-exchange market by Japanese authorities.
This could further cap the currency pair and serve as a cautionary signal for aggressive bullish traders.

articles.title: Wall Street doubts gold’s near-term strength, Main Street maintains bullish minority as central banks take center stage - Kitco
articles.summary: Wall Street doubts gold’s near-term strength, Main Street maintains bullish minority as central banks take center stage  Kitco
articles.full_text:
(Kitco News) – Gold prices suffered another sharp weekly decline as rising oil prices, persistent inflation fears, and expectations for further Federal Reserve tightening overwhelmed safe-haven demand, while Thursday's technology-led equity selloff triggered another wave of liquidations that pushed the precious metal back below $4,000 per ounce.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $4,164.69 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal managed to eke out some early gains as traders continued to assess renewed U.S.-Iran tensions and the inflationary impact of disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. But the rally quickly stalled, with gold setting its weekly high of $4,190.17 per ounce early Monday morning before sellers took control as rising energy prices and elevated Treasury yields reinforced expectations that the Fed would maintain their restrictive monetary policy.
The selling accelerated through Monday and Tuesday trading, with gold breaking below $4,150 as markets continued to digest the previous week's hotter-than-expected CPI and PPI reports. The yellow metal attempted to stabilize on Wednesday as Treasury yields eased, but the recovery proved short-lived as traders remained focused on the risk of another Fed rate hike before year-end.
Gold prices plunged Thursday as a sharp technology-led equity selloff triggered broader market liquidations, even as Treasury yields and the dollar weakened. Renewed concerns about the AI sector and speculation about possible intervention in the Japanese yen added to the uncertainty, while renewed Middle East tensions pushed oil prices higher. The selling carried over into Friday, with gold set its weekly low of $3,975.10 per ounce – its lowest level since early June – around an hour after the North American open, and prices oscillated on both sides of $4,000-per-ounce heading into the weekly close.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed Wall Street pessimism on the rise after gold’s steep slide, while Main Street saw more silver lining despite the yellow metal’s recent underperformance.
“Gold, basis spot, was sold to a new three-month low before the weekend, slightly below $3990,” said Marc Chandler, managing director at Bannockburn Global Forex. “It recovered but the technical tone still looks weak. The momentum indicators are not rising and the five- and 20-day moving averages are falling. Initial resistance is seen in the 4065-4075 area.”
“Half of the G10 central banks meet next week and only the RBNZ is likely to hike,” Chandler added. “Still, the others, including the Fed, will keep the door open to hikes before the end of the year.”
“Unchanged,” said Adrian Day, president of Adrian Day Asset Management. “More back and forth, but still think $4,000 will hold, or maybe just a little below.”
“Up,” said James Stanley, senior market strategist at Forex.com. “The $4k test has held so far, and while it may take a bit for the tide to turn, I think the case is still strong for $4k support – unless something breaks in the US economy which could lead to a risk aversion run. But even in that backdrop, I’m biased towards longer-term accumulation.”
“Up,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “The sell-off in the stock market this week triggered margin calls. As always, investors seeking liquidity to meet those margin calls turned to THE most liquid asset on earth… gold. The selling pressure took gold back below $4,000 per ounce.”
“I do not expect gold to remain below $4,000 very long,” Checkan said. “Barring any surprises from next Wednesday’s interest rate announcement from the Federal Open Market Committee, I would expect gold to bounce off these lows as bargain hunters snatch up as much cheap gold as they are able.”
Kevin Grady, president of Phoenix Futures and Options, said gold continues to trade inversely to interest rates, but there’s also broader concerns impacting the yellow metal.
“We're all thinking about rates, and I know we're following daily yields and things like that,” he said. “But it's also the long-term picture that people are looking at and seeing that there is a crack in the bond market, and even historically, that rates are higher.”
It's hard to see, because you're not really getting a lot of color,” Grady said. “A lot of commercials have decreased their trading. You're not seeing the volumes that we've had in the past. I think it's one of those things where gold has been trying to see the next leg up, and we just haven't had it.”
Grady said that a number of longs came into the market as gold posted its recent gains, and they were waiting for a good exit, but it didn’t come, and now they have no choice but to exit at lower prices and into thin liquidity.
“When you look at daily volumes at 129,000 contracts, that's what we used to do in open outcry! Once the markets went electronic, we were doing over 400,000 easily,” he said. “I think what's happening now is that it's very thin, and when you see people start to get out, it's just exacerbated the moves.”
Grady said that between the Iran war’s renewed threats of escalation, Russia-Ukraine getting worse, the risk of a hawkish Fed next week, and the looming midterm elections, people are wary of putting their money into the markets – any markets.
“That move [on Thursday], I think scared a lot of people away from saying, ‘Hey, let me go in right before a big meeting or a big decision where I don't know where it's going to be, and let me take a position.’ Because getting out of that position can be deadly.”
“I think that move yesterday is going to put a lot of people on the sidelines.”
Turning to Wednesday’s Fed meeting, Grady said that even if markets are pricing in a hold, under current conditions, they really can’t be sure
“What is the Fed going to do? The market's saying, no, he's not going to raise rates, but maybe he tries to shock people,” he said. “I don't think he should, but you just don't know. There's just too much uncertainty. A lot of people, especially professional traders, are saying, ‘This isn't trading right now, it's guessing.’”
“I was speaking with a friend of mine yesterday who's a big trader on the floor with me, in gold, and we were talking about [this],” he said “It isn't just that you’re a trader and you're putting on positions. As a trader, you're a risk manager. And if you're not a good risk manager, you're not going to be a successful trader. I think right now, when you look at the upside or downside to putting on a trade, what are the odds of this trade working? Markets have gotten so thin… I just think the upside is not worth it.”
Grady said that if gold does see a break below $4,000, we’ll soon be approaching levels where prices held during earlier selloffs.
“But I will tell you, underneath those levels is going to be stops, and everyone knows that,” he said. “Being long in front of those… it's always nice to buy in front of the support level, but when it breaks that support level, it could be dangerous. So I think people have to really watch out.”
This week, 17 analysts participated in the Kitco News Gold Survey, with the largest portion of Wall Street sentiment sliding into the bearish camp after gold’s precipitous drop below $4,000. Four experts, or 24%, expect to see gold prices gain ground during the week ahead, while seven, representing 41%, see the yellow metal declining further. The remaining six analysts, 35% of the total, said they couldn’t predict gold’s direction, or expected sideways trading next week.
Meanwhile, 161 votes were cast in Kitco’s online poll, with Main Street investors considerably more bullish than their professional counterparts despite gold’s late-week slide. 67 retail traders, or 42%, looked for gold prices to rise next week, while 41 others, or 26%, predicted the yellow metal would lose more ground. The remaining 53 investors, representing 33% of the total, expected to see consolidation during the week ahead.
Central banks will dominate next week’s economic news, with rate decisions from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Canada and Japan, but markets will also have a raft of growth, consumer and housing data to digest.
The U.S. calendar kicks off Tuesday morning with Durable Goods Orders, Consumer Confidence, and New Home Sales.
Then on Wednesday morning, the Bank of Canada will issue its monetary policy decision, followed by the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy decision in the afternoon.
Thursday morning will see the ECB’s monetary policy decision, along with Advance US Q3 GDP and PCE, and weekly jobless claims, with the Bank of Japan’s monetary policy decision coming overnight to cap the week’s key data.
Sean Lusk, co-director of commercial hedging at Walsh Trading, said the Iran conflict – and its impact on oil prices, inflation expectations, and Fed rate projections – continues to cap gold’s potential gains.
“It's just an impediment to any rally in gold,” he said. “Now, there could be an 11th hour deal over the weekend for a ceasefire, but I don't know… It looks like the market, at least the energy space, is really priced in that this thing is going to escalate in the near term. Big time.”
Lusk said he’s optimistic about productivity gains from AI, but the broader economy won’t do well for a while.
“Bond yields aren't coming off anytime soon, which means housing prices are still going to decline – obviously there's going to be winners and losers in that space – but if you do have declining home values, where the sellers far outpace buyers by a wide margin, I don't think gold in that context is still at $4,000 an ounce. It's still rather elevated here.”
“A couple things have to happen [for gold to resume its uptrend],” he said. “The strait has to be reopened, and these wars have to end. It doesn't look like either of those things are going to happen anytime soon. And it could get really ugly here before it does.”

articles.title: MSCI Inc Earnings Call: Growth, AI And Buybacks - The Globe and Mail
articles.summary: MSCI Inc Earnings Call: Growth, AI And Buybacks  The Globe and Mail
articles.full_text:
MSCI Inc ((MSCI)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.
MSCI Inc’s latest earnings call struck a distinctly upbeat tone, as management highlighted double-digit growth across revenue, EBITDA, EPS and asset-based fees. While they acknowledged pockets of weakness in Sustainability, Climate and Real Assets, the breadth of growth and AI-driven innovation left the overall sentiment strongly positive for investors following the stock.
Robust Third-Quarter Financial Performance
MSCI posted a powerful third quarter, with total revenue up 12.4%, asset-based fees climbing 25% and subscription revenue rising 8%. Adjusted EBITDA increased 12% and adjusted EPS grew 14%, underscoring solid profitability despite a still-challenging environment for traditional asset managers.
Record Asset-Based Fee Momentum
The company’s run rate grew 12%, driven by a near record asset-based fee run rate approaching $1 billion. Equity ETFs tied to MSCI indexes saw $76 billion in cash inflows, as assets benchmarked to its indexes climbed to almost $23 trillion, split between roughly $15 trillion active and $8 trillion indexed.
Aggressive Buybacks and Insider Confidence
Capital return was a major theme, with MSCI repurchasing $627 million of stock at an average price of $562 from July through mid-October. Since the start of 2024 it has bought nearly 8 million shares for $4.4 billion, while CEO Henry Fernandez signaled confidence by personally buying 57,000 shares for $30.1 million.
Subscription Growth and Stronger Retention
Subscription run rate advanced 9% as MSCI added nearly $55 million in recurring net new sales across its franchises. Overall retention improved to 95%, 30 basis points higher than a year ago, indicating clients are not only expanding relationships but also sticking with MSCI’s platforms.
Record Recurring Sales Across Core Lines
Recurring net new sales reached their best-ever third-quarter levels in Index, Analytics and Private Capital Solutions, underscoring broad product momentum. Compared with last year, PCS recurring sales jumped 88%, Analytics rose 63% and Index increased 40%, pointing to diversified growth engines.
Broad-Based Regional Growth
Sales strength was global, with recurring net new sales up 74% in EMEA, 36% in APAC and 26% in the Americas. APAC delivered its best quarter on record, fueled by strong demand for MSCI’s Analytics tools across institutional clients.
Index Business Acceleration and High Retention
Organic subscription run rate in Index accelerated to 11.7%, reflecting strong demand across client types. Growth from hedge funds, banks and brokers, wealth managers and asset owners reached 32%, 15%, 10% and 10% respectively, while Index retention stayed above 97%, including 98% with asset managers.
ETF Inflows and Custom Index Strength
Asset-based fees benefited from $76 billion of equity ETF inflows, MSCI’s second-strongest inflow quarter and focused on developed ex-U.S. and emerging markets. Custom index solutions also surged, with subscription run rate rising more than 26% as clients sought more tailored benchmarks.
Analytics and Private Capital Solutions Expansion
Analytics posted organic subscription run rate growth of 7.5%, with last-12-month recurring sales up 18% versus the prior period. Private Capital Solutions accelerated to 19% subscription run rate growth, driven by demand for transparency, data, diligence and benchmarking tools spanning private markets.
Asset Owners and Non-Manager Client Momentum
Asset owners were a standout, delivering more than 12% organic growth and over triple the recurring net new sales versus last year, supported by total portfolio solutions and integrated risk analytics. Hedge funds grew about 18%, while broker-dealers and banks posted roughly 10% growth, broadening MSCI’s revenue base.
Strategic Wins and Expanded Partnerships
MSCI highlighted a marquee win in Asia, shifting from vendor to strategic portfolio analytics partner with a major sovereign wealth fund. It also signed large Index and Analytics deals with top hedge funds, formalized a key private-assets agreement with UBS and leveraged the Vantager acquisition to secure a major U.S. bank mandate.
Innovation’s Growing Role in Revenue
New products are becoming a meaningful growth driver, with their contribution to third-quarter sales rising more than 50% year on year. Management emphasized that innovation is helping not only to win new logos but also to support retention, pricing power and expansion into new use cases and client types.
AI-Enabled Product and Model Development
AI featured prominently, as MSCI uses it to build agentic private-market tools, specialized data sets and new factor models, dramatically speeding development. The time to design and fully calibrate a new model has fallen from several weeks to a couple of hours, with ambitions to reduce that further to minutes.
New Portfolio and Risk Management Solutions
The firm launched a total portfolio management platform for asset and wealth managers alongside a tailored wealth-specific offering. Additional launches included a custom model service, new factor models, specialized data sets and lower-latency intraday multi-asset risk capabilities aimed at more active trading desks.
Progress in Climate Integration
Integration of First Street within MSCI’s climate suite is said to be on track, supported by strong client engagement and rising demand for physical-risk analytics. Climate run rate grew 8% across MSCI product lines when excluding the First Street impact, showing underlying client interest despite broader sustainability headwinds.
Real Assets Retention and Modest Growth
Real Assets saw organic subscription run rate growth of 2%, lagging other segments but benefiting from improving retention trends. Demand for broader data access via Snowflake is supporting the franchise, though growth remains modest compared with Index, Analytics and Private Capital Solutions.
Cash Collections and Free Cash Flow Outlook
Quarterly free cash flow was pressured by timing and higher interest payments tied to earlier financings, which management framed as transitory. Despite this, MSCI kept its full-year free cash flow guidance intact and stressed that performance option accruals are noncash, preserving underlying cash strength.
Opportunities in Active ETFs and Trading Tools
Management pointed to significant growth as traditional active managers convert mutual funds into ETFs, increasing demand for systematic tools. MSCI believes its trading ecosystem solutions for hedge funds, broker-dealers and market makers will also become increasingly relevant to asset managers in a more systematic ETF world.
Investor Relations Leadership Changes
The company announced a leadership transition within investor relations as it evolves its capital markets communication. Jeremy Ulan will move into a lead finance director role for client segments and solutions, while Craig Carter, currently head of corporate development, will take over as head of investor relations.
Sustainability and Climate Retention Pressure
Not everything was rosy, as Sustainability and Climate remained under pressure with elevated cancellations and one large downsell from a client cutting spending. Management cautioned that parts of the Sustainability franchise will likely continue to face challenges through the fourth quarter, weighing on growth metrics.
Muted Near-Term Sustainability and Climate Sales
MSCI still booked more than $5 million in new recurring Sustainability sales and over $2 million in Climate during the quarter. However, executives expect recurring net new sales for the combined segment to be only flat to slightly positive in the fourth quarter, signaling a near-term drag on overall momentum.
Real Assets Growth Lags Other Segments
Real Assets growth remained modest at 2% organic subscription run rate, well below the pace in Index, Analytics and PCS. While retention is improving and data access initiatives are promising, the segment is clearly a slower-growth area relative to MSCI’s core franchises.
Higher Expense Outlook for 2026
Looking ahead, MSCI expects to sit at the top end of its 2026 expense guidance ranges as it continues to invest. Acquisitions should add around $20 million of costs, higher performance stock-based compensation another $15 million to $20 million and severance roughly $10 million to $15 million more than initially planned.
Rising Interest Costs and Cash Outlays
Interest expense guidance was raised due to higher revolver usage to fund aggressive share repurchases, reflecting capital return priorities. Third-quarter free cash flow was also impacted by more than $50 million in additional cash interest payments tied to prior-year financings.
No Explicit Margin Expansion Target
CEO Henry Fernandez stated that MSCI is not targeting margin expansion, preferring to reinvest operating leverage and AI-driven savings into growth. The company aims to use AI to slow the growth rate of run-the-business EBITDA expenses from mid- to high-single digits into low-single digits and eventually negative territory.
Asset Manager Segment: Steady but Pressured
Within asset managers, organic subscription run rate growth was around 6%, including roughly 8% in Index, showing steady but not explosive progress. Management reiterated that secular pressures on the asset manager industry are likely to persist, moderating growth even as MSCI continues to gain share.
Deal Timing and Metric Lumpiness
Executives cautioned that large strategic deals can slide between quarters, causing lumpiness in operating metrics such as recurring sales. They advised investors to focus on multi-quarter trends in recurring net new sales, retention and cancellations rather than drawing firm conclusions from one quarter alone.
