- PRESS RELEASE
ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – September 2026
23 October 2026
- median consumer perceptions of inflation over the past 12 months and expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased slightly, while median expectations for inflation three years and five years ahead were unchanged;
- expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months increased, as did expectations for spending growth over the next 12 months;
- expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months decreased, while the expected unemployment rate in 12 months’ time increased;
- expectations for growth in the price of homes over the next 12 months increased, while expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged
Inflation
In September the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 3.6% from 3.5% in August. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also increased, to 3.1% from 3.0%. Median expectations for inflation three years ahead and median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.9% and 2.5% respectively. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased slightly, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Respondents in the bottom income quintile continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations, on average, than those in the top quintile. Younger respondents (aged 18-34) continued to report lower inflation perceptions and expectations than older respondents (aged 35-54 and 55-70).
Inflation results
Income and consumption
Consumers’ expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months increased to 1.1% in September from 1.0% in August. As in previous months expectations were, on average, higher in the bottom income quintile (1.5%) than in the top quintile (1.2%). Perceived nominal spending growth over the previous 12 months increased to 5.3% from 5.2%, while expected nominal spending growth over the next 12 months increased to 3.7% from 3.6%.
Income and consumption results
Economic growth and labour market
Expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months decreased in September to -1.5%, from -1.2% in August. Expectations for the unemployment rate 12 months ahead increased to 11.3%, from 11.0%. As observed in previous months, households in the bottom income quintile expected the highest unemployment rate 12 months ahead (13.6%), while households in the top income quintile expected the lowest rate (9.7%). Consumers continued to expect the future unemployment rate to be only slightly higher than the perceived current unemployment rate (10.6%), suggesting a broadly stable labour market outlook.
Economic growth and labour market results
Housing and credit access
Consumers expected the price of their home to increase by 3.5% over the next 12 months, higher than in August (3.4%). As in previous months expectations for home price growth over the next 12 months remained, on average, higher in the lowest income quintile (4.0%) than in the highest income quintile (3.2%). Expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged from July, at 4.9%. As in previous months, households in the top income quintile expected the lowest mortgage interest rates 12 months ahead (4.4%), while those in the bottom quintile expected the highest rates (5.7%). The net percentage of households reporting a tightening (relative to those reporting an easing) of access to credit over the previous 12 months increased compared with August, as did the net percentage of households expecting tighter credit conditions over the next 12 months (relative to those expecting an easing).
Housing and credit access results

articles.title: Falling Treasury yields may be hiding a darker story about the AI boom - investingLive
articles.summary: Falling Treasury yields may be hiding a darker story about the AI boom  investingLiveWinter arrives in markets  Financial Times10-year Treasury yield drops back to 5% this week as investors seek cover from AI worries  CNBCUS bond market down: Why are 10-year, 30-year, 2-year treasury yield notes are falling? Check latest predi  The Economic TimesTreasury yields log biggest drop since the 2023 banking crisis. Here’s what’s going on.  MarketWatch
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Why are investors rushing into Treasuries even as inflation fears persist?
Let's take a step back and check on the key market drivers this week. The US-Iran conflict is still raging on and geopolitical tensions remain high. So, that is underpinning oil prices once again with WTI crude breaching $100 and Brent crude hitting $114 - its highest since May.
Now, that sounds like a familiar backdrop for the bond market, doesn't it? Higher oil prices mean stronger inflation pressures, which should normally push up Treasury yields. Well, that has not been the case this week.
Instead, Treasury yields have fallen sharply, with 10-year yields even slipping back below the 5% threshold in overnight trading and holding thereabouts since. But wait a second, shouldn't falling yields then buy some relief for stocks?
You would certainly think so, especially when surging Treasury yields have been such a major bane for equities over the past two months. And yet stocks have been battered this week, with AI names in particular bearing the brunt of the pain. So, what gives?
It's one thing to suggest that investors are perhaps starting to worry about growth conditions again. But considering how long that narrative has been brushed aside and the extent of the damage we are seeing in AI stocks, I think there is perhaps a rather different problem brewing beneath the surface.
Let's jump straight into it and start with CoreWeave, shall we?
That's not the most familiar name in the AI space. However, CoreWeave might well have been the stone that started an avalanche of worries about debt financing in the entire sector.
Just take a look at the chart below, which shows how the cost of insuring against defaults among major AI-related companies has surged over the past year i.e. change in CDS spreads.
The chart might seem complicated at first glance but the underlying message is quite straightforward. And that is investors are becoming more nervous about lending money to companies involved in the AI boom.
CoreWeave stands out like a sore thumb, with its CDS spread widening by more than 500 basis points over the observed period. But what exactly does that mean?
The simple way to think about it is to picture CDS as an insurance that investors can buy to protect themselves against a company failing to repay its debt. So, a five-year CDS provides that protection over five years and the spread simply reflects the cost of obtaining it. To give more context, 100 bps equals to 1% annually.
As such, when CoreWeave's actual five-year CDS spread surged to above 1,000 bps last week, that implied roughly $100,000 annually to insure $1 million of debt. Now, that's an enormous premium to pay just to protect yourself against a potential default.
And while CoreWeave is clearly the standout, the chart also shows that the worries aren't confined to just one company. Oracle's five-year CDS has climbed towards 300 bps, while Meta and Nvidia have seen theirs approach 100 bps.
In the case of Oracle, it is being traded like junk credit due to aggressive debt-fueled infrastructure loans. Meanwhile, the five-year CDS level for Meta is near its historic peak so that helps to put things into better perspective. Having said that, I wouldn't put all these companies in the same risk category. Meta and Nvidia clearly have much stronger financial positions and liquidity than CoreWeave for example.
However, it is clear that investors are beginning to question something bigger. And that brings us back to the same question we've been asking all year, that is who is going to pay for the enormous AI infrastructure boom, and how long before those investments generate sufficient returns?
CoreWeave relies heavily on debt to finance data centres and computing infrastructure. Meanwhile, Oracle is also committing massive sums to AI expansion and Meta is also pouring billions into infrastructure. As for Nvidia, their fortunes are very much closely tied to that spending cycle.
The major concern here is that if financing becomes more expensive or AI investment slows, the consequences could spread across companies that depend on one another for revenues, financing and growth.
So, what does this have to do with the bond market and Treasury yields?
Considering the backdrop above, investors are essentially growing more uncomfortable in wanting to hold riskier corporate debt and equities. So, what other options do they have left that pays a safe and good return in this market? Well, the answer is quite simply government bonds. And that pushes Treasury prices higher and yields lower as the demand flows in.
But then, here's the catch though. Even if Treasury yields fall, corporate borrowing costs can still rise when investors demand a bigger premium for taking on credit risk. In other words, safer money is getting cheaper while riskier money is becoming more expensive.
And that might explain why tech stocks aren't able to celebrate the sharp fall in Treasury yields. Investors may be worrying more about financing risks and future profits than the immediate benefit of cheaper government borrowing.
With all that said, AI credit concerns aren't necessarily the only reason Treasuries are rallying. However, they are likely one part of the picture that could be helpful in explaining the market moves we're seeing this week.
I mean, with inflation risks still lingering and oil prices elevated, falling Treasury yields aren't exactly hinting at better economic conditions. It could simply be investors starting to worry that something else might break first instead.

Nifty logs third-longest technical correction; shallowest in its history
The NSE Nifty on Friday marked the 160th trading day below its long-term average, the longest time period since January 2012. The index has been quoting below its 200-DMA since February 27, 2026.
Listen to This Article
The Nifty 50 index on Friday completed its third-longest correction in terms of the number of trading sessions spent below its 200-day moving average (200-DMA), even as the extent of the decline remains relatively shallow compared with previous prolonged market downturns. An analysis of historical data shows that the benchmark index has now spent 160 trading sessions below its long-term average, marking its longest such stretch since January 2012. The Nifty has been quoting below its 200-DMA since February 27, 2026. However, unlike previous extended corrections, the current downturn has seen a relatively limited gap between the index and its 200-DMA. At current levels, the Nifty quotes 6.3 per cent below its 200-DMA, which stands at 24,118.  
 The 200-DMA is a widely tracked technical indicator that helps investors gauge the market trend. An index trading below this level is generally seen as being in a weaker trend and vice-versa. The markets, analysts said, have been impacted by the ongoing geopolitical conflict in West Asia, the exodus of foreign institutional investors (FIIs) from Indian equities, rising crude prices and firming bond yields. That apart, investors have rotated out of large-caps into smaller peers and into the primary markets. The broader market resilience in recent months has been more a function of liquidity than earnings, said V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist, Geojit Investments. ALSO READ: Nifty PSU vs Private Bank: Which banking index looks stronger on charts?  “Strong external headwinds in the form of elevated crude prices and high US bond yields are emboldening bears to build short positions. This is the reason why the market is declining even on days of positive FII and DII buying,” he said. Meanwhile, historical data show that the Nifty has spent at least 150 trading sessions below its 200-DMA on six occasions. The longest such stretch lasted 227 trading sessions, between May 2008 and April 2009, during the global financial crisis triggered by the US subprime mortgage meltdown. The second-longest correction lasted 188 trading sessions on two occasions — between May 2011 and January 2012, and between May and December 2001. 
Shallow correction
Despite its prolonged duration, the current correction stands out for the relatively small magnitude of the Nifty's decline below its long-term moving average. During the ongoing phase, the index's maximum deficit relative to its 200-DMA has been 11.5 per cent, while its average shortfall has stood at 4.5 per cent.
The index, he said, maintains a cautious-to-bearish bias, with the near-term direction likely to depend on its ability to sustain above the 22,800 resistance zone while holding the immediate support around 22,600–22,550.
"On the downside, the 22,600–22,550 range serves as the immediate support zone. A sustained breakdown below 22,500 could intensify selling pressure and drag the index towards the 22,300–22,200 zone," he said.

articles.title: Peso hits one-year low as Fed-Banxico rate gap narrows - Mexico News Daily
articles.summary: Peso hits one-year low as Fed-Banxico rate gap narrows  Mexico News Daily
articles.full_text:
In just seven weeks, the Mexican peso has depreciated nearly 10% against the US dollar, and on Thursday fell to its weakest level against the greenback in over a year.
The Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate on Thursday was 18.71, representing a depreciation of 9.7% for the peso since Sept. 4, when it closed at 16.89 to the dollar — its strongest level in over two years.
The last time the peso closed at a weaker level than 18.71 was on Sept. 4, 2025.
The U.S. Federal Reserve’s decision in mid-September to increase its key interest rate to a target range of 3.75% to 4% is seen as a key factor behind the peso’s recent depreciation as the hike reduced the differential between the Fed’s rate and that of the Bank of Mexico (currently 6.5%). The smaller spread weakened one of the supports of the so-called “super peso,” reducing the appeal of “carry trade” operations.
Other factors have also contributed to the recent depreciation of the peso. They include a greater aversion to risk amid the U.S.-Iran war and uncertainty over the future of the USMCA free trade pact.
Peso’s decline on Thursday was modest, but extended the currency’s slide
The USD:MXN closing rate on Thursday represented a 0.2% depreciation for the peso compared to its position at the end of trading on Wednesday.
The peso has depreciated 1.1% this week after closing at 18.50 to the dollar last Friday, according to the Bank of Mexico.
The depreciation on Thursday came after the national statistics agency INEGI reported that Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate was 3.62% in the first 15 days of October, up from 3.45% in September.
The peso appreciated slightly after the publication of the inflation data on Thursday morning, but it weakened later in the day to close weaker than it did on Wednesday.
The gap between interest rates in Mexico and the US could narrow further soon
While Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate appears likely to increase for a third consecutive month in October, most analysts don’t anticipate that the Bank of Mexico will make any change to its key interest rate following its final two monetary policy meetings for 2026, scheduled for Nov. 5 and Dec. 17.
In contrast, 100 of 100 economists polled by Reuters in recent days expect the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise its interest rate in December. Such a hike would further narrow the gap between the Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate and the Fed’s, potentially weighing on the peso.
Where will the peso be at the end of the year?
The consensus forecast of analysts and economists from 37 banks, brokerages and research organizations who were recently surveyed by Citi is that the USD:MXN rate will be 18.20 at the end of 2026.
Expectations ranged from 16.80 to 18.90, Citi said in an article published on Tuesday.
The bank noted that the consensus forecast increased to 18.20 from 18.00 in its previous “Mexico Expectations Survey.”

articles.title: Yen jumps as oil, AI and France worries rattle markets - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Yen jumps as oil, AI and France worries rattle markets  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
By Karen Brettell
NEW YORK, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The yen was on track for its strongest daily gain in almost a month on Thursday, as investors sought safety amid fragile equity markets, elevated crude prices from the drawn-out war in the Middle East, and doubts over future returns from artificial intelligence.
The US dollar, meanwhile, rose against the euro. Worries about social unrest in France and a worsening fiscal outlook for the country outweighed concerns about the AI trade, which pushed US stocks lower.
"AI is making people nervous, as is oil ... and as is France," said Chris Scicluna, head of economic research at Daiwa Capital Markets.
Oil prices climbed about 3% to a five-month high after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region.
The Japanese yen strengthened 0.75% to 156.96 per dollar.
Some of the move in the yen may also be due to its approaching the key 160 level, which is seen as increasing the odds of further intervention by Japanese authorities to shore up the currency.
Kevin Ford, lead FX and macro strategist at Convera, called it "the intervention premium," noting that "every time the yen gets closer to the 160 line, that's where there's higher speculation that the central bank will intervene."
Against the Swiss franc, another traditional safe haven, the dollar weakened 0.42% to 0.821 francs per dollar.
The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.08% to 101.60, with the euro down 0.09% at $1.1222.
The dollar has become increasingly tied to capital flows and to growth and inflation expectations linked to the AI trade. It fell last week as fears over the AI outlook grew. On Thursday, however, concerns about France outweighed those fears.
"You have these competing stories and weak points between US AI-related credits and then France's sovereign credit, and we've seen this push and pull in the last couple of days where at times one is more of a concern than the other," said Erik Nelson, global head of FX strategy at Wells Fargo. "As long as France is more of a concern than US AI credits, then you're going to see the euro underperform."
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that "illegitimate" protests would be banned in the coming days and blamed "seditious" ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend's riots and looting.
Concerns about France's ability to manage its huge debt burden have hurt French government bonds and raised worries about other heavily indebted euro zone countries. The spread between France and Germany's 10-year note yields reached 177.7 basis points on Thursday, the widest gap since 2011.
Sterling strengthened 0.05% to $1.3401. The Australian dollar weakened 0.11% to $0.7019.
In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 4.27% to $81,023.
(Additional reporting by Amanda Cooper and Tom Westbrook; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria and Andrea Ricci )

articles.title: ECB caught in the French drama - ing think
articles.summary: ECB caught in the French drama  ing think
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank meeting on 29 October is not expected to result in an interest rate hike. Instead, the French crisis is increasingly eroding the need for additional rate hikes
Back in September, the ECB surprised markets with a more hawkish message, at least between the lines. With headline inflation higher for longer and core inflation expected to increase in 2027, the stage seemed set for at least one more rate hike at the December meeting. Some even speculated about a back-to-back increase in October.
One month later, and after a severe fiscal and political crisis in France, the ECB is unlikely to repeat the hawkish tone at next week’s meeting. At face value, macro developments since the last meeting would still justify another rate hike. Headline inflation increased again in September and most leading indicators point to continued resilience in the eurozone economy. However, the surge in bond yields on the back of the French crisis is already imposing a new restrictive monetary policy stance. In fact, the surge in German bond yields since the September meeting has already had roughly the same impact on growth and inflation as an additional 25bp rate hike. For France, it's closer to a 50bp hike. Or in other words, the bond market has taken over the ECB’s job.
All of this means that the ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December. This is when new staff projections will be available and when there will also be more insights into whether higher energy prices will eventually bring knock-on effects on the rest of the economy or not. In fact, there are three main parameters that, in our view, will determine the ECB’s path going forward: i) the length and intensity of the war in the Middle East. The longer oil prices remain elevated, the higher the probability of more rate hikes; ii) the knock-on effects of higher energy prices. So far, there has hardly been any pass-through of higher energy prices in the rest of the economy. If this remains the case, the need for further rate hikes drops. If it doesn’t, the likelihood of new rate hikes goes up. iii) France. Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely (and less needed).
Because it's France
Even if France does not play a role in the ECB’s policy statement next week, it will be an important element at the press conference. Political and fiscal concerns in France, and the resulting widening in French spreads, have raised questions about whether the ECB could intervene through the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which allows it to purchase securities issued by member states whose financing conditions have deteriorated for reasons not justified by country-specific fundamentals. However, before activating it, the Governing Council considers a cumulative set of criteria to determine whether the countries concerned are pursuing sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies. In practice, this includes compliance with the EU fiscal framework, which would, at a minimum, require the proposed French budget to be fully adopted.
The ECB has nevertheless left itself some discretion, stating that the intervention criteria “will be dynamically adjusted to the unfolding risks and conditions to be addressed”. This brings back memories of the famous “because it’s France” by former European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker. Generally speaking, the ECB will be in a difficult position: intervening too quickly in support of France may be viewed unfavourably by other member states and interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules. That argues strongly against early intervention. Also, don’t forget that the leadership changes at the ECB over the next months (Schnabel, Lane, Lagarde) could also affect how the ECB views TPI.
Given the challenges of justifying the activation of TPI at present, we expect the ECB to adopt a three-pronged approach to address the French crisis.
- The first line of defence is a more dovish approach to policy rates. As bond markets are currently taking over the ECB’s job of inserting a more restrictive monetary stance on the economy, there is less need for the ECB to hike rates aggressively, or to hike rates at all. In fact, the ECB has already started to prepare for this option, as ECB president Christine Lagarde recently noted that “while growth has been resilient, since our last meeting long-term interest rates have risen notably, which will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise".
- The second line of defence would be a covert return to bond purchases. The ECB could instead pause quantitative tightening temporarily and reinvest maturing bonds in its portfolio 'flexibly', sending a positive signal to bond markets. This had already happened during the Covid period.
- Last but not least, should contagion in eurozone bond markets intensify, we expect the ECB to eventually trigger the TPI. As long as France remains non-compliant with the European fiscal rules, the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France.
All in all, next week’s ECB meeting looks set to be uneventful on action but clearly not on words.

articles.title: UK Inflation Hits 3.5% as Jackdaw Gas Gets Approval Ahead of Budget - EBC Financial Group
articles.summary: UK Inflation Hits 3.5% as Jackdaw Gas Gets Approval Ahead of Budget  EBC Financial Group
articles.full_text:
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September 2026, up from 3.1% in August, as motor fuel prices climbed at their fastest annual pace since 2022. Hours later, the government approved production at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, where first gas could arrive before the end of October.
Jackdaw is expected to add to domestic gas supplies this winter, although ministers acknowledged that the project would not reduce household energy bills. Meanwhile, September government borrowing reached £24.5 billion and central government debt interest hit £10.9 billion, adding fiscal pressure ahead of the 28 October Budget.
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, its highest since October 2025.
Motor fuel prices rose 29.8% year on year, with petrol averaging 169.5p and diesel 192.5p per litre.
Core CPI rose to 2.8%, while services inflation increased to 3.7%.
Jackdaw received approval on 21 October and could lift UK gas output by 6% at peak, but is not expected to lower household bills.
September borrowing of £24.5bn and debt interest of £10.9bn exceeded forecasts, while net debt passed £3 trillion.
The 28 October Budget and 5 November BoE decision are next, with Bank Rate currently at 3.75%.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) put CPI at 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, above the 3.4% consensus and the highest rate since October 2025. Transport contributed the most to annual inflation, adding 0.94 percentage points to the overall CPI rate. Motor fuel prices rose 29.8% over the year, compared with 23.0% in August.
Petrol averaged 169.5 pence per litre in September, its highest since August 2022, while diesel reached 192.5 pence, a level last recorded in July 2022. Both prices rose amid disruptions to global oil markets following the Middle East conflict that began in late February 2026.
Price pressures extended beyond fuel. Core CPI rose to 2.8% and services inflation to 3.7%, while goods inflation reached 3.2%, its highest since September 2023. Food inflation remained unchanged at 1.3%.
| CPI Measure (Annual %) | August 2026 | September 2026 | 
|---|---|---|
| Headline CPI | 3.1% | 3.5% | 
| Core CPI | 2.6% | 2.8% | 
| Services | 3.4% | 3.7% | 
| Goods | 2.7% | 3.2% | 
| Transport | 4.6% | 6.6% | 
| Motor fuels | 23.0% | 29.8% | 
| Housing and household services | 4.9% | 5.3% | 
| Food and non-alcoholic drinks | 1.3% | 1.3% | 
Source: ONS, Consumer price inflation, UK: September 2026, released 21 October 2026.
The North Sea Transition Authority granted development and production consent for Jackdaw on 21 October, after Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh agreed the regulator could proceed. The field sits approximately 250km east of Aberdeen and connects to the existing Shearwater hub.
Operator Adura can now proceed towards production, with first gas possible before the end of October. At peak output, Jackdaw is expected to increase UK gas production by approximately 6%, with a field lifespan of up to 11 years.
Energy Minister Michael Shanks told Parliament that Jackdaw would not lower household energy bills, a position the Energy Secretary reiterated in a broadcast interview. UK wholesale gas prices remain linked to international markets, limiting the effect of additional domestic production on consumer prices.
September’s inflation acceleration was driven largely by petrol, diesel and kerosene, all refined from crude oil, while Jackdaw produces natural gas and condensate. Housing and household services inflation nevertheless reached 5.3% in September, before the latest quarterly energy price cap increase took effect on 1 October.
The government has positioned Jackdaw as an energy-security measure that could reduce reliance on imported gas. Alongside the approval, Chancellor John Healey announced a £2 billion Energy Wealth Fund, initially financed by government funding and designed to receive future North Sea tax revenues for investment in renewable and low-carbon energy projects.
Public sector net borrowing reached £24.5 billion in September, £1.9 billion above the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) forecast and the second-highest September figure on record.
Central government debt interest payable totalled £10.9 billion, 16.6% more than a year earlier and £2 billion above forecast. Borrowing for the financial year to September exceeded the OBR’s forecast by £6 billion.
Of September’s debt interest bill, £4 billion reflected accrued capital uplift on index-linked gilts, largely attributable to Retail Prices Index (RPI) movements between June and July rather than September’s inflation reading.
The £4 billion represents accrued index-linked interest, payable at redemption rather than as a cash payment during September. Annual RPI inflation stood at 3.9% in September, with future index movements affecting the government’s debt-servicing liabilities.
Public sector net debt also exceeded £3 trillion for the first time, reaching £3,005 billion. However, the provisional debt-to-GDP ratio stood at 94.0%, slightly below its year-earlier level. Borrowing above forecast adds pressure to the government’s fiscal plans ahead of the Budget.
| Public Finances, September 2026 | Figure | Comparison | 
|---|---|---|
| Public sector net borrowing | £24.5bn | £1.9bn above OBR forecast | 
| Central government debt interest | £10.9bn | £2.0bn above forecast, up 16.6% annually | 
| RPI capital uplift within that interest | £4.0bn | Accrued index-linked gilt interest | 
| Public sector net debt | £3,005bn | First reading above £3 trillion | 
| Net debt to GDP | 94.0% | Below year-earlier ratio | 
Source: ONS, Public sector finances, UK: September 2026, released 21 October 2026.
The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75% on 17 September by six votes to three, with three members supporting an increase to 4%. Its next decision is scheduled for 5 November, alongside a new Monetary Policy Report.
September’s CPI figures are the final inflation release before that meeting, with October’s data due on 18 November. Markets had already priced a quarter-point increase to 4% as highly likely before the release, while a Reuters survey on 15 October found that 54 of 63 economists expected that outcome.
Services inflation reached 3.7% after Governor Andrew Bailey said on 16 October he had seen limited evidence of the energy shock spreading into wages and broader domestic prices.
Expectations for further tightening in December nevertheless eased after the release. FXStreet reported that the implied probability of another increase fell to about 48% from 58% as investors weighed persistent inflation against weaker consumer demand.
Jackdaw’s approval is unlikely to materially affect near-term rate expectations, given its production timetable and the UK’s continued exposure to international gas prices.
Sterling showed little reaction to the inflation surprise, with GBP/USD trading near $1.34 on 21 October after touching a session low around $1.3364. With a November rate hike already heavily priced in, stronger inflation figures offered little additional support for the pound. The above-forecast borrowing figures also kept fiscal concerns in focus.
UK government bonds rallied across the yield curve. The 10-year gilt yield closed near 5.38%, down approximately five basis points, after trading around 5.36% intraday. The 30-year yield finished near 5.79%, retreating further from the 6% threshold breached earlier in October.
The yield declines coincided with reduced expectations for a December Bank Rate increase, despite stronger September inflation. Longer-dated gilts remain sensitive to the government’s borrowing requirements and prospective issuance.
Attention now turns to the Budget on 28 October and the Bank of England’s 5 November decision. The government’s updated fiscal plans and the central bank’s inflation assessment will provide the next major tests for sterling and UK government bonds.

articles.title: Euro Approaches 920 Pesos as Dollar Hits New High in Cuba's Informal Market - CubaHeadlines
articles.summary: Euro Approaches 920 Pesos as Dollar Hits New High in Cuba's Informal Market  CubaHeadlines
articles.full_text:
As of 8:00 PM Cuban local time, the informal currency market in Cuba closed this Friday with the U.S. dollar and the euro experiencing gains. Both currencies ended the day surpassing their previous session values, while the MLC showed a notable decline, though this should be cautiously interpreted due to the limited volume of transactions.
The U.S. dollar wrapped up the day at 830 Cuban pesos (CUP), reflecting an increase of 3.5 CUP from the previous session's 827 CUP. Over the past week, the dollar has surged by 27.5 CUP, rising from 803 CUP just seven days ago, marking a 3.4% increase.
When compared to the past month, the current rate stands 105.5 CUP higher than the levels recorded at the end of September, though this change may partially reflect methodological adjustments in the index.
Throughout the last month, the dollar has fluctuated between a low of 725 CUP and today's high of 830 CUP, highlighting its influence in the informal market amid a persistent currency shortage.
Euro's Climb in the Cuban Market
The euro ended the day at 919 CUP, up from 915 CUP the previous day, marking an increase of 3.5 CUP. Over the past week, the euro has climbed 21 CUP from 898 CUP, representing a 2.3% rise.
In the last 30 days, the euro has gained 93 CUP. However, similar to the dollar, this figure should be approached with caution as it could include methodological adjustments.
Today's closing at 919 CUP is the highest in the last month, surpassing the dollar by 89 CUP, reinforcing its dominant position in Cuba's parallel market.
MLC's Volatile Position
The MLC ended the day trading at approximately 570 CUP, though this figure is indicative given the low transaction volume. Compared to the previous day, the MLC dropped by 105.5 CUP, a 15.6% decrease.
Over the last week, it has fallen 61.5 CUP from 632 CUP seven days ago. Over the past month, it has fluctuated between a low of 457 CUP and a high of 742 CUP, illustrating the volatility and irregularity of its market. Without physical existence, its use is restricted to state-run stores that accept it, limiting its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Exchange Rates and Economic Impact
The exchange rate for the U.S. dollar to CUP stands at 830 CUP. The euro is at 919 CUP, while the MLC is at 570 CUP (indicative value, limited data). The official exchange rate set by the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III) is significantly lower, at 738 CUP per dollar and 827 CUP per euro, highlighting the persistent foreign currency scarcity in the state banking system and the high demand for dollars and euros among the population, whether for emigration, importing goods, protecting savings, or making private sector purchases.
In an environment of sustained inflation, low state salaries, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, each fluctuation in the informal market directly impacts internal prices and Cubans' purchasing power.
With the informal dollar at 830 CUP compared to the official 738 CUP, the 92 CUP disparity per unit imposes a real penalty on those without access to foreign currencies through state channels, which, in practice, includes the vast majority of the population.

articles.title: Euro Falls for Third Straight Day vs. Dollar as French Fiscal Worries, Crude Oil Surge Weigh; NY Close at $1.1202 - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Euro Falls for Third Straight Day vs. Dollar as French Fiscal Worries, Crude Oil Surge Weigh; NY Close at $1.1202  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
In the New York foreign exchange market on the 23rd, the euro fell against the dollar for a third consecutive session. The closing level of $1.1202 per euro represented roughly a $0.0014 move toward a weaker euro and stronger dollar from the previous New York close of $1.1216. Uncertainty over French politics and fiscal policy, combined with a crude oil surge driven by escalating Middle East tensions, prompted euro selling, and during the Tokyo afternoon session the pair briefly hit the day's low of $1.1185. After the New York session opened, the euro pared some losses to around $1.1212, but the rebound was limited. Rising U.S. long-term yields and the final October reading of the University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index, which came in at 48.0 versus a market forecast of 46.3, weighed on the market and pushed the pair back into the upper $1.11 range.
Closing levels for major currency pairs were as follows:
| Currency Pair | NY Close on 23rd | Previous NY Close | Change | 
|---|---|---|---|
| EUR/USD | $1.1202 | $1.1216 | About $0.0014 toward weaker euro | 
| Dollar-yen | 156.87 yen | 156.77 yen | About 10 sen toward stronger dollar | 
| EUR/JPY | 175.72 yen | 175.84 yen | About 12 sen toward weaker euro | 
Note: Figures are compared with the previous business day's New York market close.
The dollar-yen pair rebounded slightly for the first time in four business days, closing at 156.87 yen. Yen buying and dollar selling led early, with the pair briefly falling to around 156.32 yen before 10 p.m. as European equities and Japanese and U.S. stock futures declined. However, once the day's low of 156.08 yen set during the Tokyo morning session was seen as a support line, buying back gained the upper hand, and yen selling and dollar buying tied to rising U.S. long-term yields lifted the pair to around 157.08 yen. Stronger-than-expected U.S. economic data also underpinned the market.
EUR/JPY fell for a third consecutive session, closing at 175.72 yen. Shortly after 10 p.m., it briefly touched 175.10 yen, its lowest level in about a year since October of last year, but buying linked to the dollar-yen's recovery pared losses to around 175.83 yen. The day's reference ranges were 156.08–157.16 yen for dollar-yen, $1.1185–$1.1226 for EUR/USD, and 175.10–176.22 yen for EUR/JPY.
Behind the euro selling are concerns over French fiscal policy. Amid uncertainty over the outcome of the 2027 French Presidential Election and the outlook for deliberations on a budget plan aimed at reducing the fiscal deficit, the French 10-year bond yield briefly rose to the 5.1% range during the previous day's trading on the 22nd, marking its highest level in about 24 years since 2002. Euro selling led in the foreign exchange market, and in the New York session on the 22nd the pair briefly hit a session low of $1.1189 shortly before 11:30 p.m. The preliminary October eurozone consumer confidence reading, which came in at -17.9 versus a market forecast of -17.0, also weighed on the market.
Still, the euro's downside was limited. On the previous day, the 22nd, selling ran its course and the decline stalled; when the U.S. 10-Year Treasury Yield, a benchmark for U.S. long-term rates, fell below the 5% threshold and briefly hit the 4.93% range, its lowest in about a month, dollar selling gradually took over and the euro pared its losses to around $1.1231. In the Tokyo market on the 23rd as well, euro selling led after France's preliminary October manufacturing and services Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) readings both came in below market forecasts, but the pair found a floor once the previous day's low of $1.1189 was seen as near-term support.
France's fiscal deterioration is easily perceived as an issue directly tied to confidence in the euro currency. Rising government bond yields in France, the eurozone's second-largest economy, reduce the relative appeal of euro-denominated assets as a benchmark for regional interest rates. Meanwhile, the direction of U.S. long-term yields continues to drive the dollar's trajectory, and the battle over the 5% threshold is amplifying swings in EUR/USD in both directions. The crude oil surge is seen as a factor worsening the trade balance of the eurozone, which is highly dependent on energy imports, and is capping the euro's upside.
Many market participants expect the outcome of France's budget deliberations and the level of U.S. interest rates to be the near-term focus. That EUR/JPY is trading near a one-year low suggests risk-averse flows of yen buying and euro selling continue. Depending on upcoming European and U.S. economic indicators and headlines on the Middle East situation, the euro's downward trend could strengthen further.

articles.title: Treasury Yields Snapshot: October 23, 2026 - Advisor Perspectives
articles.summary: Treasury Yields Snapshot: October 23, 2026  Advisor Perspectives
articles.full_text:
The yield on the 10-year note finished October 23, 2026 at 5.00% while the 2-year note ended at 4.69%.
The chart below overlays the daily performance of several Treasury bonds, starting from the pre-recession equity market peaks, along with the Federal Funds Rate (FFR) since 2007.
This next table shows the highs and lows of yields and the Federal Funds Rate (FFR) since 2007.
A Long-Term Look at the 10-Year Treasury Yield
Here is a long-term view of the 10-year yield starting in 1965, well before the 1973 oil embargo that triggered the era of 'stagflation' (economic stagnation coupled with inflation)
Inverted Yield Curve
An inverted yield curve is when longer-term Treasury yields are lower than their shorter term counterparts. The next chart displays the latest 10-2 spread. Typically, the spread turns negative for a period before rising again prior to recessions, as illustrated in the four recessions shown on this chart. For this reason, the 10-2 spread is widely considered a reliable leading indicator for recessions. The lead time between a negative spread and the onset of a recession varies, with recessions beginning anywhere from 18 to 92 weeks after the spread goes negative.
One false positive is seen in 1998, where the spread briefly went negative without leading to a recession. In the case of the 2009 recession, the spread went negative multiple times before rising again. Most recently, the spread was continuously negative from July 5, 2022, to August 26, 2024. The last time the spread was negative was on September 5, 2024.
If we consider the first negative spread date as the starting point, the average lead time to a recession is 48 weeks, or about eleven months. If we instead use the last positive spread date before a recession, the average lead time is 18.5 weeks, or about 4.25 months.
For another perspective on the yield curve, the 10-3mo spread below uses an even shorter-term maturity. The lead time to recessions based on this spread (after it turns negative) ranges from 34 to 69 weeks. Like the 10-2 spread, we see the same false positive in 1998, as well as multiple instances of the spread turning negative before rising again ahead of the 2009 recession. Recently, the spread was negative from October 25, 2022 to December 12, 2024. Since February 26th the spread has swung back and forth from positive to negative territory.
If we consider the first negative spread date as the starting point, the average lead time to a recession is 48 weeks, or about eleven months. If we instead use the last positive spread date after the spread had been negative, the average lead time is 13 weeks, or about three months.
The 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage
The Federal Funds Rate influences the cost of borrowing for banks. When the Fed increases this rate, banks often raise their lending rates, which can impact mortgage rates, among other things. Therefore, a rising FFR generally leads to higher mortgage rates, and vice versa. However, this was not the case recently when the Fed began their rate cutting cycle in September 2024 and mortgage rates moved in the opposite direction. With that said, mortgage rates have been on the decline as of late, following a similar fashion of the FFR. The latest Freddie Mac Weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed rate at 7.32%, down slightly from last week.
Now let's see the 10-year against the S&P 500 with some notes on Federal Reserve intervention. Fed policy has been a major influence on market behavior.

articles.full_text: Federal farm safety-net payments are expected to reach a record $13.8 billion for the 2025 crop year, reflecting the growing importance of government assistance to American agricultural producers. USDA says payments through the Agriculture Risk Coverage and Price Loss Coverage programs will be the largest since Congress established them in the 2014 farm bill. The programs provide financial protection when commodity prices or farm revenues fall below established thresholds. USDA says the payments cover eligible crops including corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, rice and peanuts. The department cautions that the $13.8 billion estimate represents gross payments before applicable reductions. articles.title: What To Expect From Wednesday’s Federal Reserve Meeting - Investopedia
articles.summary: What To Expect From Wednesday’s Federal Reserve Meeting  Investopedia
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- The Federal Reserve’s policy committee is likely to keep its key interest rate flat when it meets to set monetary policy on Wednesday.
- Economists expect the Fed to raise interest rates at future meetings to combat high inflation, but say there is no rush to raise them for a second consecutive meeting following September’s rate hike.
- Higher interest rates push up borrowing costs on all kinds of loans and can dampen inflation but risk slowing down the economy.
Federal Reserve officials are widely expected to leave the central bank’s key interest rate unchanged when they meet on Wednesday, signaling patience in their fight against inflation.
Financial markets were pricing in a one-in-ten chance that policymakers on the Federal Open Market Committee will vote to raise the fed funds rate by a quarter-point when they meet Wednesday, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool, which forecasts rate movements based on fed funds futures trading data.1
In recent weeks, Fed officials have publicly discussed whether to follow up on September’s quarter-point rate hike to counter higher-than-expected inflation. Although some Fed officials have voiced concerns, others have advocated a wait-and-see approach.
A higher fed funds rate means higher borrowing costs on all kinds of loans, which could discourage spending and subdue inflation. But it could also drag on the job market and the economy overall.
The Fed is balancing its dual mandate from Congress to keep inflation low and employment high. With inflation running above the Fed’s inflation goal for a fifth year and unemployment hovering near historic lows, most experts expect the Fed to raise interest rates again in December even if they forego an October hike.
“All signs are that the Federal Reserve will need to continue lifting interest rates in the near term, yet comments from a few key officials suggest they’re unlikely to do so at the October policy meeting,” Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a commentary.
What This Means For The Economy
If the Fed pauses its rate hike campaign in October, it would allow officials more time to assess how much the Iran war’s fuel price hikes are pushing up inflation before taking action again.
Recent comments from two key FOMC members—Fed Governor Michelle Bowman and John C. Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York—suggested they didn’t favor rate hikes at back-to-back meetings.
The recent Fed remarks indicated that most officials will support hiking rates by a quarter point at every other meeting, which would mean the next two rate hikes will take place in December and March, David Mericle, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs, wrote in a commentary.
Related Education
Aside from the interest rate decision, the main point of interest from the Fed meeting Wednesday will be Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference. If he sticks to form, however, he will avoid giving hints about future monetary policy decisions. Unlike previous Fed chairs, Warsh has stuck to a policy of not giving “forward guidance” to financial markets.
Still, Warsh’s words, however cryptic, could offer some clues.
“Chair Warsh is unlikely to offer any direct forward guidance in his press conference, but we expect he will implicitly endorse a December rate hike,” Ruchir Sharma, an economist at Nomura, wrote in a commentary. “His characterization of recent inflation data and market financial conditions could provide some clues around the threshold for additional tightening in 2027.”

articles.title: Anthropic Is Racing to Price Its IPO Before the Thanksgiving Dealmaking Freeze - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: Anthropic Is Racing to Price Its IPO Before the Thanksgiving Dealmaking Freeze  The Motley FoolWhat some of Anthropic’s backers are worth before its IPO  Yahoo FinanceAnthropic logged net loss of over $80 billion in first half of 2026  ReutersThe Story of Anthropic’s Cap Table: VCs Showed Up Late to the Party, Toting All the Cash They Could Wrangle  Newcomer | SubstackAnthropic’s Elevator Problem: Persuading Investors to Share Its AI Dream  The I...
articles.full_text:
Anthropic is gearing up for one of the largest initial public offerings (IPOs) in history, and its public debut could make waves across the broader stock market. Investors probably won't have to wait long for the company's IPO and the resulting fervor.
The company is reportedly aiming to carry out its public debut before Thanksgiving, getting ahead of the informal freeze on dealmaking that tends to immediately precede and follow the holiday. While it's possible that the public debut could slip into early December, itself a popular window for companies going public, signs point to the company conducting its IPO in mid-November.
Will Anthropic become the biggest IPO in history?
In June, Space Exploration Technologies had its IPO and listed its first batch of publicly available stock at a price of $135 per share. The listing price valued the company at $1.77 trillion -- a level that made SpaceX's IPO the largest ever. While there were expectations that Anthropic would price its stock at a level that would value the company at roughly $2 trillion and set a new valuation record, that's now looking less likely.
Following some recent volatility for the broader market, concerns about valuations in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, and updates on Anthropic's business momentum, many analysts expect the company to debut at a valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion. Some estimates suggest that the company could be valued as low as $1.2 trillion at its IPO.
According to a leaked draft version of the company's IPO prospectus, Anthropic generated roughly $16.3 billion in sales across this year's first half -- up from sales of roughly $1.1 billion across the same period last year. That's incredible growth and reflects surging demand for the company's Claude AI software suite, which offers top-tier tools for coding, analysis, and other forms of content generation. On the other hand, the business posted a loss of roughly $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026.
Investors also took a measured approach to reports about the company's third-quarter performance, which suggested that sales in the period had increased 45% on a sequential basis to reach $16.8 billion. While that still represents an incredible rate of growth, some analysts had been expecting the rate of expansion to be even stronger given the momentum across the first half of the year.
Even though Anthropic is unlikely to dethrone SpaceX in terms of IPO size, there's still a good chance that the company will conduct a successful public debut next month. With the company using lots of cash as it spends on compute resources and scales rapidly, going public will provide the AI leader with an influx of capital that can be used to fuel its growth.

articles.title: Downgrade by Fitch Ratings the latest setback for JTA - Jacksonville Daily Record
articles.summary: Downgrade by Fitch Ratings the latest setback for JTA  Jacksonville Daily Record
articles.full_text:
A downgrade in the Jacksonville Transportation Authority’s credit rating will not have immediate financial repercussions for the authority but will further damage its reputation among investors, JTA Chief Financial Officer Randall Barnes said Oct. 23.
Speaking to the City Council Financial Audit and Oversight Committee, Barnes noted that Fitch Ratings dropped JTA two spots, from AA+ to AA-, skipping a AA rating on the way down. Due to JTA’s financial insecurities, the move was to be expected, Barnes said.
“They did cite diminished financial resilience and management practices that reflect weak budgeting practices and controls. I think that’s been pretty apparent as we’ve gone throughout this process over the last few weeks and months,” Barnes told the committee. “Our reserve balances have been depleted and our cash balances are low, and we haven’t done a great job of managing our budget.”
Fitch’s credit rating is not directly tied to any of JTA’s debt, Barnes said, meaning that the change would not immediately affect the authority’s borrowing costs. JTA recently took out a $25 million line of credit to pay down its bills, and then took a $30 million loan from its Local Option Gas Tax revenue to pay down that line of credit.
“That’s the important thing for investors: The issuer default rating is really just an overall view of JTA’s financial position, essentially,” Barnes said. “While the rating down there obviously is never good, Double A minus is still a good rating.”
Barnes also said the work JTA is doing with the city, as well as an independent auditor it will contract, would be viewed positively by ratings agencies.
After finishing fiscal year 2025 with an $18.9 million shortfall, JTA projected a $39 million deficit heading into its fiscal year 2027 budget. To address it, the authority announced plans to cut services and lay off nearly 200 employees.
Barnes’ statements to the committee come as Council members, city staff and JTA work to find out what led to the authority’s financial crisis.

articles.title: Weak cobalt pricing sentiment across Antaike and LME Week - Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.summary: Weak cobalt pricing sentiment across Antaike and LME Week  Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.full_text:
Cobalt market participants at the recent Antaike Nickel and Cobalt Forum (13–15 October) and LME Week (19–23 October) events in China and London respectively have uniformly reported weak pricing sentiment. This is driven by soft LCO demand and large stocks of cobalt sulphate, precursor cathode active material (pCAM) and recycled material in China. Huayou, Greatpower, Tengyuan and CTT have halted metal production, while Greatpower’s salt line is running at only 20% utilisation.
Several sources told Benchmark they expect the DRC to cut export quotas by 25% next year, with some traders anticipating an announcement in late October or early November, whilst others are expecting intervention in January or February 2027.
“A 25% quota cut would land on a market that is already well supplied with intermediates, so the price response will depend on how quickly Chinese stocks are drawn down,” said George Ingall, senior analyst at Benchmark.
Black mass emerges as key feedstock
Chinese sulphate producers increasingly rely on recycled material, and several sources told Benchmark the cheapest sulphate in the market comes from black mass, with most estimates of recycled cobalt supply sitting between 30kt–45kt per year.
During Antaike’s Forum, European cobalt metal prices sat at $21–23/lb, which was well above the $16–17/lb heard in China. During LME Week, the European market corrected down, with transactions heard in the range of $17.5-19.5/lb. Market participants also tempered hopes that Indonesia can fill any DRC shortfall, with expectations voiced of Indonesian MHP output of 40–50kt rather than the 60–70kt expected in China.
Dislocation raises demand for transparent reference prices
“With prices this fragmented, reliable reference points matter more than ever,” Ingall said.

The anchor book saw participation from marquee global institutional investors, including Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, one of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds managed by Norges Bank Investment Management, and global asset manager Schroders. Domestic mutual funds accounted for a significant share of the anchor allocation, with all five of India’s largest mutual fund houses — HDFC Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, SBI Mutual Fund, Nippon India Mutual Fund and Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund — participating in the book.

The Rs 1,200-crore IPO of EAAA India Alternatives is entirely an offer for sale (OFS), through which promoter Edelweiss Securities and Investments Private Limited will divest 72.07 lakh shares. The company will not receive any proceeds from the issue, with the proceeds accruing to the selling promoter.
The IPO has a price band of Rs 1,585-1,665 per share and will remain open for subscription from October 26 to October 28.
Axis Capital, Jefferies, Motilal Oswal and Nuvama are the book-running lead managers to the issue. Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas, Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas and Linklaters are among the legal advisers associated with the offering.
About EAAA India Alternatives
EAAA India Alternatives is an alternative investment management platform focused on India’s real assets and private credit markets. The company manages investment funds and provides alternative investment solutions to domestic and global institutional investors, high-net-worth individuals, ultra-high-net-worth individuals and family offices.
Its operations are organised primarily across two verticals — Real Assets and Private Credit — alongside portfolio management services and other investment solutions.
The Real Assets business invests in infrastructure, commercial real estate, perpetual capital and energy transition opportunities through equity, quasi-equity and debt instruments. Its Private Credit business provides financing across performing credit, special situations, real estate credit and investment-grade credit. The platform also offers co-investment opportunities through portfolio management services.

Summary
