articles.title: Fed may hold in October, but analysts see a tougher call ahead - Invezz
articles.summary: Fed may hold in October, but analysts see a tougher call ahead  Invezz
articles.full_text:
powered by
If oil stays elevated and the Fed is forced to “tighten into a supply shock,” the economy slows while energy-related costs remain sticky. That combination typically supports energy infrastructure and services demand (maintenance, production support, logistics) even as broad growth cools. Buy XES to capture persistent energy capex/opex and resilience versus cyclicals.
Key Risk: A fast oil normalization (geopolitics de-escalate or supply disruption reverses) that drives crude back toward ~$80 and crushes energy services pricing power.
Warsh is signaling no forward guidance, and the Fed is likely to keep the door open to December tightening because core inflation is still running hot and oil-driven inflation may be feeding broader prices. With the October meeting lacking fresh dot plots, markets will keep repricing the path higher on any hawkish wording, pushing yields up. Short IEF (or sell 2Y futures) to benefit from higher front-end rates.
Key Risk: Warsh clearly emphasizes employment risk and signals December is unlikely, causing a sharp drop in front-end yields.
- Futures price an 86% chance of an October hold; December remains uncertain.
- Economists disagree on whether oil pressures justify tightening as hiring weakens.
- Warsh’s refusal to guide markets puts the statement and vote under scrutiny.
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged next week, but the decision may offer little clarity on what comes next.
With inflation running above target, oil prices elevated and hiring showing signs of weakness, policymakers face competing reasons to tighten further or wait.
Futures-based estimates of CME FedWatch probabilities put the chance of a hold at 88%, against 12% for a quarter-point increase.
The Fed’s October 27-28 meeting follows its September rate increase, which came amid renewed inflation pressures.
A UBS note published October 19 also identified an unchanged October rate as its base case, followed by measured further tightening.
The firm said markets were pricing a more aggressive tightening path than it expected.
But the central question is not simply whether the Fed will hold next week.
Investors will be looking to Chair Kevin Warsh for clues about conditions that could prompt another increase in December, and whether the central bank is giving enough weight to employment risks.
Warsh’s communication strategy leaves markets guessing
Warsh has made clear that he does not intend to provide the kind of forward guidance used by previous Fed chairs.
Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, he said: “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”
That approach is likely to make the statement, voting record, and press conference particularly important.
The October meeting will not include a new Summary of Economic Projections, which is published at selected meetings, leaving investors without an updated set of interest-rate projections.
Tracy Shuchart, Senior Economist at NinjaTrader, expects limited guidance from Warsh.
“He has been consistent since he took the chair that the Fed is out of the forward guidance business, he doesn’t prejudge meetings, and he still won’t submit a dot,” the economist told Invezz.
“Expect the same on the 28th. Anyone waiting for him to tee up December is going to be disappointed.”
Patrick Boyle, a visiting professor of finance and former hedge fund manager, said the wording of the statement could take on greater significance in the absence of forward guidance.
He suggested investors watch how the Fed characterizes the labour market.
A shift in its language from describing conditions as “solid” to saying they have “softened” could indicate that policymakers view the weak September employment report as more than temporary noise.
The voting record could also provide clues. Boyle noted that September’s decision was unanimous and said a dissent in either direction would offer insight into the committee’s debate over December.
JoAnne Bianco, Senior Investment Strategist at BondBloxx, similarly said markets should focus less on the immediate decision and more on whether the Fed leaves the door open to additional tightening.
“The more important question is whether Chair Kevin Warsh characterizes inflation as a temporary setback or evidence that policy needs to become more restrictive,” she told Invezz.
Oil prices raise questions about the source of inflation
The expected decision to hold rates comes against a difficult inflation backdrop.
US consumer prices rose 0.6% in September from a month earlier, lifting the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% from 3.4%.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually, up from 2.4% in August.
Bureau of Labor Statistics data also showed that gasoline prices rose 9.1% in September.
Producer prices added to the concerns. The UBS note said September’s 1.3% monthly increase was the largest in four and a half years, exceeding the 0.5% consensus forecast.
Although energy accounted for much of the increase, UBS noted that prices rose across a broader range of goods and services.
Brent crude was trading near $113 a barrel on Friday, October 23, after a surge linked to renewed concerns about Middle East supply disruptions.
The challenge for the Fed is that higher interest rates cannot directly resolve a disruption to oil supplies.
Raising borrowing costs may instead weaken demand and economic activity, even as households and businesses face higher energy bills.
Shuchart said the Fed has repeatedly treated oil price shocks as transitory and indicated that monetary policy should look through them.
But she argued that September’s inflation report made that approach harder to sustain.
“The problem is the September CPI didn’t look transitory,” she said, pointing to the rise in core inflation and the possibility that energy costs were feeding into transportation services, airfares, freight and goods prices.
“The Fed is tightening into a supply shock with a hiring stall underneath it,” Shuchart said.
Rebecca Homkes, an Economist and Lecturer at London Business School, also highlighted the difficulty of using interest rates to address an energy shock.
“Interest rates are a crude tool for a complicated world, and an incredibly blunt one against the supply shocks driving price levels up,” she said.
But Homkes argued that the policy context makes it harder for the Fed to assume that an oil-related increase in prices will be temporary.
She referred to the Trump administration’s policy environment, saying that rather than simply looking through an energy shock, policymakers may have to anticipate further disruptions.
“With the Trump administration, it’s more ‘look for it:’ another shock will come soon,” Homkes told Invezz.
Robert R. Johnson, Professor of Finance, Heider College of Business, Creighton University, made a related but distinct argument.
He said that describing the inflation problem as an oil-driven shock assumes the pressure is transitory, while the war with Iran and the Trump administration’s tariff policy could continue contributing to higher prices.
Johnson told Invezz that both the tariff policy and the war were “unforced errors” by the administration, arguing that neither appeared close to resolution.
His comments challenge the idea that policymakers can treat the current inflation pressure as a single, temporary supply disruption.
In his view, the sources of price pressure extend beyond oil itself.
The implications for monetary policy remain uncertain. Homkes said higher rates can worsen a slowdown if supply shocks push firms to reduce hiring or investment.
At the same time, she said September’s inflation reading, economic growth and the latest personal consumption expenditures inflation data suggested that policy was not yet too restrictive.
A weak labour market complicates the case for further tightening
The inflation problem is only one side of the Fed’s dilemma.
The other is the labour market, where the latest report showed payroll growth falling short of expectations.
US employers added 29,000 jobs in September, compared with expectations of 90,000, while the unemployment rate stood at 4.2%.
Revisions to the July and August payroll figures reduced employment growth across those two months by a combined 60,000.
The BLS employment report showed that employment changed little across major industries.
Shuchart argued that the employment side is deteriorating faster than the inflation debate gives it credit for, pointing to weak payroll growth, downward revisions, an unemployment rate of 4.2% and negative real wages.
“That is not a labor market that absorbs a second hike quietly,” Shuchart told Invezz.
Bianco offered a more measured assessment. She said the labour market was cooling through reduced hiring rather than a meaningful increase in layoffs, describing the pattern as normalization rather than contraction.
“We do not think policymakers will place excessive weight on one weaker payroll report,” she said, adding that payroll data can be volatile from month to month.
Bianco said the Fed would likely need to see several consecutive months of weak payroll growth, a sustained increase in unemployment, slowing wage growth and broader weakness in hiring intentions before becoming more concerned.
That distinction matters for the December decision. A labour market that is gradually losing momentum may allow the Fed to wait for more evidence.
A sharper deterioration, however, could make another rate increase harder to justify even if inflation remains above target.
Johnson said the Fed’s dual mandate means policymakers must balance stable prices against full employment.
"The Fed has a dual mandate of stable prices and full employment, and it shifts its focus when one becomes more problematic than the other,” Johnson said.
He argued that inflation is currently the more pressing concern, while also not

articles.title: USD/UZS Outlook Hinges on Fed and Uzbekistan Rate Decisions - UzDaily.uz
articles.summary: USD/UZS Outlook Hinges on Fed and Uzbekistan Rate Decisions  UzDaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The USD/UZS exchange rate rose above 12,000 soums per US dollar in October before partially recovering. At the time of writing, the currency pair was trading below 11,900, remaining approximately 1% below its level at the start of the year.
Economic growth is not the main concern for the national currency. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its forecast for Uzbekistan’s economic growth in 2026 from 6.8% to 7.8%, and for 2027 from 6% to 6.5%. The World Bank expects growth of 7.9% this year. The economy expanded by 8.5% in the first half of the year.
The main source of pressure on the soum remains the trade and balance of payments position. According to the IMF’s revised estimate, Uzbekistan’s current account deficit will reach 5.1% of GDP in 2026, up from 3.9% a year earlier.
In June, the fund had forecast that the deficit would narrow to 3.2% of GDP. The revised outlook indicates that the country continues to spend more abroad on imports and other payments than it earns, sustaining demand for foreign currency.
Inflation rose to 6.4% in September from 6.2% in August, marking its first acceleration in three months. The rate remains above the Central Bank of Uzbekistan’s 5% target. Petrol prices increased by 20% year on year, while propane prices rose by nearly 49%.
Uzbekistan’s policy rate stands at 14%, with the next monetary policy decision scheduled for 28 October.
With inflation accelerating, a rate cut is considered unlikely. High real interest rates remain one of the main factors supporting the Uzbek soum.
Gold accounts for more than 90% of the Central Bank of Uzbekistan’s international reserves. As a result, falling gold prices reduce the value of the reserves even if no gold is actually sold.
Gold prices continued to decline this week. On Friday, prices fell below US$4,000 per troy ounce and briefly dropped below US$3,990, their lowest level since mid-July. This followed a decline of nearly 3% in the previous session.
The fall in gold prices was linked to weakening investor interest in artificial intelligence-related assets. Market participants increased gold sales to cover losses on other investments.
Although the probability of a US Federal Reserve rate hike at its next meeting is estimated at less than 10%, this has so far failed to support the precious metal.
Gold also remains under pressure from high oil prices, which are sustaining inflation risks. Since late February, when the conflict between the United States and Iran began, gold prices have fallen by more than 20%, increasing the risk of a further decline in the value of Uzbekistan’s gold and foreign exchange reserves.
The oil market, by contrast, has been rising. Brent crude was trading at around US$114 per barrel, up nearly 4% for the week and heading towards a third consecutive weekly gain.
Although oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have almost returned to pre-crisis levels, reports of possible new strikes against Iran following the US midterm elections have sustained a geopolitical risk premium in prices. This factor could keep oil above US$100 per barrel through the end of 2026 and maintain upward pressure on fuel prices in Uzbekistan.
The key events next week will be interest rate decisions by the US Federal Reserve and the Central Bank of Uzbekistan, both scheduled for 28 October.
Analysts expect USD/UZS to trade within a range of 11,800–12,100 over the coming week. Keeping the policy rate unchanged would preserve high real interest rates and limit the dollar’s appreciation.
However, a further acceleration in inflation, an additional decline in reserves or another surge in oil prices could increase the likelihood of the exchange rate moving towards 12,100 soums per US dollar.

articles.title: A Costly Climate: Sovereign Credit Ratings and the Clean-Energy Transition - orfonline.org
articles.summary: A Costly Climate: Sovereign Credit Ratings and the Clean-Energy Transition  orfonline.org
articles.full_text:
India’s long-awaited rating upgrade is a reminder that the price attached to a country’s risk can determine how quickly and how well it can reduce that risk
Image Source:  Getty Images 
Japan Credit Rating Agency (JCR) recently raised India’s sovereign credit rating from BBB+ to A-, the first time in over 35 years that any agency has rated India in the A range. This is significant because the Big Three — Fitch, Moody’s, and S&P — have barely moved in decades. Fitch has maintained its rating for India at BBB- since 2006; Moody’s has kept it at Baa3 since downgrading it from Baa2 in 2020, in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic; and although S&P upgraded India from BBB- to BBB in August 2025, its first such move in 18 years, the rating still sits in the lowest band of investment grade.
A sovereign credit rating exists to assess the risk of lending to a government and to communicate that risk to investors so that they can price it. This shapes the cost of debt available not only to the government but also to projects across its economy. It raises an uncomfortable question: what happens when the price attached to a country’s risk makes it harder for that country to actually reduce that risk, and who bears the heaviest burden as a result? The question is most pressing for climate action and the energy transition, where the investment required is large, urgent, and precisely the kind that a weak rating makes more expensive.
The cost of capital is made up of a risk-free rate of return plus sovereign risk premia, which are shaped by macroeconomic (country-level) and microeconomic (project-, sector-, and business-level) conditions. Sovereign credit ratings are one input into the premium, alongside market conditions and a country’s fiscal, monetary, and external credibility. A weaker rating therefore tends to mean a higher premium. That premium does not stop at the government: investors financing a solar plant or a transmission line in the same country price in the same country risk, so private projects, too, face higher required returns.
Renewable projects feel this more than most investments. Solar, wind, grids, storage, and related infrastructure typically require most of their capital expenditure (CapEx) upfront and earn it back gradually over decades. That structure makes their viability particularly sensitive to the cost of capital. The consequence is not that every project becomes unbankable, but that some get delayed, scaled back, or can proceed only with outside guarantees.
The relationship is not one-directional. The same climate and energy risks that countries need investment to reduce can themselves weaken sovereign creditworthiness. Climate-related disasters or energy shocks can damage infrastructure and economic output, raise public spending on reconstruction, and strain already constrained fiscal positions. Climate vulnerability can push up borrowing costs across a country’s entire sovereign yield curve.
A 2026 IMF working paper links climate disasters to a higher probability of government default. It estimates that the odds of a sovereign default rise by about two to three percent for every percentage-point increase in disaster-related losses as a percentage of GDP. The paper calls the resulting bind an “impossible trilemma,” where countries must increase adaptation investment, keep debt sustainable despite high borrowing costs, and avoid the higher default risk that delays bring. Another IMF study finds that climate vulnerability lowers sovereign credit ratings and raises borrowing costs, with larger effects in emerging and developing economies (EMDEs).
Climate vulnerability weakens a country’s credit standing and raises its borrowing costs; higher costs constrain the investment needed to reduce that vulnerability; and the resulting exposure to further climate-related fiscal damage feeds back into weaker credit ratings
OECD research reinforces the point: in developing countries (excluding China), the cost of capital for clean-energy projects is at least twice what it is in Europe or the US, for reasons that have less to do with the technology than with how investors price the country itself. Similarly, IEA estimates put the cost of capital for a typical solar photovoltaic (PV) project in EMDEs (excluding China) at two to three times the level in advanced economies in 2021.
The result is a self-reinforcing loop, which some call a climate-investment trap: climate vulnerability weakens a country’s credit standing and raises its borrowing costs; higher costs constrain the investment needed to reduce that vulnerability; and the resulting exposure to further climate-related fiscal damage feeds back into weaker credit ratings. The loop, however, is not equally tight everywhere, and India and Africa show why.
India has sat in the lowest investment grade category for more than two decades, yet its clean-energy build-out has continued. Clean energy took 83 percent of power-sector investment in 2024, and India now ranks third globally in installed renewable-energy capacity. This does not mean the loop described above is flawed; rather, India has channels that route around it: a developing but still bank-dominated financial system, where state-linked lenders such as REC and IREDA raise money on the strength of the government’s backing, and an economy large enough that most of its clean-energy private capital is domestic, not foreign. Foreign direct investment in sectors such as power generation has risen steadily, but domestic capital remains the major source.
The loop bites hardest when a country is heavily dependent on foreign capital and rated more harshly than its fundamentals warrant. When a country has other financing channels, as India does, a weaker-than-ideal rating, which the government argues does not do justice to its fundamentals, cannot entirely derail the build-out.
Much of Africa has no such buffer, and its experience shows how low ratings affect economies without these roundabout channels. The continent’s average external debt-to-GDP ratio almost doubled from 16 to 31 percent between 2011 and 2021, which contributed to negative outlooks on the ratings of many countries. As of June 2023, only Botswana and Mauritius held investment-grade sovereign ratings in Africa. The continent holds roughly 18 percent of the world’s population but draws a mere 2 percent of global clean-energy investment. One reason is a higher weighted average cost of capital (WACC): African countries receive renewable-energy finance at rates at least twice those in Europe or the US, which pushes up production costs downstream. Infrastructure default risk in Africa is, in fact, among the lowest globally, yet investment risk is perceived to be high, resulting in low financing.
Read together, India and Africa highlight two consequences of the same mechanism. The loop bites hardest when a country is heavily dependent on foreign capital and rated more harshly than its fundamentals warrant. When a country has other financing channels, as India does, a weaker-than-ideal rating, which the government argues does not do justice to its fundamentals, cannot entirely derail the build-out.
Clean-energy projects carry risks beyond sovereign creditworthiness, including regulatory, political, foreign-exchange, offtake, and project-level risks that push up required returns on their own. This does not mean that credit ratings should look past climate risk, or that ratings alone determine borrowing costs. The problem arises when countries need capital to reduce the risks that investors are already pricing, when climate finance has to rely heavily on commercial-rate borrowing in a high-risk country, and when a rating struggles to tell different kinds of borrowing apart.
When the risk is closer to mispricing, as the gap between Africa’s low infrastructure default rates and its high risk premium suggests, subsidy alone does not fix the distortion. What is needed is better climate-risk data and rating methodologies that can distinguish resilience-related borrowing from broader structural fiscal weakness.
Where the constraint is genuine capital scarcity, the remedies are well known. Guarantees, concessional and blended finance, and risk-sharing facilities, along with long-term structural fixes such as developing domestic bond and derivatives markets to reduce dependence on international capital, have been discussed extensively by the IEA and the OECD, and most are already in practice.
However, when the risk is closer to mispricing, as the gap between Africa’s low infrastructure default rates and its high risk premium suggests, subsidy alone does not fix the distortion. What is needed is better climate-risk data and rating methodologies that can distinguish resilience-related borrowing from broader structural fiscal weakness.
Climate-resilient deferral clauses (CRDCs) already point in this direction. Recognised by S&P and Fitch, they let a country pause payments after a “pre-defined” disaster. If they meet certain rules and verifiable triggers, a well-structured pause does not automatically count as a default. But the clauses are optional and narrow, as Grenada’s hurricane clause shows. CRDCs are only a temporary emergency mechanism after a shock: they pause debt already owed, but do not distinguish fresh post-disaster borrowing to build resilience from fiscal slippage, nor do they treat resilience-linked debt differently from other borrowings when assessing creditworthiness. Even where agencies reward resilience, the debt raised to build it counts against the sovereign today, while the credit benefit arrives later, if at all. Extending the same logic would mean treating borrowing tied to verified adaptation or transition investment differently from other borrowing, both in debt metrics and in rating assessments.
The point is not to strip sovereign risk out of climate finance, but to ensure that markets can tell a country investing in resilience from one sl

articles.title: What the Fed’s Balance Sheet Could Mean for the Debt - Bipartisan Policy Center
articles.summary: What the Fed’s Balance Sheet Could Mean for the Debt  Bipartisan Policy Center
articles.full_text:
This is the first in a two-part series on the Federal Reserve and its impact on the national debt.
In June, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh announced five task forces to examine potential policy changes at the central bank. One task force is focused on potential changes to the size and composition of the Fed’s balance sheet, which grew significantly during the Fed’s response to the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. Although the Fed operates independently within the federal government, its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and other assets affect the federal budget directly, through the earnings it remits to the Treasury Department, and indirectly, through their effects on interest rates and federal borrowing costs.
This issue brief describes the size, makeup, and trends in the Fed’s balance sheet and examines how the Fed’s activities impact the nation’s fiscal outlook as the national debt continues to grow.
The Federal Reserve’s Balance Sheet
The Fed’s balance sheet is distributed across the 12 banks that make up the Federal Reserve System. The assets and liabilities on the balance sheet reflect the Fed’s role in conducting the nation’s monetary policy and supporting financial market stability.
On a consolidated basis, the Fed holds approximately $6.7 trillion in assets as of October 2026 (see table below). This includes $4.5 trillion in Treasury securities and $1.9 trillion in mortgage-backed securities, both of which are managed by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York—on behalf of the Federal Open Market Committee—in its System Open Market Account. Smaller holdings include unamortized premiums on securities held outright, foreign currency-denominated assets, gold certificates, International Monetary Fund special drawing rights certificates, and other financial instruments.
The Fed acquires these assets mainly by creating liabilities. The largest are deposits held by banks, mostly reserve balances, at $3.0 trillion, and Federal Reserve notes (paper currency in circulation), at $2.4 trillion. The New York Fed also holds the Treasury General Account, the federal government’s checking account with a current balance of nearly $900 billion, as a liability owed to the Treasury Department. Together with other liabilities and capital of $48 billion, these items total approximately $6.7 trillion, matching the Fed’s assets.
The Fed earns income on its assets, mostly interest on its securities, and pays expenses, chiefly interest on the reserves that banks hold with it. After covering its costs, the Fed has historically sent any remaining profits to the Treasury Department. These payments are known as remittances.
Changes to the Balance Sheet’s Size
During the Great Recession, the Fed acted aggressively to provide liquidity to banks and financial markets through emergency loans and lending facilities. Between September and November 2008, its assets more than doubled, from approximately $925 billion to more than $2.2 trillion. Most of this lending was temporary and repaid over the following years.
The Fed also cut its benchmark interest rate to nearly 0% in December 2008 but still needed more fuel for the economy. It turned to quantitative easing (QE)—purchasing longer-maturity Treasurys and agency mortgage-backed securities to lower long-term interest rates. Interest rate cuts are constrained near zero, but QE has no hard floor—the Fed can keep buying for as long as economic conditions demand, though purchases are limited by the supply of securities and by risks such as inflation. And while rate cuts primarily impact short-term rates, QE lowers the interest rate on whatever maturity length the Fed chooses to purchase.
The central bank carried out three rounds of QE between 2008 and 2014. Unlike the emergency loans, which were repaid, the purchased securities stayed on the balance sheet, leaving it durably larger than before the crisis.
Beginning in 2017, the Fed engaged in a period of quantitative tightening (QT)—allowing maturing securities to roll off its balance sheet without reinvesting the proceeds—but ended the effort in 2019 amid strains in short-term funding markets. It initiated another round of QE during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, again expanding its holdings of Treasurys and mortgage-backed securities. This pushed the Fed’s assets to nearly $9 trillion by 2022. A second round of QT began that year and ended in 2025. In December 2025, the Fed began buying Treasury bills to keep reserves ample, bringing assets to today’s $6.7 trillion.
During economic expansions, the balance sheet has contracted more slowly than it grew during recessions, and it has not returned to its pre-2008 size. One reason for this is growth in demand for the Fed’s liabilities, including currency, the Treasury General Account, and bank reserves. In 2019, the Fed adopted a policy of maintaining ample reserves—enough reserves in the banking system to control short-term interest rates without frequent intervention—which limits how much the balance sheet can shrink. The Task Force on Balance Sheet Policy is reviewing that framework.
A Maturity Shift in the Treasury Securities Held
The Fed has significant discretion over the maturity of the Treasury securities it holds. QE has shifted its holdings toward longer maturities. Securities with 10 or more years to maturity grew from approximately 10% of the Fed’s Treasury holdings in 2007 to about one-quarter by 2013, helped by Operation Twist—a 2011–2012 program in which the Fed sold short-term Treasurys to buy long-term ones and thereby lower long-term rates. More recently, shorter-term securities rolled off the portfolio faster than longer-term ones, lifting the 10-plus-year share to more than one-third.
That composition is beginning to shift. In late 2025, after ending QT, the Fed began buying only Treasury bills, rather than long-term maturities, to maintain ample reserves. Future adjustments by the Fed could take one of two approaches:
- Match the maturity mix of outstanding Treasurys so the Fed’s portfolio does not tilt the market toward any particular maturity.
- Match the maturity of the Fed’s own liabilities, which are mostly bank reserves and currency that can be withdrawn on short notice. This approach would favor short-term securities, closer to the Fed’s traditional preference for Treasury bills.
Examining these alternative frameworks is one of the charges given to the Task Force on Balance Sheet Policy. If the Fed moved toward shorter maturities, it could do so in one of two ways:
- Exclusively purchase bills to maintain ample reserves, and, over time, as the balance sheet grows, reduce the share of longer-term Treasurys. This is the path it is currently on.
- Allow long-term Treasurys to run off the balance sheet when they mature, replacing them with shorter-term assets.
Reweighting the balance sheet toward shorter-term Treasurys has a stabilizing effect on the Fed’s net income, which is the interest it earns on its holdings minus its costs, chiefly the interest it pays on bank reserves. Short-term securities mature quickly, so the Fed’s portfolio yield adjusts—alongside the interest it pays on reserves—instead of remaining locked into the low yields from earlier QE. Today, the Fed is vulnerable to interest rate swings, as interest costs can grow to exceed the revenues generated by a balance sheet acquired in an earlier, lower-rate era. That mismatch is exactly what happened in 2022: as the Fed raised rates, its interest costs rose above its earnings, and it stopped remitting excess profits to Treasury.
If the Fed chooses to run off long-term Treasurys, however, increased market supply could cause private investors to demand a higher term premium for these securities. This conflicts with the Fed’s mandate to promote moderate long-term interest rates. Moreover, elevated long-term interest rates have real-world implications for everyday Americans—they raise what Treasury pays to borrow, and they depress private lending, particularly in the housing market, where mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury yields.
The Intersection of Fiscal and Monetary Policy
The Treasury Department and the Fed make portfolio decisions independently, but their choices interact. In the low-rate environment after the Great Recession, Treasury tilted its issuance toward long-term securities to lock in favorable rates and reduce the need to refinance, partially counteracting the Fed’s efforts to lower long-term rates. Since 2020, Treasury has shifted toward heavier bill issuance and recently increased buybacks of long-term Treasurys. The Fed, in contrast, has begun reducing its tilt toward long-term securities, but still maintains a large portfolio of them. Because the two institutions pursue different goals—the Fed’s include price stability, maximum employment, and moderate long-term interest rates, while Treasury’s is financing the government at low cost—their strategies can pull in different directions.
The Fed holds approximately 14% of the federal government’s nearly $32 trillion marketable debt—Treasury securities that investors can trade, which excludes approximately $8 trillion in intragovernmental borrowing. That is more than any other single entity. The Fed’s actions can influence yields across the Treasury market, and with them the government’s borrowing costs. Net interest costs on the national debt surged after the Fed started raising interest rates in 2022, as the debt itself continued to grow, and now exceed $1 trillion annually. Allowing long-term securities to mature without rolling over would put upward pressure on long-term yields, thereby increasing interest costs for the federal government.
On the other hand, a Fed balance sheet weighted more heavily toward short-term Treasurys would more closely align the interest the Fed earns with the interest it pays. That would reduce the risk of losses when rates rise and allow remittances to resume more quickly, partially offs

articles.full_text:
When the European Central Bank (ECB) meets next Thursday, it is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, partly because rising government bond yields are already pushing up borrowing costs across the eurozone.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has played down hopes of a rescue, saying the solution to France's debt problems lies at home.
The yield on France's 10-year government bond traded above 5% on Friday after rising to that level on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The gap with German 10-year bonds, the eurozone's safest debt, was above 170 basis points.
Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was at 5.5%, and the gap with German 30-year bonds was even wider at 184 basis points.
On Thursday, the cost of France's five-year credit default swaps, contracts that insure investors against a government default, also climbed above 100 basis points for the first time since October 2012, when the eurozone was going through its sovereign debt crisis.
Lawmakers remain split over next year's budget, which includes €43 billion in spending cuts and additional revenue measures that the government has no majority to push through.
Ratings agency Moody's, which rates France Aa3, its fourth-highest grade, with a negative outlook, delivers its verdict on Friday evening, and a downgrade is widely expected. A one-notch cut to A1 would put France's rating at the equivalent level to those assigned by S&P and Fitch.
Civil unrest is adding to investors' concerns.
More protests are expected this weekend, and Paris police prefect Patrice Faure has advised business owners in a letter to hire private security.
French trade unions, unanimously disappointed after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday, have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, one of France's biggest unions, urged workers to "generalise the strike".
Bonds doing the ECB's job
The case for another rate hike is still there.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices.
Yet German yields have climbed so much since September that their effect on growth and inflation roughly matches a 25 basis point hike, Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, estimated in an investor note on Thursday.
"For France, it's closer to a 50 basis point hike," Brzeski wrote, adding that "the bond market has taken over the ECB's job".
Brzeski expects the ECB to wait for new staff forecasts in December before deciding on its next hike.

articles.title: Dollar-yen stuck in upper 156 range as euro hits fresh lows on French political concerns - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Dollar-yen stuck in upper 156 range as euro hits fresh lows on French political concerns  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The dollar-yen pair traded heavily in the European foreign exchange market on the 23rd. At 20:00 it stood at 156.79 yen, about 16 sen firmer for the yen (weaker for the dollar) from 156.95 yen at 17:00. The pattern of selling into rallies above 157 yen continued, and with yen-buying pressure for risk-aversion purposes persistent, softness in Japanese, US and European stock indices also weighed on the pair, which was pushed back to the mid-156 yen level at one point.
The dollar-yen fell to 156.08 yen during Tokyo hours on the day, marking its lowest since September 18. Japan's September National Consumer Price Index (excluding fresh food and energy) came in above market expectations and was cited as a factor. It later rebounded to 157.16 yen, supported by dollar buying from commercial accounts and stocks trimming losses, but the upside was limited amid uncertainty over the outlook.
The euro was also heavy against the dollar. At 20:00 it stood at 1.1195 dollars, slightly weaker for the euro from 1.1198 dollars at 17:00. Persistent concerns over France's deteriorating fiscal position weighed on the market, and the euro broke below the previous day's low of 1.1189 dollars to hit a fresh low of 1.1185 dollars. The subsequent rebound was confined to around 1.12 dollars.
EUR/JPY also moved weakly. At 20:00 it stood at 175.53 yen, about 23 sen weaker for the euro (firmer for the yen) from 175.76 yen at 17:00. The dollar-yen's loss of momentum and the euro's slow decline against the dollar capped the upside, and the pair was pushed back to just above an intraday low of 175.20 yen.
Reference ranges for major currency pairs on the day were as follows.
| Currency Pair | Low | High | 
|---|---|---|
| Dollar-yen | 156.08 yen | 157.16 yen | 
| EUR/USD | 1.1185 dollars | 1.1226 dollars | 
| EUR/JPY | 175.20 yen | 176.22 yen | 
Note: Ranges from Tokyo to European trading on the 23rd.
Behind the euro's weakness is uncertainty over French politics and fiscal policy. In the previous day's trading on the 22nd, the spread between French and German government bonds widened to 175 basis points on concerns over France's fiscal deterioration, a development that weighed on sentiment and pushed EUR/USD down to 1.1193 dollars. EUR/JPY also extended losses to 175.55 yen to hit a year-to-date low before rebounding to the lower 176 yen level as the dollar-yen was bought back.
In Tokyo trading on the 23rd, preliminary October purchasing managers' index (PMI) readings for France's manufacturing and services sectors both came in below market expectations, adding to euro selling. EUR/USD briefly fell to 1.1191 dollars but halted its decline once the previous day's low of 1.1189 dollars was seen as near-term support. The dollar-yen briefly hit a fresh intraday high of 157.16 yen, supported by dollar buying against the euro and rising US long-term yields in off-hours trading, but moves were dominated by euro-related transactions and the range was limited.
Market participants said a wait-and-see stance was strengthening ahead of the weekend amid concerns over France's political situation and deteriorating public order. According to foreign exchange order information, stop-loss buying was confirmed above the current level at 157.15 yen, while buying was seen scattered below at 156.65 yen, with little appetite to aggressively build new positions.
The dollar-yen is expected to see heavy upside pressure in the lower 157 yen range, while commercial buying is likely to support the downside in the lower 156 yen range. With concerns over French fiscal policy continuing to weigh on the euro, trading in EUR/JPY near its year-to-date low is likely to shape sentiment across yen crosses. Going into next week, French political developments and major countries' stock price moves will remain in focus.

articles.title: 155-Year Historical Analysis Shows 10-Year U.S. Treasury Yield Is 'Too High' - KuCoin
articles.summary: 155-Year Historical Analysis Shows 10-Year U.S. Treasury Yield Is 'Too High'  KuCoin

Author: Jim Paulsen
Compiled by Deep潮 TechFlow
DeepChain Overview: Amid soaring U.S. Treasury yields reaching multi-decade highs and Wall Street gripped by fears of “higher for longer” driven by geopolitical tensions, massive debt issuance, and AI-related capital expenditures, legendary Wall Street strategist Jim Paulsen takes a different approach, analyzing a comprehensive 155-year historical dataset dating back to 1871 with full-dimensional quantitative insight. The data reveals a startling yet undeniable conclusion: once the unique anomaly of 1970–1985—driven by an unprecedented demographic dividend and high leverage fueling runaway inflation—is excluded, today’s 10-year yield of slightly above 5% is higher than at 96% of all historical periods. Whether compared to the current inflation rate of 3.7%, or to post-war nominal GDP, real GDP, or non-farm payroll growth rates, today’s yield demonstrates a powerful contractionary effect exceeding that of 70% to 84% of historical periods. Historical precedent consistently shows that such “excessively high” borrowing costs inevitably stifle real economic activity; current yields are far from low, and have already approached the cyclical peak that the economy cannot sustain over the long term.
Paulsen Perspectives is an independent publication supported by its readers. To receive the latest articles and support my research, please consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Since a sharp sell-off in bonds pushed U.S. Treasury yields to multi-decade highs, most investors remain deeply anxious about the possibility of further rises in Treasury yields. The key drivers intensifying this yield panic include: the potential for a secondary inflation spike triggered by conflict in Iran; surging U.S. federal debt and fiscal pressures leading to a surge in new Treasury issuance; corporations borrowing heavily to fund massive capital expenditures for AI data centers and infrastructure, competing with the government for capital; and the Fed’s continued signaling that the federal funds rate may rise further. Although this list of concerns sounds daunting—and these forces may indeed continue pushing bond yields higher over the coming months—U.S. Treasury yields may have already approached their peak, driven by a surprisingly simple yet potentially more critical logic: compared to long-term historical levels, current 10-year U.S. Treasury yields are already quite “high.”
Figure 1 shows the complete historical trajectory of the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield since 1871. Currently, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield stands at 5.12%, which may appear relatively low compared to the peaks reached over recent decades. Indeed, as seasoned financial market analysts clearly recall, during the first half of the 1980s, the 10-year yield frequently traded above 10% and reached a historic high of nearly 16% in 1981. In other words, today’s 10-year yield is roughly half of what it was during the early 1980s and only about one-third of the 1981 historical peak. Undoubtedly, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield hit an all-time low of nearly 0.5% in 2020 and remained significantly below its historical average for most of the period following the Great Recession from 2008 to 2010. Therefore, although it has recently risen to multi-decade highs, many investors still perceive considerable room for further upward movement before it is truly considered “too high.”
Figure 1: Long-term historical chart of the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield from 1871 to 2026
However, it is also noteworthy from this chart that, apart from the unprecedented and prolonged wave of high inflation experienced by the United States in the 1970s—that is, excluding the unusual period roughly between 1970 and 1985—the current 10-year Treasury yield has rarely been significantly higher than its present level since 1871. In essence, as long as we exclude this unique 15-year period in U.S. economic history (and given that the U.S. is extremely unlikely to revisit such a scenario in the foreseeable future), today’s 10-year yield is effectively approaching the upper bound of its long-term historical range. Next, we will present the historical percentile distribution of the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield since 1871 on a chart and compare it with several key economic fundamentals to demonstrate that the current 10-year yield is already at a “relatively high” level compared to the vast majority of U.S. history.
Historical percentile distribution of the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield
Figure 2 shows the historical percentile ranking of the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield over the past 155 years, from 1871 to 2026. Although current levels are far below their historical absolute peak, they remain higher than 76% of all historical periods since 1871! In fact, excluding the unique period of hyperinflation in the U.S. from 1970 to 1985, the current 10-year yield is higher than 96% of all historical periods! In short, throughout the entire history of the U.S. economy, the 10-year Treasury yield has rarely risen significantly higher than it is today. Will yields continue to rise? Certainly possible! But measured against long-term historical norms, the current 10-year yield is already in a range that would historically be defined as “extremely high.”
Figure 2: Historical percentile distribution of 10-year U.S. Treasury yields from 1871 to 2026
Yield historical percentile adjusted for current inflation rate
Figure 3 examines the historical percentile rank of the current 10-year U.S. Treasury yield among all months since 1871 in which the annual Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rate was less than or equal to the current inflation level. Essentially, this chart assesses the “relative water level” of the 10-year yield—its percentile position relative to its own historical range—during past periods when inflation was no more severe than today’s 3.7%. Compared to all historical months since 1871 with inflation no worse than today’s, the current 10-year yield is higher than 84% of those periods! Indeed, while the U.S. is currently combating elevated inflation, the degree of monetary tightening implied by today’s 10-year Treasury yield is more restrictive than in 84% of historical months with comparable inflation levels.
Figure 3: Percentile distribution of 10-year U.S. Treasury yields during historical months with inflation rates not exceeding 3.7%.
Historical percentile of the spread between yield and nominal GDP growth rate
From a historical perspective, how does the current 10-year yield compare to the pace of overall U.S. nominal GDP growth? Figure 4 examines the spread between the 10-year yield and annual nominal GDP growth since 1915. Specifically, the chart shows the historical percentile distribution of the "yield minus GDP growth" spread after excluding all recession periods and the first quarter of new expansions. Recessions and the first quarter of new recoveries are excluded because, during recessions (and at the outset of new recoveries), nominal economic activity typically performs exceptionally weakly relative to yield levels, while yields tend to decline less sharply than nominal GDP growth during downturns. During past recessions, this spread reached very high levels, but these elevated readings did not reflect a contractionary yield structure; they merely reflected the objective reality of an economic recession. Today, as with all historical samples in this chart, the U.S. economy is in a normal expansion phase.
Figure 4: Percentile distribution of the spread between 10-year U.S. Treasury yields and nominal GDP growth rates during non-recession periods from 1915 to 2026
As shown in Figure 4, the current spread between yields and nominal GDP growth is higher than 69% of historical periods since 1915. Can the spread between U.S. Treasury yields and nominal economic growth widen further? Certainly. However, given that the current yield-GDP spread is already above nearly 70% of historical levels, it is difficult to maintain that today’s U.S. Treasury yields are “too low” relative to overall economic activity.
Contractionary test of yield spread relative to real GDP and employment growth rates
When comparing the current 10-year U.S. Treasury yield to real GDP growth and annual employment growth, does it appear relatively tight or loose within the historical context since World War II? Figures 5 and 6 show the spreads between the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield and annual real GDP growth, and between the yield and annual non-farm employment growth, respectively, since 1948. Consistent with the approach used for nominal GDP, all recession periods have been excluded from the statistics for real GDP and employment data.
Figure 5: Percentile distribution of the spread between the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield and real GDP growth rate since 1948
Figure 6: Percentile distribution of the spread between the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield and non-farm payroll growth since 1948
In both scenarios—whether compared to actual GDP growth or employment growth—the current 10-year yield exhibits a notably “high and contractionary” profile. Compared to the entire postwar era, the spread between the current 10-year yield and actual GDP growth is higher than 73% of historical periods; the spread relative to employment growth is higher than 78% of historical periods. Historically, the only period during which U.S. Treasury yields sustained a spread above current levels relative to real economic activity was the high-inflation era of the late 1970s through the 1980s.
Summary and Key Points
For many investors who still clearly remember the rare surge in bond yields during the 1970s and 1980s, today’s 10-year yield of slightly above 5% may not seem particularly high. However, as the series of charts above strongly demonstrates, current 10-year Treasury yields are already quite elevated when compared to the full 155-year historical record—or even just to the postwar period since World War II—and li

articles.title: SK hynix pulls back from Solidigm IPO following shareholder opposition, regulatory pressure - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: SK hynix pulls back from Solidigm IPO following shareholder opposition, regulatory pressure  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
The decision came after shareholders opposed the move, arguing that Solidigm's separate listing would deepen the "parent-company discount," in which the market value of a parent's stake in a subsidiary is not fully reflected in the parent's share price.
SK hynix headquarters in Icheon, Gyeonggi, on Aug. 24NEWS1
SK hynix said on Friday that it has suspended plans to list its indirect subsidiary Solidigm on the U.S. stock market, roughly 80 days after preparations for the initial public offering (IPO) first came to light in August.
“Considering recent capital market conditions and stock price trends, we concluded that we need to reassess whether an IPO would be the most beneficial option for SK hynix and its existing shareholders at this time,” SK hynix said in a regulatory filing. “We have therefore decided to suspend our review of both a pre-IPO investment round and an IPO.”
Solidigm was established after SK hynix acquired Intel’s NAND flash memory and solid-state drive (SSD) operations in 2021.
SK hynix had been pursuing a Nasdaq listing for Solidigm to secure funding for production facilities in the United States and investments in technology.
However, the company decided to halt the listing process after shareholders opposed the move, arguing that Solidigm’s separate listing would deepen the so-called parent-company discount, in which the market value of a parent’s stake in a subsidiary is not fully reflected in the parent’s share price.
Under the current ownership structure, SK Inc. controls SK Square, which in turn controls SK hynix; SK hynix controls AI Company and Solidigm. SK Inc., SK Square and SK hynix are all publicly listed companies. Solidigm accounts for approximately 13 percent of SK hynix’s corporate value.
GoogleAdmanager-KJD
Pressure on SK hynix also mounted after senior financial regulators raised the possibility of applying restrictions on split listings, also referred to as duplicate listings, in which a subsidiary goes public while its parent is already listed.
Financial Services Commission (FSC) Chairman Lee Eog-weon said that Solidigm’s proposed U.S. listing would be “subject to the guidelines on split listings” at a comprehensive parliamentary audit of the National Assembly’s National Policy Committee on Thursday.
“The guidelines on split listings apply to both overseas and domestic listings,” the FSC chairman said. “As parent companies, SK Square and SK hynix must fulfill the five obligations based on their fiduciary duties to shareholders.”
Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) Gov. Lee Chan-jin also addressed the issue at a parliamentary audit on Monday.
“We are continuing to monitor the Solidigm issue,” the FSS governor said. “We will also consider ways for the FSS to convey its concerns about split listings to SK hynix.”
Semiconductor industry sources cited a broader downturn in chip stocks as another factor behind the decision, following growing calls for a slower pace of AI investment and macroeconomic volatility, including rising U.S. Treasury yields.
SK hynix shares have fallen more than 35 percent on the Kospi over the past month. Shares of Sandisk, which also produces NAND flash memory, have dropped around 40 percent from its June peak.
With semiconductor stocks declining across global markets, concerns grew that Solidigm would struggle to secure its anticipated valuation even if it proceeded with the listing.
SK hynix, however, left open the possibility of reviving the IPO, emphasizing that Solidigm’s growth potential and need for investment remain unchanged. The company believes that if Solidigm secures an appropriate market valuation through an IPO, it could also increase shareholder value at SK hynix.
“Attracting external capital through an IPO would increase SK hynix’s consolidated cash flow, which allows us to secure funding for capital expenditures while also strengthening our capacity to return capital to shareholders through dividends, share buybacks and cancellations,” an SK hynix representative said.
“[A listing would also] allow the market to reassess Solidigm’s growth potential, which is not yet fully reflected in SK hynix’s corporate valuation,” the representative added. “We will continue to explore various options that can support Solidigm’s growth while maximizing the interests of existing shareholders, taking into account the timing and scale of investments and how they will be financed.”
Securities analysts said the decision could boost SK hynix shares.
“Suspending the review of Solidigm’s U.S. listing could help ease concerns surrounding split listings at SK hynix,” said Yang Hyun-kyung, an analyst at iM Securities. “Because the decision reflects shareholders’ concerns about potential damage to shareholder value, it could reduce fears of a valuation discount and equity dilution associated with a separate subsidiary listing.”

articles.title: The decline in U.S. Treasury yields may be masking deeper concerns underlying the AI boom. - Moomoo
articles.summary: The decline in U.S. Treasury yields may be masking deeper concerns underlying the AI boom.  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
Let's take a step back and first review several key market drivers this week. The U.S.-Iran conflict continues to escalate, with geopolitical tensions remaining at elevated levels. This has once again provided support for oil prices—WTI crude has broken above $100, while Brent crude has climbed to $114, its highest level since May last year.
At first glance, this seems like a familiar backdrop for the bond market, doesn't it? Higher oil prices typically signal mounting inflationary pressures and, by extension, should push U.S. Treasury yields higher. Yet this week, that hasn't been the case.
On the contrary, U.S. Treasury yields have plunged, with the 10-year yield briefly falling below the 5% threshold during overnight trading and hovering near that level. But hold on—shouldn't lower yields provide some relief for the stock market?
Of course you'd think so—especially over the past two months, when soaring U.S. Treasury yields have been a major drag on equity markets. Yet this week, stocks suffered a severe blow, with the AI sector bearing the brunt. So what's really going on?
One narrative suggests that investors may be growing concerned once again about U.S. economic growth rather than inflation. However, given that this storyline has long been sidelined by the market and the severity of the sell-off in AI‑related stocks, I believe the underlying issue may point to a wholly different kind of risk.
Let's get straight to the point and start with CoreWeave.
In the AI field, this is not a household name. However, CoreWeave may well be the "first domino" to spark industry-wide concerns about debt financing.
Please see the chart below, which illustrates the changes over the past year in the costs incurred to hedge against default risk for major AI‑related companies—specifically, the fluctuations in CDS (credit default swap) spreads.
At first glance, this chart may seem somewhat complex, but the underlying message is quite straightforward: investors are growing increasingly cautious about lending money to companies caught up in the AI boom.
CoreWeave stood out in this regard, with its CDS spread widening by more than 500 basis points over the observation period. But what does this actually mean?
A simple way to think about it is this: you can imagine a CDS as a type of insurance that investors purchase to hedge against the risk of a company defaulting on its debt. A five-year CDS provides protection for up to five years, and the spread reflects the cost of obtaining that protection. For ease of understanding, 100 basis points equate to 1% per year.
Last week, when CoreWeave's actual five-year CDS spread surged above 1,000 basis points, it amounted to paying roughly $100,000 annually to insure $1 million of debt. This was undoubtedly an astonishingly high premium, merely to guard against the risk of a potential default.
Although CoreWeave is clearly the most prominent case, the chart also shows that this concern is not limited to any single company. Oracle's five-year CDS has climbed to nearly 300 basis points, while Meta and NVIDIA's CDS are also approaching 100 basis points.
Take Oracle, for example: due to its aggressive reliance on debt financing to support its infrastructure loans, it is being traded by the market as a junk‑grade credit. Meanwhile, Meta's five‑year CDS spreads have approached their historical peaks, which helps us better grasp the current situation. That said, I don't believe these companies should be placed in the same risk category. Compared with CoreWeave, Meta and NVIDIA clearly enjoy far stronger financial strength and liquidity.
However, it is clear that investors are beginning to question a broader issue. This brings us back to the question the market has been repeatedly raising over the past year: Who will foot the bill for this massive AI infrastructure boom? And how long will it take for these hefty investments to generate sufficient returns?
CoreWeave relies heavily on debt to finance its data centers and computing infrastructure; Oracle is likewise investing heavily in its AI expansion; Meta is also pouring billions of dollars into infrastructure. As for NVIDIA, its fortunes are closely tied to this spending cycle.
The biggest concern here is that if financing becomes more expensive or AI investment slows, the fallout could ripple through companies that are interdependent in terms of revenue, funding, and growth.
So, what does all this have to do with the bond market and U.S. Treasury yields?
Given the aforementioned backdrop, investors are growing increasingly uneasy about holding higher‑risk corporate bonds and equities. So, in this market environment, what options remain that can deliver both safety and decent returns? The answer is straightforward: government bonds. Consequently, as buying pressure mounts, Treasury prices rise, pushing yields lower.
But here's a key point: even as U.S. Treasury yields decline, corporate borrowing costs may still rise when investors demand higher risk premiums to compensate for credit risk. In other words, safe‑haven capital is becoming increasingly cheap, while riskier capital is growing more expensive.
This may well be why tech stocks have been unable to celebrate the sharp drop in U.S. Treasury yields. Investors are likely more concerned about financing risks and future profitability than about the immediate benefits of lower government borrowing costs.
In summary, concerns about AI creditworthiness may not be the sole driver behind the rise in Treasury yields. However, as part of the explanation for this week's market dynamics, it is likely to be a rather useful piece of the puzzle.
It's important to note that, with inflation risks still lingering and oil prices remaining elevated, a decline in U.S. Treasury yields does not necessarily signal an improvement in economic conditions. Rather, it may simply reflect investors' growing concerns that something else could collapse first.

articles.full_text:
Event-Driven M&A Trading in Hong Kong: Opportunities and Risk Analysis
Hong Kong event-driven trading focuses on M&A, privatization, and tender offers. This guide decodes the Takeover Code framework, mandatory thresholds, privatization methods, arbitrage spreads, and key risks—deal failure, timing, liquidity—with recent case studies.
TL;DR: Event-driven trading in Hong Kong stocks revolves around corporate actions such as mergers and acquisitions, privatizations, and s. The analytical focus centers on the gap between the offer price and , as well as whether the transaction can be successfully completed. This type of strategy involves risks including transaction failure, timing concerns, and issues. Before participating, investors must understand the regulatory framework of Hong Kong's Code on Takeovers and Mergers.
Whenever a listed company announces a privatization proposal or acquisition offer, stock prices typically experience significant volatility in response to the news. This has given rise to an analytical approach centered on corporate events, known as event-driven trading. Event-driven trading in Hong Kong stocks specifically focuses on mergers and acquisitions, restructurings, and privatizations, examining the gap between offer prices and market prices. However, whether the transaction can be completed and how long it will take are variables that must be considered. The following analysis breaks down the operational logic, regulatory requirements, and key risks behind Hong Kong stock merger and acquisition events.
What is Event-Driven Trading in Hong Kong Stocks?
Event-driven trading is an analytical approach based on specific corporate events, distinct from simply following overall market trends. Common events include corporate mergers, acquisitions, privatizations, and s.
Core Analysis Logic
The analytical focus lies in comparing the acquirer's "offer price" with the target company's "current market price." These typically differ, reflecting market expectations regarding whether the transaction will be completed. Therefore, assessing the probability of transaction completion is the core of this type of analysis.
Common Types of Corporate Actions
Common scenarios in Hong Kong stocks include privatization proposals from controlling shareholders, comprehensive acquisition offers from third parties, and absorption mergers between listed companies. The approval thresholds for various types of actions differ.
Understanding the Code on Takeovers and Mergers, and Share Buy-Backs
Hong Kong corporate mergers and acquisitions are regulated by the Code on Takeovers and Mergers, and Share Buy-Backs formulated by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). The core principle is to ensure that shareholders receive sufficient information and time to make decisions (Data source: Hong Kong SFC Code on Takeovers and Mergers).
Mandatory Offer Threshold
If an investor and persons acting in concert with them acquire 30% or more of the voting rights in a company, they are generally required to make a mandatory general offer to the remaining shareholders (Data source: same as above).
Two Routes for Privatization
A scheme of arrangement (Rule 2.10) requires approval at a court meeting by at least 75% of votes attached to shares held by independent shareholders, with opposition votes not exceeding 10% of votes attached to all independent shares held. Compulsory acquisition (Rule 2.11) requires acceptance by at least 90% of independent shareholders within 4 months from the date of dispatch of the offer document (Data source: same as above). These different thresholds directly affect whether the transaction can be completed. To understand basic Hong Kong stock trading rules, refer to the Hong Kong Stocks Beginner's Guide.
Where Does the Price Spread in M&A Arbitrage Come From?
The Gap Between Offer Price and Market Price
The spread generally reflects the market's comprehensive judgment on completion probability, expected timeframe, and capital costs. This is not a prediction of stock price movements, but rather an assessment of whether the risk-reward ratio is reasonable.
Key Variables Affecting Outcomes
Whether a transaction can be completed is affected by factors such as whether shareholders oppose it, whether the acquirer cancels the proposal, and . If the proposal fails to obtain the required number of votes, it becomes void. The case reviews below include relevant examples.
Review of Recent Hong Kong Stock Privatization Cases
The following are factual statements from public reports and do not constitute any operational recommendations.
Privatization Actions by Major Institutions
In October 2025, HSBC proposed to privatize Hang Seng Bank through a scheme of arrangement at HKD 155 per share, representing a premium of approximately 30.3% over the closing price on the last trading day prior to the announcement (October 8, 2025) of HKD 119. The proposal was subsequently approved by shareholders and became effective on January 26, 2026. Hang Seng Bank shares were delisted on January 27, 2026 (Data source: HSBC Group Hang Seng Bank Privatization Page; HSBC Scheme Document Despatch Announcement).
Example of a Rejected Proposal
In May of the same year, although a privatization proposal from an apparel brand company offered a premium to market price, opposition votes at the court meeting exceeded the 10% upper limit stipulated in Rule 2.10, and the proposal thus became void (Data source: Company Announcement). This case illustrates that whether the offer price is acceptable to independent shareholders is key to whether a scheme of arrangement can be implemented.
Major Risks of Event-Driven Trading
Transaction Failure and Timing Risk
A transaction may fail to complete due to shareholder opposition, regulatory rejection, or the acquirer's cancellation. Once failed, the stock price may experience adjustment. Even if completed, the process may take several months, during which capital is tied up.
Liquidity and Execution Risk
Trading volume in the relevant shares may decline after the announcement, and bid-ask spreads may widen. Order execution methods will also affect transaction efficiency. You can refer to the Difference Between Limit Orders and Market Orders.
Tools and Information Sources to Note When Participating
Corporate merger and acquisition announcements are generally required to be disclosed through the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKExD) "HKEXNEWS" platform. Investors should pay attention to company circulars and shareholder notices to understand the terms and approval progress. Longbridge has market data tracking functions that enable users to monitor changes in stock prices and trading volumes. You can visit Longbridge Market Data for details. The AI investment research assistant PortAI can also help organize key points in announcements (Further reading: How AI Tools Assist the Research Process). For trading in stocks, ETFs, REITs, options, and warrants in the Hong Kong market, you can check the Longbridge Investment Products Overview.
Conclusion
Event-driven trading in Hong Kong stocks revolves around corporate actions such as mergers and acquisitions, privatizations, and tender offers. The core analysis focuses on the gap between offer price and market price, as well as whether the transaction can be smoothly completed. Cases ranging from successful privatizations to rejected proposals demonstrate that such transactions involve uncertainties including shareholder opposition, regulatory approval, and liquidity concerns. Past performance cannot serve as a guide to future results.
Which tool to choose depends on your investment objectives, risk tolerance, market outlook, and experience level. Jio Platforms Ltd’s initial public offering crossed another threshold on its closing day as the IPO became the first issue globally to receive over 1 crore applications. This surpasses the earlier global record of Waaree Energies, who received 97 lakh applications.
Bidding for the $3.2 billion issue continues, with the IPO subscribed nearly 7 times and investors bidding for over 147 crore shares against 19.75 crores offered. The final application count is expected to be even higher, which could set another benchmark globally for IPOs of large telecom and technology companies.
Jio Platforms Ltd, the largest company by market share in India’s telecom sector, opened for public offering on Wednesday with investors fully subscribing within 100 minutes. This makes it one of the fastest-subscribed offerings in India.
Retail investors fully subscribed to the issue on Thursday (October 22, 2026), signalling positive and increased sentiment towards public offerings of large Indian conglomerates.
Typically, foreign investors and institutional buyers wait until the last day before bidding to gauge investor sentiment.
However, Jio Platform’s issue was bidded over 10 times by qualified institutional buyers on day 2. According to the latest data from NSE, QIB demand has risen as high as nearly 15 times. Retail investors’ demand crossed 2.03 times with biddings worth 17.29 crore shares against 8.5 crore shares reserved.
As per reports, bids were largely placed on the upper end of the price band at Rs 1,119, with total demand now exceeding $15 billion.
Anchor investors including Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, BlackRock and Fidelity have received bids of over $25 billion to reserved shares worth $854 million. The IPO will close on Friday and Jio Platforms Ltd will get listed on the exchanges on October 28.

articles.title: Take Five: AI trade meets the Fed - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Take Five: AI trade meets the Fed  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - An eye-catching week is in store as rate-setters at the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan announce policy decisions, while investors will gauge whether results from Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft can fuel the next leg of the AI rally.
An election in Brazil, a gathering of China's top leadership and a closely watched British budget add political risk to the agenda.
Here's all you need to know about the coming week in financial markets by Lewis Krauskopf in New York, Kevin Buckland in Tokyo, and Dhara Ranasinghe, Marc Jones and William Schomberg in London.
1/ MOVE OVER
It's a packed week for central banks. The Fed, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of New Zealand meet on Wednesday, the ECB on Thursday, and the BOJ a day later.
The Fed, ECB and BOJ face no immediate pressure to hike rates after tightening last month.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will be pressed on his view on the rate outlook. The ECB is sure to face questions about surging French borrowing costs that risk becoming a flashpoint, while the BOJ may raise its inflation forecasts in a post-meeting report.
Markets expect Canada and New Zealand to hike rates to contain inflation, with all policymakers grappling with the extent to which high oil will fuel broader price pressures.
2/ HYPERSCALER HOT SEAT
A big week for US corporate earnings will be headlined by reports from three of the largest companies at the heart of the huge AI capital investment theme that has driven up equities.
Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon — three of the so-called hyperscalers — will post results at a time investors are becoming wary of the risks of the spending on data centres.
The week will be critical to determining if the third quarter lived up to high expectations for US profit growth, with about one-third of S&P 500 companies reporting.
Other high-profile firms set to report include drugmaker Eli Lilly, oil majors Exxon and Chevron, and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar.
3/ FISCAL TIGHTROPE
British finance minister John Healey will announce his first budget on Wednesday, when he will try to offer some relief from higher energy prices to households, but without unsettling the bond market by ramping up borrowing.
That means Healey may have to accept a narrowing of his room for manoeuvre to meet his fiscal rules. Analysts polled by Reuters think he can allow his headroom to almost halve to around £15 billion ($20 billion) without spooking the market.
Banks might bear the brunt of tax increases, and the share prices of Britain's biggest lenders have fallen in the run-up to Healey's high-profile debut.
