articles.title: Fitch outlines impact of Indonesia downgrade by MSCI - IDNFinancials
articles.summary: Fitch outlines impact of Indonesia downgrade by MSCI  IDNFinancials
articles.full_text:
JAKARTA - Fitch Ratings believes MSCI's proposal to reclassify Indonesia's stock market as a Standalone Market could add risks to the credit profiles of the government, banks and corporates.
However, in a report published on Wednesday (21/10), Fitch emphasised that the impact of the proposed reclassification would depend on Indonesia's external and domestic funding conditions. The global rating agency warned that declining investor confidence could lead to increased foreign capital outflows.
Fitch also said the MSCI proposal was already reflected in Indonesia's sovereign rating of 'BBB', whose outlook was revised to Negative on 4 March 2026.
"However, the reclassification itself is unlikely to have a material direct credit impact," Fitch wrote.
As previously reported by IDNFinancials.com, MSCI has proposed changing Indonesia's stock market classification from Emerging Market to Standalone Market, placing it in the same category as Zimbabwe and Argentina. However, MSCI is still consulting market participants and will announce its decision by the end of June 2027 at the latest.
For the government, Fitch believes sustained external pressure could trigger a surge in borrowing costs and erode Indonesia's external buffers. This risk would be particularly pronounced if the country's foreign exchange reserves continued to decline amid weak confidence among global investors or deteriorating governance.
According to Bank Indonesia (BI) data, Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 146.3 billion at the end of September 2026. Fitch said reserves sufficient to cover 5.3 months of imports would provide a buffer against short-term pressure on Indonesia.
However, Fitch highlighted BI's substantial short-term liabilities, driven by an increase in its net short foreign exchange position over the past year to USD 32 billion as of August 2026.
Impact on banks and mining companies
In the banking sector, Fitch believes direct reliance on stock market funding is relatively limited, given Indonesian banks' strong capital ratios. However, prolonged foreign capital outflows could tighten liquidity and increase borrowers' debt refinancing risks, potentially weakening banks' asset quality.
A prolonged stock market correction could also worsen loan-to-value ratios for shares pledged as collateral for bank loans in Indonesia.
Fitch also stressed that higher funding costs could delay renewable energy projects requiring substantial investment.
On the other hand, Fitch noted that companies in the energy and mining sectors have a wider range of funding options, including domestic bank loans, offshore bonds and internal cash flows. Companies such as PT Pertamina (Persero), MIND ID and PT Freeport are considered to have adequate liquidity and funding.
Following MSCI's proposal, Fitch said the government's policy response would be a determining factor in future credit ratings.
Indonesia's government has responded in different ways to MSCI's latest proposal. President Prabowo openly stated that MSCI's statements were merely intended to intimidate the Indonesian nation.
Meanwhile, Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said Indonesia's economy remained solid amid various pressures from global markets. Airlangga also stressed that MSCI's assessment would not disrupt the national economy as a whole. (KR/ZH)

articles.title: Why is Indonesia facing a rare MSCI downgrade and what's at stake? - CNA
articles.summary: Why is Indonesia facing a rare MSCI downgrade and what's at stake?  CNA
articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE: About US$65 billion was wiped off the value of Indonesian stocks on Oct 16 after global index provider MSCI proposed downgrading the country's stock market from emerging market to "standalone" status.
The Jakarta Composite plunged 11.6 per cent following the announcement, marking its biggest one-day fall since the 1998 Asian financial crisis.
The proposal caught investors by surprise, as it went further than MSCI’s initial warning in January that Indonesia could be demoted to “frontier market” status.
If implemented, the downgrade could trigger billions of US dollars in foreign outflows from Southeast Asia's largest economy, even as Indonesian authorities pursue reforms aimed at addressing concerns over market transparency and trading practices.
But the downgrade is not yet a done deal. MSCI has given Indonesia time to demonstrate meaningful and lasting improvements before reaching a final decision next year.
What does a standalone status mean, why is MSCI considering such a drastic downgrade, and how could it affect Indonesia’s stock market?
THE INFLUENCE OF MSCI
MSCI, originally known as Morgan Stanley Capital International, is one of the world's largest index providers, alongside rivals such as FTSE Russell and S&P Dow Jones Indices.
Its influence lies in the widespread use of its benchmarks by global fund managers, who rely on them to guide investment allocations and measure the performance of their portfolios.
About US$10 trillion in assets are benchmarked against MSCI's Emerging Markets Index, making its decisions on which countries and companies to include potentially consequential for investment flows.
A country's inclusion in or exclusion from these indexes can therefore influence how much foreign capital enters or leaves its stock market.
WHAT A STANDALONE DOWNGRADE MEANS
MSCI classifies global equity markets into four categories: developed, emerging, frontier or standalone.
Frontier markets are smaller, less developed or less accessible than emerging markets.
To qualify, a market must have at least one company meeting MSCI’s minimum size and liquidity requirements, among other criteria, and demonstrate a degree of accessibility to foreign investors
Asian markets in this category include Vietnam, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
Standalone markets, meanwhile, sit outside MSCI’s developed, emerging and frontier market indexes.
They are broadly classified into two groups: newly eligible markets and markets previously classified under the developed, emerging or frontier market categories.
According to MSCI, a market may be reclassified as standalone if there is a severe deterioration in its accessibility, size or liquidity.
Markets in this category include Argentina, Lebanon, Nigeria and Ukraine. None are in the Asia-Pacific region.
For Indonesia, a downgrade from emerging to standalone status would mean its stocks being removed from major emerging market indexes tracked by investment funds worldwide.
Funds that passively track these indexes, or are ranked against them, would be forced to sell their Indonesian holdings. Actively managed funds benchmarked against them could also reduce their exposure.
If Indonesia’s market is downgraded to standalone status, it would become the largest economy in the standalone category, at more than twice the size of Argentina, the next largest.
CONCERNS OVER TRANSPARENCY AND MARKET FUNCTIONING
MSCI's concerns go beyond the size and liquidity of Indonesia's stock market to more fundamental questions about how it operates, analysts told CNA.
Allspring Global Investments' portfolio manager Gary Tan said the index provider's core concerns centre on Indonesia's market transparency, price formation and the credibility of regulatory enforcement.
Similarly, Eastspring Investments said MSCI's proposed downgrade reflects questions about the integrity and credibility of Indonesia's trading mechanisms.
In January, MSCI first warned that Indonesia could lose its emerging market status, citing opaque share ownership structures, suspected coordinated trading activity and inadequate enforcement.
It said its clients had flagged concerns about the reliability of market data, particularly information on the proportion of shares available for public trading, known as free float, and how shareholders were classified.
These made it difficult for investors to determine how many shares were genuinely available for trading.
Concerns that some stock prices may have been artificially supported also raised questions about the reliability of market prices and the effectiveness of regulatory oversight, MSCI said.
Indonesian officials, however, have questioned the basis of MSCI's assessment and called for greater transparency over its methodology.
President Prabowo Subianto told his Cabinet earlier this week that the global index provider was trying to "intimidate" the country.
Hanif Dhakiri of the National Awakening Party, who sits on the parliamentary committee overseeing finance affairs, called for MSCI's methodology to be transparent, objective and consistently applied across countries.
"We should not be defensive in the face of criticism, but neither should we accept judgements without examining their basis and objectivity," he told Reuters.
MSCI, in an emailed response to Reuters, said its decisions follow transparent and rules-based methodologies.
WHY MSCI IS CONSIDERING A MORE SEVERE DOWNGRADE
Last week, MSCI went a step further, saying that demoting Indonesia’s market to frontier status might not adequately reflect the severity of these problems.
The global index provider said Indonesian authorities had failed to make “sufficient progress” in demonstrating consistent implementation of market reforms and their sustained impact.
Weak enforcement also remained a concern, it added.
Mr Tan said MSCI may be concerned that downgrading Indonesia to a frontier market instead of a standalone status would simply transfer its unresolved underlying market issues into another MSCI index.
"This would be more disruptive, as Indonesia would leave (the emerging market index) without the offsetting inflows from frontier index funds," he added.
Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital, suggested that MSCI's earlier removal of several Indonesian companies from its Indonesia index may also have influenced the severity of its latest proposal.
"This may have had a bearing on the severe approach this time around," he told CNA.
"MSCI has already made it clear that it will downgrade Indonesia unless it makes progress on its demands to sanction market abuse, although it has not been specific as to what it wants."
Following MSCI's proposal, Indonesia's Financial Services Authority disclosed fines of millions of dollars for market participants involved in trading violations - including three of the companies MSCI had cut from its index.
BILLIONS OF DOLLARS IN POTENTIAL OUTFLOWS
A downgrade could trigger billions of US dollars in capital outflows as international funds sell Indonesian equities to align their portfolios with MSCI's revised classifications.
Indonesia has been classified as an MSCI emerging market since 1989.
Losing that status would mark a significant change for a market that was, until recently, a favourite among foreign investors.
The impact would be quite severe in terms of passive money outflows and active money outflows, Mr Mackintosh said.
Banks estimate that a downgrade could trigger US$3 billion to US$6 billion in outflows from passive emerging market funds.
UBS also warned that active investors could withdraw another US$15 billion.
Beyond the immediate selling pressure, a downgrade could affect how international investors assess Indonesian assets.
It could impact Indonesia's currency negatively and increase the cost of capital in the country, Mr Mackintosh said.
However, Eastspring Investments cautioned that the eventual impact would depend on the index providers’ final decisions, how any reclassification is implemented and how investors respond to Indonesia's ongoing capital market reforms.
The projected outflows are also estimates rather than guaranteed withdrawals, with actual selling likely to depend on the composition of investment portfolios and the timing of any index changes.
In the near term, uncertainty surrounding this reclassification review may prolong volatility in Indonesian equities, particularly amid limited domestic catalysts and persistent external pressures, it said.
The market could face a prolonged period of uncertainty over the next six to nine months, until MSCI reaches its final decision before June next year, Eastspring Investments added.
A WINDOW TO AVERT A DOWNGRADE
Analysts said Indonesia still has an opportunity to retain its emerging market status, but will need to demonstrate that its reforms are producing lasting improvements in market conduct and transparency.
MSCI has given the country time to address the concerns raised by investors and demonstrate that its reforms are delivering lasting improvements in market transparency, conduct and enforcement.
The index provider is consulting institutional investors until next April, with a final decision expected by June.
Macquarie Group's head of ASEAN equity research Jayden Vantarakis told CNA that regulators must take sufficient action to address concerns over market conduct and convince institutional investors to oppose the proposed reclassification.
Similarly, Mr Tan said Indonesia must demonstrate tangible improvements in transparency, trading practices and enforcement.
"Ultimately, MSCI will need confidence that these measures will remain effective after the current index freeze is lifted," Mr Tan explained.
Indonesian authorities have already introduced a series of measures since MSCI first raised its concerns in January.
Top officials were replaced by figures widely known and trusted by markets. Its financial regulator and stock exchange introduced tighter measures and adopted refor

Increasing EV production, expanding battery manufacturing capacity, and growing investments in renewable energy storage are supporting demand for battery-grade copper foil, which serves as the anode current collector in lithium-ion batteries.
Growing emphasis on sustainable manufacturing is encouraging copper foil producers to improve resource efficiency, reduce production waste, and optimize copper utilization. Copper foil is an essential component of lithium-ion battery anodes, and improvements in foil thickness, production yields, and material recovery can help reduce copper consumption per unit of capacity. Manufacturers are increasingly focusing on process optimization, recycling production scrap, and improving the recovery of copper from manufacturing waste.
Technological advancements in electrodeposited copper foil production are expanding the performance capabilities of high-quality copper foil. Manufacturers are improving electrodeposition processes, drum surface characteristics, thickness control, and surface-treatment techniques to produce thinner foils with consistent physical and electrical properties. These developments are particularly important for ultra-thin copper foil measuring 5 µm or less, including 4.5 µm and 4 µm grades, which can help reduce current collector weight and increase the proportion of active materials within a cell. Improvements in tensile strength, elongation, surface uniformity, and handling characteristics are also helping manufacturers address the processing challenges associated with thinner foil.
Market Dynamics
Increasing demand for lithium-ion batteries across EVs, ESS, and consumer electronics is driving demand for copper foil. Copper foil functions as the anode current collector, providing electrical conductivity and supporting electron transfer during charging and discharging. Growth in EV production, expansion of manufacturing capacity, and investments in electrification are increasing the requirement for reliable, high-performance current collector materials. Automakers and manufacturers are also focusing on improving energy density, driving range, charging performance, and weight efficiency, supporting the use of advanced copper foil grades.
The expansion of energy storage installations and continued demand for portable electronic devices are further broadening copper foil consumption across applications. Grid-scale and commercial energy storage systems use lithium-ion technology to support renewable energy integration, electricity balancing, and backup power requirements. Meanwhile, smartphones, laptops, tablets, and other portable electronics require compact cells with reliable electrical performance. These applications create demand for copper foil with different thicknesses and performance characteristics, depending on design and operating requirements.
High capital investment and stringent production requirements can constrain the manufacturing and adoption of battery-grade copper foil. Producing ultra-thin grades requires precise control over thickness uniformity, surface roughness, tensile strength, elongation, and defect levels. Pinholes, surface imperfections, or variations in material properties can affect electrode processing, battery performance, and manufacturing yields. Production facilities also require specialized equipment, high-purity copper inputs, controlled operating conditions, and rigorous quality assurance, increasing capital and operating expenditure.
The expansion of renewable energy generation and the increasing deployment of battery-based energy storage systems are creating opportunities for copper foil manufacturers. Solar and wind installations require storage solutions to manage intermittent electricity generation, improve grid stability, and support reliable power delivery. Lithium-ion batteries are increasingly used in utility-scale storage projects, commercial and industrial installations, and residential energy storage systems, supporting demand for copper foil used in battery anode current collectors. Investments in grid modernization, renewable energy integration, and distributed energy infrastructure are creating additional opportunities for suppliers serving the energy storage systems segment.
Analyst Perspective
The copper foil for battery industry is increasingly benefiting from the expansion of lithium-ion battery manufacturing across electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and consumer electronics. Growing emphasis on battery energy density, weight reduction, charging performance, and production efficiency is encouraging the adoption of advanced copper foil grades, particularly ultra-thin products measuring 5 µm or less. Manufacturers are investing in electrodeposition technology, precision thickness control, and surface treatments to improve mechanical strength, electrode adhesion, and production consistency. At the same time, capacity expansion, copper price volatility, and evolving battery technologies are shaping competitive strategies.
Application Insights
The electric vehicles segment dominated the copper foil for battery market, accounting for a revenue share of 65.5% in 2025. Its dominance is primarily attributed to the growing adoption of electric passenger cars, commercial vehicles, buses, and two-wheelers powered by rechargeable battery systems. Copper foil functions as the anode current collector in lithium-ion batteries, supporting electrical conductivity and efficient operation. Rising EV production, expanding manufacturing capacity, and investments in vehicle electrification are driving demand for battery-grade copper foil.
The ESS segment is projected to grow at the fastest CAGR of 17.2% during the forecast period. Growth is driven by increasing deployment of battery storage to support renewable energy integration, grid stability, peak-load management, and backup power requirements. Expanding solar and wind power installations are increasing the need for storage solutions that can manage fluctuations in electricity generation and improve power supply reliability. Lithium-ion batteries are being deployed across utility-scale projects, commercial and industrial facilities, and residential installations, supporting demand for copper foil used in battery manufacturing.
Thickness Insights
The 6 µm segment dominated the copper foil for battery industry, accounting for 65.9% of the total revenue share in 2025. Its leading position is supported by a balance of electrical conductivity, mechanical strength, processability, and material efficiency in lithium-ion battery manufacturing. Battery cell manufacturers widely use 6 µm copper foil to optimize current collector weight while maintaining the performance and reliability required for high-volume electrode production. Increasing battery demand across EVs, ESS, and consumer electronics continues to support adoption.
The ultra-thin segment (≤5 µm, including 4.5 µm and 4 µm grades) is projected to grow at the fastest CAGR of 21.6% during the forecast period. Growth is driven by battery manufacturers' efforts to reduce current collector weight and increase the proportion of active materials within battery cells, thereby improving energy density. This is particularly important for EV batteries, where weight reduction and driving range are key performance considerations. Advancements in electrodeposition technology, thickness control, tensile strength, and surface treatment are improving the commercial feasibility of ultra-thin foil production.
Regional Insights
Asia Pacific dominated the copper foil for battery market with a revenue share of 85.0% in 2025. The region is a major hub for battery-grade copper foil production and consumption, supported by an extensive lithium-ion battery manufacturing ecosystem across China, Japan, and South Korea.

articles.title: Norway’s $2.3tn Wealth Fund Loses $30bn as Rising Bond Yields Hit Returns - Tekedia
articles.summary: Norway’s $2.3tn Wealth Fund Loses $30bn as Rising Bond Yields Hit Returns  Tekedia
articles.full_text:
Norway’s $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund recorded a loss of nearly $30 billion in the third quarter as rising interest rates weakened returns on fixed-income investments, underscoring the pressure higher borrowing costs can place on even the world’s largest institutional investors.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the fund, reported an accounting loss of 278 billion kroner, equivalent to about $29.7 billion, for the three months ended September. Fixed-income investments were the main source of the decline, delivering a negative return of 3.5% as government bond yields climbed.
“The fund’s return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments,” NBIM Deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement.

The loss followed a strong first half, when the fund generated a return of 12.95% and a record profit approaching $185 billion. The reversal shows how quickly market conditions can change for a portfolio exposed to global equities and debt securities, even when its investments are spread across countries, sectors and asset classes.
The third quarter was marked by a broad sell-off in global bond markets as investors reassessed inflation risks, government borrowing requirements and the outlook for interest rates. Rising yields generally push down the market value of existing bonds, particularly those with longer maturities, because their fixed payments become less attractive relative to newly issued securities.
NBIM’s fixed-income portfolio accounts for just over a quarter of its total investments. Around 70% of those holdings are allocated to government bonds, with the remainder invested in corporate debt. The fund holds 1,664 bonds across 51 countries, giving it broad exposure to sovereign borrowing costs and credit-market conditions.
The scale of its portfolio means even relatively modest changes in bond valuations can translate into substantial financial swings. Government securities are often treated as a source of stability within diversified investment portfolios, but they are not immune to losses when interest rates rise sharply.
Last month, NBIM said it wanted to reduce its holdings of U.S. Treasuries as part of a broader plan to lower its allocation to government-issued debt. The proposed shift comes as investors weigh the implications of persistent fiscal deficits, rising public debt and the cost of financing government spending.
A reduction in sovereign bond exposure could limit some interest-rate risks, depending on how the fund reallocates its capital. However, moving away from government debt also changes the portfolio’s balance of risk and may reduce the diversification benefits those securities provide during periods of equity-market stress.
Equities represent approximately 72% of the fund’s portfolio, but they provided only a modest offset to the weakness in bonds. The fund’s stock investments returned 0.5% in the third quarter, with performance varying considerably across sectors.
“Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell,” Grande said.
Energy stocks benefited from rising oil prices during the quarter as the U.S.-Iran war continued. NBIM holds positions in major oil and gas companies, including Exxon Mobil, Shell and Chevron, giving it exposure to movements in global energy markets.
By contrast, utilities and real estate companies came under pressure as higher interest rates increased financing costs and reduced the relative appeal of income-generating investments. These sectors are sensitive to borrowing costs because of their capital-intensive operations and reliance on long-term financing.
The broader U.S. stock market also delivered mixed results during the quarter. The S&P 500 rose 2.03%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 1.9% and the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.2%. The average change across the three indexes was approximately 0.6%, a sharp slowdown from the double-digit gains recorded in the previous quarter.
NBIM owns small stakes in about 7,100 companies across most countries and holds approximately 1.5% of all listed companies globally, making it the world’s largest single investor. Its biggest positions include a $65.4 billion stake in Nvidia, alongside substantial investments in Apple, Alphabet, and Microsoft.
The fund’s extensive ownership gives it considerable influence over corporate governance through shareholder voting and engagement. However, its size also exposes it to broad market movements, particularly when the largest publicly traded companies account for a significant share of global equity valuations.
During the summer, NBIM Chief Executive Nicolai Tangen cautioned investors against expecting a continuation of the strong gains recorded in the first half of the year.
“For sure, we should not be expecting the same kind of returns going forward as we’ve seen over the last six months,” he said at the time.
Beyond stocks and bonds, the fund invests in real estate and renewable energy infrastructure. Those portfolios returned 0.4% and 7.5%, respectively, in the third quarter, although their relative size limits the extent to which they can offset losses elsewhere.
Established in 1998 to invest Norway’s oil revenues for future generations, the fund is designed to convert finite petroleum wealth into a diversified pool of international assets. Its quarterly performance is therefore influenced not only by individual company results but also by global interest rates, inflation expectations, commodity prices and investor appetite for risk.
The latest loss does not, by itself, indicate a structural deterioration in the fund’s finances. Market valuations fluctuate, and the portfolio is built around a long investment horizon. But the quarter demonstrates that diversification cannot eliminate market risk when several major asset classes are affected by the same macroeconomic forces.

Investing.com-- Asian currencies and the U.S. dollar were largely subdued on Friday as investors weighed rising energy costs and geopolitical tensions, while the yen held firm after a safe-haven rally driven by concerns over global growth and technology-sector valuations.
The US Dollar Index traded largely flat at 101.60 by 03:33 GMT, remaining near a three-week low. It was set for a second straight weekly loss.
Yen hits 1-mth high on weaker dollar, safe-haven demand
The Japanese yen's USD/JPY pair edged up 0.1% to 156.90 yen on Friday, after dropping nearly 1% in the previous session.
The yen strengthened to its highest level in more than a month, as investors sought safety amid concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence-related investments and escalating Middle East tensions.
Meanwhile, falling U.S. Treasury yields reduced support for the greenback. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield approached a one-month low of 4.953%, reflecting demand for safer assets.
Oil prices remained a major concern for regional currencies, with Brent crude trading near $114 a barrel on Friday after surging 4% on Thursday as attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened fears of supply disruptions.
Higher crude prices threaten to fuel inflation and complicate the monetary policy outlook across Asia, particularly for energy-importing economies such as Japan, India and South Korea.
Asia FX subdued; central bank meetings awaited
Elsewhere in Asia, the Chinese yuan's onshore USD/CNY and offshore USD/CNH pair traded largely unchanged, remaining near four-year lows.
The South Korean won's USD/KRW pair edged 0.2% lower, while the Singapore dollar's USD/SGD traded flat.
The Indian rupee extended losses on Friday, erasing most of sharp gains recorded earlier this week on RBI's support measures.
The USD/INR pair rose 0.3% to 95.109, after jumping 0.4% in the previous session. It had fallen for nine straight sessions through Wednesday.
The Australian dollar's AUD/USD pair edged down 0.1%.
Investors were also preparing for a series of major central bank decisions next week.
The U.S. Federal Reserve is expected to hold interest rates at 3.75%-4.00% on October 28, while the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan are due to announce policy decisions on October 29 and 30, respectively.
For the yen, attention will centre on the Bank of Japan's inflation outlook and signals on the timing of further rate increases, while traders will also remain alert to the possibility of Japanese currency intervention.

articles.title: IMF warns Pakistan’s external position may weaken as Middle East war fuels inflation - Profit by Pakistan Today
articles.summary: IMF warns Pakistan’s external position may weaken as Middle East war fuels inflation  Profit by Pakistan Today
articles.full_text:
Fund expects imports to rise and remittances to moderate over medium term; inflation reaches 11.1% in August as IMF flags further monetary tightening and higher borrowing costs
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected that Pakistan’s external position will weaken over the medium term as imports increase and remittances moderate, while warning that the prolonged Middle East conflict could intensify inflationary pressures, increase government borrowing costs and require further monetary tightening.
In its October 2026 Regional Economic Outlook, titled “Steering Through Uncertainty: Strengthening Resilience in Challenging Times”, the Fund said Pakistan faced risks from tighter global financial conditions because of its large gross financing requirements, while higher food and energy prices had already pushed consumer inflation to 11.1% year-on-year in August.
The IMF said external positions were expected to strengthen over the medium term in Egypt, Jordan and Morocco, supported by lower commodity prices and export diversification, but weaken in Pakistan as imports rise and remittances moderate.
The projection follows a period of relative resilience in Pakistan's external sector, with remittance inflows remaining broadly stable during the first half of 2026 despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict.
According to the report, net remittances as a share of GDP remained broadly stable in Pakistan, Morocco and Tunisia compared with the corresponding period of 2025, while Egypt recorded higher inflows.
The IMF noted that the impact of the conflict on external positions had differed considerably across the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (MENAP) region and the Caucasus and Central Asia (CCA).
Among MENAP oil exporters directly affected by the conflict, higher energy prices and reduced imports had offset the effect of lower export volumes on trade balances. By contrast, goods trade balances generally deteriorated among MENAP oil importers during 2026, with Jordan an exception because of stronger exports.
The report also noted that capital outflows which emerged after the conflict began had largely dissipated across the region, while exchange-rate depreciation pressures remained contained as of August.
Most regional economies recorded nominal effective exchange-rate appreciations between February and August, with depreciation confined mainly to Egypt, Algeria and Tunisia.
Sovereign borrowing spreads also narrowed across most economies, while stronger sovereign issuers continued to access international capital markets.
However, the IMF warned that a reversal in market sentiment could tighten global financial conditions and expose fiscal and financial vulnerabilities across the region.
Higher oil prices than those assumed in the baseline could renew inflation concerns and prompt major central banks to maintain higher interest rates for longer than currently expected.
The Fund specifically identified Pakistan, alongside Algeria and Egypt, among countries where concerns over rising government debt could increase borrowing costs beyond baseline projections because of large gross financing requirements.
It warned that higher borrowing costs could heighten fiscal sustainability concerns, while economies dependent on external financing and facing weaker external positions could experience capital outflows, exchange-rate depreciation pressures, wider sovereign spreads and tighter domestic financial conditions.
The IMF also highlighted risks to banking systems in countries where financial institutions hold substantial government securities.
An abrupt repricing of financial assets could reduce lending to the private sector, weaken investment and economic growth, and reinforce the relationship between fiscal vulnerabilities, banking-sector conditions and the wider economy.
Pakistan was identified alongside Egypt and Tunisia among countries where supervisors should monitor sovereign-bank linkages because of banks' substantial holdings of government securities.
The Fund advised financial supervisors to continue monitoring liquidity, funding conditions and asset quality, particularly in sectors exposed to the conflict, including tourism, transport and trade-related activities.
Where liquidity pressures emerge, it recommended temporary and targeted support against adequate collateral, accompanied by a clear exit strategy.
For economies with flexible exchange rates, including Pakistan, the IMF said foreign exchange intervention should be reserved for disorderly market conditions.
It noted that exchange-rate flexibility could help preserve reserves and facilitate external adjustment in Pakistan and Egypt, although depreciation could also increase inflation through higher import prices.
The appropriate balance between exchange-rate adjustment and monetary tightening would depend on individual country circumstances, the report said, adding that credible macroeconomic frameworks and transparent communication could help contain risk premiums and preserve market access where external buffers were limited and financing needs were large.
The impact of the Middle East conflict on inflation
The IMF said inflationary pressures had increased across several MENAP economies during 2026 as higher food prices, energy costs and shipping expenses affected domestic prices, with the sharpest increases among oil importers recorded in Egypt and Pakistan.
Consumer inflation reached 14.5% year-on-year in Egypt and 11.1% in Pakistan in August, reflecting higher food and energy-related prices, with exchange-rate depreciation contributing additionally to inflation in Egypt.
The Fund said inflation in MENAP oil-importing economies was expected to accelerate during 2026 before declining from 2027, although the moderation would be slower than anticipated in its April projections.
It revised the inflation outlook upward by 3.6 percentage points for Egypt and 1.5 percentage points for Pakistan compared with April.
The report noted that the Middle East conflict had disrupted energy production and trade routes, contributing to volatility in international commodity prices and raising inflation expectations.
International oil prices increased from approximately $65 per barrel in January to nearly $118 at the end of March before fluctuating around $90 per barrel. Renewed hostilities subsequently pushed Brent crude above $100 per barrel in September, approximately 50% above pre-war levels.
Prices of refined petroleum products increased more sharply than crude oil after late February, with jet fuel rising approximately 85%, diesel 68% and gasoline 45%.
The IMF attributed these increases to reduced supplies from the Gulf, the loss of global refining capacity since the Russia-Ukraine and Middle East conflicts began, and low inventories.
Natural gas prices were approximately 150% above pre-conflict levels in September, although additional liquefied natural gas supplies from outside the Gulf partially offset the supply shortfall.
The Fund also reported increases of approximately 25% in international wheat and diammonium phosphate prices since late February, while urea prices declined by around 12%.
These developments have contributed to higher inflation across regional economies, although the extent of their transmission to domestic prices has varied depending on subsidies, price controls, exchange-rate arrangements and initial economic conditions.
The IMF noted that subsidies, price controls and fixed exchange rates had limited the transmission of international price increases to consumer inflation in several Gulf economies.
In contrast, inflationary pressures increased more sharply in some oil-importing countries, including Pakistan, where food and energy prices contributed to the rise in consumer inflation.
The report said monetary policy responses had differed across countries since the conflict began.
Among MENAP economies with flexible exchange rates, Pakistan was the only country to increase interest rates after the start of the conflict in February 2026.
The Fund noted that inflation expectations had increased in parts of the region, particularly among some oil importers, while limited monetary policy responses had contributed to a modest easing in policy stances as forward-looking real interest rates declined.
It warned that monetary authorities should remain prepared for renewed inflationary pressures if the conflict continued longer than assumed in its baseline projections.
The IMF identified Pakistan and the Kyrgyz Republic as countries where inflation was already above target and the monetary policy stance appeared accommodative, with forward-looking real policy rates below estimated neutral levels.
It said this combination made the need for preparedness to tighten monetary policy particularly evident in the two countries.
The report stressed that monetary policy should remain the primary response if inflationary risks materialised, supported by prudent fiscal policies, especially in countries with limited fiscal space.
It cautioned that governments should avoid using fiscal stimulus to offset tighter monetary policy where fiscal space was constrained, as additional borrowing could increase sovereign risk premiums and worsen debt sustainability concerns.
The Fund instead recommended a combination of monetary tightening to keep inflation expectations anchored and cautious fiscal policies to safeguard sustainability, while allowing temporary, targeted and budget-neutral support for households most affected by higher commodity prices.
Pakistan's growth and fiscal outlook
Despite rising inflation and external risks, the IMF said Pakistan's economic activity had remained broadly resilient during the first half of 2026.

articles.title: Treasury sweeps biotech into proposed COINS Act restrictions, but spares Big Pharma’s China licensing deals - Fierce Biotech
articles.summary: Treasury sweeps biotech into proposed COINS Act restrictions, but spares Big Pharma’s China licensing deals  Fierce BiotechUS Treasury drops Venezuela from countries facing outbound US investment restrictions  ReutersTrump's China biotech rules leave investors guessing  AxiosTreasury proposes major restrictions to U.S. investment in Chinese biotech sector  STATU.S. Treasury Wants to Rein In Deals for Chinese Biotech and AI  Barron's
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Treasury Department is moving to restrict American investment in China’s life sciences industry, releasing long-anticipated proposed rules that add biotechnology to the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act.
Published Thursday, the draft regulations (PDF) categorize “pharmaceutical compounds” as a “prohibited technology” that would trigger an outright ban on certain outbound transactions with “countries of concern,” such as China. The definition of pharmaceutical compounds runs the gamut of different modalities, spanning small molecules, polymers, vaccines, blood products, allergenics, cell and gene therapies, monoclonal antibodies and other recombinant therapeutic proteins, as well as their delivery systems.
If implemented in its current form, the rules would cause additional headaches for U.S. biopharmas looking to tap into China’s biotech innovations. But despite the sweeping scope of the ban covering various types of drug molecules, biopharma business development teams can breathe a measured sigh of relief.
The proposed rule largely spares the regular in-licensing deals and fee-for-service drug R&D collaborations that have driven the majority of multi-billion-dollar deals between Western biopharma companies and their Chinese counterparts. This detail fits the description of a Reuters report in September, which said the Treasury was working on rules that would continue to allow pharma companies to strike most licensing deals for Chinese drugs.
In an accompanying Q&A (PDF), the Treasury Department outlined the types of investment that would be covered under its rules: “Under the proposed rule, certain transactions that involve the acquisition of equity, provision of debt financing that is convertible to equity or that carries certain rights, greenfield investments or other corporate expansions, the creation of joint ventures, or certain LP investments would be covered.
“Activities that do not meet the definition of a covered national security transaction would not be subject to the program except where they are undertaken to evade or avoid the proposed rule,” the agency explained.
Therefore, traditional asset licensing agreements, where Western drugmakers pay cash, milestones and sales royalties for ex-China rights to drugs, fall outside the scope of covered transactions.
The language of the rules matches the current text of the COINS Act itself. COINS was enacted as part of the fiscal year 2026 national defense bill, giving the Treasury the power to scrutinize—or outright prohibit—American investments in sensitive foreign sectors involving countries it views as adversaries. While the law does not name biotech, it allows Treasury to add new sectors when devising specific rules.
When calls for including biotechnology in the COINS Act emerged earlier this year, Laurie Burlingame, a lawyer at Morse, Barnes-Brown & Pendleton, who specializes in life sciences transactions, explained to Fierce that a pure sectoral expansion of the law likely wouldn’t cover pharma licensing deals, as the law is highly focused on equity investments rather than usual product transactions.
Several high-profile U.S. Big Pharma deals with Chinese companies have drawn scrutiny from Washington’s China hawks in their COINS Act expansion push. But those transactions appear to be pure licensing agreements based on public announcements. These include Bristol Myers Squibb’s potential $15.2 billion deal with Hengrui Pharma covering 13 early-stage programs.
However, some other transaction types that have gained traction lately would fall victim to the rules.
The COINS Act lists “acquisition of an equity interest” in a Chinese entity as a “covered national security transaction.” This provision would prevent U.S. venture capital firms from investing in Chinese biotechs, and it would also impact future deals resembling Pfizer’s recent partnership with 3SBio.
When Pfizer in-licensed a PD-1xVEGF bispecific antibody from 3SBio last year, the New York pharma made a $100 million equity investment in the Chinese biotech. That deal structure would be prohibited under the proposed Treasury rules.
Burlingame previously raised concerns over the COINS Act’s potential impact on the “NewCo” model, in which venture capitalists form a new U.S. biotech based on assets licensed from China. The Chinese licensor often takes an equity stake in the new firm to capture long-term upside.
Under existing COINS language, only Chinese ownership of 50% or above would make the NewCo a target as a Chinese entity. But the proposed Treasury rules’ anti-evasion clause could subject any future China deals that involve an equity interest component to additional scrutiny.
In addition, “entrance into a joint venture” also marks a notable transaction category regulated by the COINS Act.
In its proposed rules, the Treasury deliberately chose not to define “joint venture,” instead, it “refers to the plain English meaning of the term, i.e., as involving the contribution of capital and/or assets by two parties and the sharing of profits and losses.”
This murky definition adds uncertainties to some deals. In Pfizer’s $10.5 billion, 12-asset collaboration with Innovent Biologics, the two companies will co-develop four programs globally and share the development costs, plus U.S. and European profits or losses. Although this unincorporated partnership doesn’t necessarily fit the common idea of a joint venture business, it does involve the contribution of capital from both parties to fund R&D and profit-sharing, and the Treasury said that its term “would not require the establishment or formation of a new entity.”
It’s not immediately clear if the Treasury means to crack down on this deal structure. If it does, the Pfizer-Innovent accord could face regulatory actions—only transactions completed before the enactment of the COINS Act on Dec. 18, 2025, are exempt from the Treasury rules, if implemented.
Following the release of the draft rules, the biopharma industry has reacted with a cautious tone, warning against any broadly restrictive provisions as they study the policy’s details.
“The Administration is correct that biotechnology is a strategic technology industry for the United States. We need policies and initiatives that maintain and advance our global leadership in biotech, particularly as we compete with China,” John Crowley, president and CEO of the influential biotech industry lobby group Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO), said in a statement Thursday.
“The details of the proposed Treasury Department rules matter. We cannot restrict our way to success,” he continued. “As Treasury considers comments on the proposed rule, we need to ensure that we do not have an overly broad approach that would create uncertainty for innovators and investors and that may unintentionally risk weakening U.S. biotech competitiveness.”
In a separate statement, Kendalle Burlin O’Connell, CEO and president of Massachusetts biotech trade association MassBio, said that “efforts to address national security risks must be carefully targeted to avoid undermining the innovation ecosystem that has made the United States a global leader in developing new medicines.”
“For Massachusetts’ biotech industry, international partnerships and licensing agreements can bring promising scientific discoveries into the U.S. drug development pipeline, where American companies invest in and advance potential new therapies,” she added. “Preserving the ability to develop breakthrough innovations from our own world-leading domestic pipeline while also identifying promising innovations from elsewhere is essential to maintaining America's competitive advantage and access for U.S. patients.”
The Treasury Department is seeking comments until Dec. 7, 2026. Apparently recognizing the risk of collateral damage to public health and legitimate business conduct, the agency is explicitly asking for feedback on “whether and how ‘pharmaceutical compounds’ […] should be more precisely scoped to focus on advanced or frontier technologies.”
Editor's Note: The story was updated to clarify the 50% equity interest threshold is for determination of an entity as a covered foreign (Chinese) person.

articles.summary: ASX data center shares remain cheap after downgrade  Morningstar
articles.full_text:
Near-term pain, long-term potential.
NextDC (ASX.NXT) announced reduced fiscal 2027 guidance of 22% to a midpoint of $487.5 million for net revenue, 36% to a midpoint of $255 million for adjusted EBITDA, and 14% to a midpoint of $4,750 million for capex, reflecting delays to electricity network upgrades supplying its M3 site.
Why it matters: NextDC’s stock fell around 42% in response to the guidance changes, having already fallen 34% since its full-year results announcement, but we see this selling as overdone.
- While earnings from this site will likely be delayed and may be reduced should alternative power costs be more expensive, we don’t see such a large reduction in the business’ medium-term outlook. Its assets, both current and planned, are still in great demand.
- Management will pause future land acquisitions and capital expenditure on projects not backed by customer contracts until it has more clarity on M3 revenue. It has no plans to raise equity and is in discussions on a joint venture for the S4 data center.
The bottom line: We decrease revenue, EBITDA, and capex forecasts in line with guidance. We reduce our fair value estimate for NextDC to $12.00 from $15.60 previously. NextDC’s price/book ratio is around 0.8, with most data center companies trading at well over 1. We see it as undervalued at these levels.
Long view: Community concerns over data centers may increase developer costs and force new data centers further away from built-up areas. However, this will affect all developers, will likely be factored into new contracts, and will likely make existing data centers even more valuable.
- Absent a major setback for artificial intelligence development, we expect data center demand to remain very strong and believe NextDC is still well positioned to capitalize on this, given its existing assets, supplier relationships, reputation, and expertise.
NextDC hit by M3 electricity delays, but its strong long-term growth prospects remain
NextDC has a big opportunity in front of it, with ample room to increase its data center footprint in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region and reap the financial benefits that its larger scale should provide. The firm is already a primary provider of cloud on-ramps to the biggest global cloud providers, and we expect its importance for cloud connectivity and artificial intelligence compute power in Australia to grow.
NextDC benefits from industry trends, including increasing use of cloud computing and artificial intelligence, that are driving exponential growth in data creation.
While the firm remains focused on deepening its presence in important Australian markets, which we think is smart, it is also addressing various Asian markets with operational data centers in Kuala Lumpur and Japan, with one in Auckland also planned. The Australian market is less penetrated by global companies than other parts of the world are, and NextDC has an opportunity to be a leader in the country.
The firm currently has four data centers in Sydney and three in Melbourne to go along with two in Perth, two in Brisbane, and one each in Adelaide, Canberra, Darwin, and Newman. NextDC also already owns land and has plans in place to expand its capacity materially in some of these markets, especially with another three data centers in Sydney and two in Melbourne.
As NextDC gains size, we expect it will see some of the intracontinental benefits that firms like Digital Realty and Equinix have globally. Namely, it will enable its customers to use it to connect their points of presence throughout the continent and to connect to their cloud providers.
We expect interconnection services to become increasingly important for NextDC as more businesses transition to hybrid cloud storage models. In 2025, interconnection revenue contributed around 8.6% of NextDC’s net recurring revenue. Given the potential capital requirements from the extreme data center demand from AI, we expect NextDC to use joint ventures to lower the total project cost of capital and maximize its return on equity.
Bulls Say
- NextDC is well placed to benefit from industry megatrends, including the growing adoption of cloud computing, the Internet of Things, and AI, leading to exponential growth in data creation.
- The shift to cloud-based services increases the need for enterprises to connect to numerous cloud providers, and the connection is fastest, safest, and most efficient in a co-located data center.
- With the Australian market less penetrated by the biggest global data center providers, NextDC has an opportunity to be one of the biggest providers on the continent.
Bears Say
- Rapid technological advancements could reduce the space required by tenants to store data and leave NextDC with excess capacity and margin deterioration.
- NextDC is heavily reliant on cloud providers, which could choose to attract customers to their own facilities, undermining its business model.
- Increasing adoption of virtual connectivity solutions may reduce demand for physical space and physical connections in NextDC’s data centers.

articles.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6758 – Reuters estimate - investingLive
articles.summary: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6758 – Reuters estimate  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- PBOC CNY reference rate setting for the trading session ahead.
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.
China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.
Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.
Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.
As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.
In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

articles.full_text: People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loansJack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.” Continue reading...
